title: AirPods 5 vs AirPods 4: here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple today unveiled AirPods 5, available to order now starting at just $129, the new version of its entry-level AirPods. The biggest takeaway is that — among a sea of Apple price increases — the new AirPods are actually cheaper than ever, despite coming with Active Noise Cancellation as standard, and a few other niceties. Here’s what’s new compared to the outgoing AirPods 4 … more…
fullText:
Apple today unveiled AirPods 5, available to order now starting at just $129, the new version of its entry-level AirPods. 

The biggest takeaway is that — among a sea of Apple price increases — the new AirPods are actually cheaper than ever, despite coming with Active Noise Cancellation as standard, and a few other niceties. Here’s what’s new compared to the outgoing AirPods 4 …

There are two models of AirPods 5, AirPods 5 and AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case. This replaces the old lineup of AirPods 4 and AirPods with ANC models.

We’ll cover the differences in the AirPods 5 line a bit further down, but first here’s what’s new across both models compared to AirPods 5.

Upgraded active noise cancellation

Active noise cancellation is now available on all AirPods 5 models. Customers previously had to spend $179 for AirPods 4 with noise cancellation included, but that is now standard with AirPods 5. So if noise cancellation in an open-ear design is what you cared about most, you just saved $50 compared to the same AirPods options a week ago. 

Apple also says that the quality of noise cancellation on AirPods 5 is greatly improved, up to 50 percent better compared to AirPods 4. AirPods 5 noise cancellation uses new algorithms and a new acoustic architecture to achieve this. 

Apple claims AirPods 5 offer the best noise cancellation of any earbuds that rest on the ear. (AirPods Pro will still offer the world’s best noise cancellation overall, thanks to their in-ear design with plastic tips that physically plug the ear).

More natural Transparency mode

As well as noise cancellation, Apple has also improved the quality of Transparency mode compared to AirPods 4. Transparency mode helps the user hear the sounds of the world around them, as if their headphones were not in their ears. On AirPods 5, Transparency mode more naturally represents the sounds of voices and nearby environmental sounds.

Improved sound quality 

Based on the learnings from AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 5 feature a richer, more detailed sound profile compared to AirPods 4. This is enabled through hardware changes, like the new multiport acoustic system as well as next-generation Adaptive EQ. The acoustic architecture enables Apple to deliver sound more precisely to a range of human ear shapes and sizes, dynamically adjusting how the audio is delivered on the fly for best results.

Better water and dust resistance 

Apple has also updated the durability of the AirPods when it comes to water, dust and sweat resistance. The old AirPods 4 had an IP54 rating. The new AirPods 5 boast an IP57 rating, which should make them survive better when exposed to water and the elements, although still not waterproof. 

Lower price with ANC included 

All of the above new features are included with AirPods 5, priced at just $129. This is the same price as AirPods 4, except now you get all the active noise cancellation features in the base model. The upgraded AirPods 5 is priced at $149, which is $30 less than the old higher-end AirPods 4 option.

What do you get if you upgrade to AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case

For the jump from $129 to $149, you get a few niceties although nothing dramatic. Firstly, the AirPods come with a wireless charging case, supporting both Qi chargers and the Apple Watch charging puck. It also integrates a speaker for use with Find My.

Secondly, you actually get better battery life if you opt for the $149 model. The base $129 configuration offers the same 4 hours of listening time with ANC enabled as the AirPods 4, but the $149 model offers an extra hour of listening on a single charge. Including the case, that means 22 hours of total listening time. 

Thirdly, new with AirPods with Wireless Charging Case is a fan-favorite feature from AirPods Pro: the addition of the volume swipe gesture on the stem. This lets you raise or lower the volume just with a quick swipe on the earbud, without needing to reach for your phone or use Siri.

It’s up to you whether these differences are worth the extra $20 at checkout, but nevertheless, it still represents much better value overall than the equivalent AirPods 4 lineup. After today’s introduction, Active Noise Cancellation is now available at a $50 lower price point … and even the more expensive model is still $30 less than AirPods 4.

AirPods 5 are available to pre-order right now from the Apple Store, with first deliveries shipping on September 18.

title: Samsung has just one piece of advice for Apple’s first iPhone foldable
snippet: Samsung has been pushing the foldable market ahead for several years now and, arguably, makes some of the best foldable devices out there. But Apple is about to make its long-awaited debut with the first iPhone foldable, and Samsung has some advice. more…
fullText:
Samsung has been pushing the foldable market ahead for several years now and, arguably, makes some of the best foldable devices out there. But Apple is about to make its long-awaited debut with the first iPhone foldable, and Samsung has some advice.

Speaking to Wired, Samsung’s Hee-Cheul Moon, head of the company’s Advanced Mechanical R&D group, and Seungki Choi, head of Smartphone R&D group, discussed Apple’s incoming debut on the market. Samsung’s sentiment towards an Apple foldable hasn’t changed since last year – it’s “absolutely welcome” as Apple will bring some much-needed attention and legitimacy to the foldable space.

Moon says:

Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized. 

Weight is a key aspect that Samsung is focused on, though, with Moon saying that the key “to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device.” Samsung has cut a huge amount of weight out of its foldables since the first generation, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 weighing in at just 201g, less than even most slab smartphone flagships. Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214g, for example. Meanwhile, as Wired points out, Apple’s foldable is expected to weigh around 230-241g while the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233g.

	

Samsung has certainly figured out a lot over the years from its foldables, but thickness and weight are perhaps the biggest improvements you’ll find if you pick up an older generation and compare it to the latest models. 

With Apple’s first foldable iPhone – apparently called “iPhone Duo” – set to have the same core form factor as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, these two devices are set to battle. Apple is expected to be a major player in the foldable space within a year or so, despite Android’s major head start in this market. 

All will be revealed later today – stay tuned to our sister site 9to5Mac for more!

title: Harvey hits $15.5B valuation, months after reaching $11B
snippet: The legal AI startup and VC darling has nearly doubled its valuation in nine months.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

11:34 AM PDT · September 9, 2026

Image Credits:Harvey

		

							

											
									

					

	

Harvey, the legal AI startup that VCs can’t get enough of, has raised another $550 million in funding, this time at a $15.5 billion valuation, the company announced on Wednesday.

The round was co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners and follows the previous $200 million round at an $11 billion valuation announced in March. And that was just a few months after an $8 billion valuation from a round in December. 

With this latest infusion of capital, the company has raised more than $1.55 billion total and nearly doubled its valuation in about nine months. Like Databricks, the company didn’t name the round, though it has completed at least eight priced rounds since 2023 (five of them since 2025), PitchBook estimates. Since a couple of those were considered extension rounds, this one could be considered a Series F.

The fresh cash comes a couple of weeks after Harvey announced its first in-house model, Harvey Tenet, built from open-weight model Kimi K3 and post-trained with legal data with the help of inference provider Fireworks (which also helped Cursor train its homegrown model). In addition to offering a model, Harvey is encouraging its customers to adopt and post-train their own open-weight models. So Harvey is quickly becoming an example of how an entire industry — law — can both heavily use AI and not rely on proprietary frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 unveiled with upgraded health tracking system
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are official. Apple has announced its two new Apple Watch models as part of its product event today. An upgraded health tracking system is key to both models. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are official. Apple has announced its two new Apple Watch models as part of its product event today. An upgraded health tracking system is key to both models.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 details

While both new models feature a familiar design, an upgraded heart rate monitor is key to the new health sensing system. 

For example, the new system now measures heart rate data every five seconds, a 60x frequency increase over previous models. 

Apple is also measuring HRV every five minutes. The new system is called the most accurate heart rate sensor in a wearable, according to Apple. 

Apple is also introducing a new readiness feature. This is based on activity, vitals, and sleep data.

Readiness is a new feature based on activity, vitals, and sleep data

Audio Intelligence

Additionally, Apple is adding a new Audio Intelligence feature to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

This includes sound recognition, like doorbells. There’s also a “live rewind” feature that lets you go back 15 seconds to transcribe what someone just said. It’s invoked by double-clicking the Digital Crown, which used to be multitasking.

Apple has published a new support document that details what audio intelligence does and how it works.

Siri recaps is another new feature. When enabled, it can summarize things like meetings, based on audio notes. Apple Watch also gains a new Siri Modular face as part of the new system.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on Apple’s new S11 chip. It includes A20 Pro-derived CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine components.

Colors, prices, availability

Colors include space gray, black, light gold, and bronze aluminum. Ceramic Shield 2 protects the front glass.

Radiant gold and natural make up the polished titanium finishes. Ceramic returns in pearl white and a new dark blue option. Hermes adds gold to the lineup.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 includes a larger battery with over two days of battery life. Black and natural titanium remain the two finish options. There’s also a new titanium band. 

Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are available for pre-order from today. Both launch on September 18. Pricing remains the same as the Series 11 and Ultra 3, from $399 and $799, respectively.

title: iPhone 18 Pro can authenticate that your photo wasn’t edited with AI
snippet: Apple is introducing a new Reference Image feature as part of the new iPhone 18 Pro, which digitally authenticates that the image you took with the camera has not been altered later by AI. If edits have been made, users can see the ‘digital negative’ original and compare the differences. This is Apple’s answer to the rise of synthetic AI-generated imagery. Reference Image ensures that people looking at your photos know if it reflects the true reality or not. more…
fullText:
Apple is introducing a new Reference Image feature as part of the new iPhone 18 Pro, which digitally authenticates that the image you took with the camera has not been altered later by AI. If edits have been made, users can see the ‘digital negative’ original and compare the differences.

This is Apple’s answer to the rise of synthetic AI-generated imagery. Reference Image ensures that people looking at your photos know if it reflects the true reality or not.

Reference Image incorporates Apple Private Cloud Compute to sends some details about the photo you take with the iPhone 18 Pro lenses, essentially creating a cryptographic signature. 

The Reference Image indicators are not just limited to showing on the phone you took them with. You can also share the signed images with other people, including the reference signatures for later authentication.

Apple Reference Image will not be available in the European Union or China. 

For Apple’s image generation features, including Image Playgrounds or the new Apple Intelligence editing tools like Extend and Spatial Reframe, the generated images will include SynthID markers.

title: Apple shares more details about Apple Intelligence usage limits and terms
snippet: Apple today published a new support article that provides more detail on Apple Intelligence usage terms, limits, and restrictions. Here’s what the company says. more…
fullText:
Apple today published a new support article that provides more detail on Apple Intelligence usage terms, limits, and restrictions. Here’s what the company says.

A bit of context

When Apple first announced the new Apple Intelligence during WWDC26, the company said “some images, including image generation,” would have usage limits, because “they rely on powerful server models.”

The company added that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans and would also include Apple Intelligence support for compatible home cameras.

Earlier today, Apple reaffirmed these limitations during the “Surprise and Shine” event. However, it didn’t offer further details on what those limits will be or how much additional access iCloud+ subscribers will get.

Now, the company has published a new support article titled “Learn about Apple Intelligence usage limits,” where it goes into more detail on these limitations.

‘Increased access will be available for a fee’

According to Apple, the following features will rely on server-side models and may be subject to usage limits:

Siri AI

Intelligent Photo Editing Tools including Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing

Image Playground

AFM 3 Cloud and AFM 3 Cloud Pro Models in Shortcuts

Developer apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

Apple says that it will implement usage limits on these and other Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features “in the future,” but does not offer specifics on what those limits will look like or when they will take effect.

The company does confirm, however, that once users reach those limits, the affected features will become unavailable for a period of time before access is restored.

Apple also notes that the limits themselves won’t necessarily be the same across features, but that users will be able to pay for increased access:

Limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other factors. Increased access to such features will be available for a fee.

As for the Apple Intelligence features that will work with home cameras, the company says:

Some Apple Intelligence features in the Home app, such as video summaries, are available for a limited number of cameras depending on your iCloud+ plan — up to 1 camera in the 2 TB plan, up to 2 cameras in the 6 TB plan, and up to 5 cameras in the 12 TB plan. Supported camera counts and other iCloud+ plan features may change over time.

Apple adds that both Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage will be subject to the Apple Intelligence Usage Terms, which also outline restrictions on excessive or abusive use, availability and device requirements, age restrictions, and how Apple may enforce violations.

Here are two of the most relevant tidbits:

Unreasonable Use

Excessive, abusive, automated, fraudulent, illegal or otherwise unreasonable use, including use that materially impacts service availability or other users, may be restricted, throttled, suspended, or subject to additional limits. We may determine what constitutes unreasonable use based on factors including usage volume, frequency, request complexity, system demand, and patterns of use.

Enforcement

Apple reserves the right to investigate and take action against any use that violates these Usage Terms, including restricting, suspending, or terminating access to Apple Intelligence Features. Apple may update these Usage Terms from time to time, and continued use of Apple Intelligence after changes constitutes acceptance of the updated Usage Terms.

12:21 PM PDT · September 9, 2026

Image Credits:Apple

		

							

											
									

					

	

Duo, Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.

The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to the hype. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.

Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer. 

“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Wednesday’s event.

Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections,” as well as a multilayer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

title: Apple releases iOS 27 RC ahead of public launch
snippet: Apple has released the first iOS 27 release candidate for testing. The update brings Apple’s next major iPhone software release one step closer to public launch, with Siri AI leading the list of changes. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the first iOS 27 release candidate for testing. The update brings Apple’s next major iPhone software release one step closer to public launch, with Siri AI leading the list of changes.

iOS 27 reaches release candidate stage

Following a summer of testing, Apple is now preparing the software for release to everyone.

This is the version Apple intends to ship publicly if testing doesn’t uncover any issues that require another build. Apple can release additional RC versions before the final rollout.

Developers can download the update through Settings > General > Software Update. If you’re already running the iOS 27 developer beta, check there for today’s release.

iOS 27 is all about Siri AI

The biggest part of iOS 27 is Siri AI, Apple’s revamped assistant with more conversational responses, personal context, on-screen awareness, and expanded actions in apps.

Apple also introduced a dedicated Siri app for returning to previous conversations, a new interface centered on the Dynamic Island, and a Siri mode in Camera that brings Visual Intelligence into the experience.

Beyond Siri, Apple has announced AI features across Photos, Safari, Mail, Messages, Shortcuts, and other apps.

More iOS 27 features and changes

iOS 27 also builds on last year’s Liquid Glass redesign with additional customization, including a transparency slider.

Other changes include keywords and star ratings in Photos, customizable slideshows, Dual Capture in FaceTime, custom EQ for AirPods, and easier card switching with Apple Pay.

Apple has also focused on performance, with improvements planned for app launches, Photos loading, AirDrop transfers, and switching between Wi-Fi and cellular connections.

title: TCL’s first NXTPAPER phone with AMOLED is also one of its most flagship-like, coming to US
snippet: After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series. more…
fullText:
After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series.

TCL’s NXTPAPER display tech is more than just a matte coating, but the one part that takes the whole thing down a notch has been the panel technology. While NXTPAPER displays typically look good, they lack the vibrance and brightness of the AMOLED (or OLED) panels used on most other modern smartphones. That’s finally changing, with the first new releases dropping this week.

TCL P80, P80 Pro, and P80 Ultra offer up a 1.5K NXTPAPER AMOLED display and some of the highest-end packages TCL has put together so far – though still not quite in flagship territory. All three phones are based on MediaTek chips, with Ultra and Pro using Dimensity 7400 Elite and the base model a Dimensity 7300 Elite. These are upper-mid-range chips that are still a whole lot more powerful than what TCL’s phones usually bring to the table. They’ve all got a 6.83-inch display.

The TCL P80 Ultra has two 50MP cameras on the back including a telephoto lens, up to 512GB of storage, 8GB of RAM, a 6,800 mAh battery, and IP68 dust/water resistance.  TCL P80 Pro is virtually identical, but the second 50MP camera is now an 8MP ultrawide. The base TCL P80 also has a 50MP main camera and 8MP ultrawide, but has the aforementioned drop in chipset, as well as limiting itself to 256GB of storage at most, while still offering 8GB of RAM. It also drops down to a 6,000 mAh battery. 

	

These phones launch in Europe starting today at €349, €429, and €549, respectively.

TCL says these phones will come to the US eventually, but there’s no exact word on when. TCL is supporting the Ultra with 7 years of OS and security updates, while the Pro and base models drop to 3 years of OS updates, but stick with 7 years of security updates.

title: Google Chrome starts two-week release cycle with version 153
snippet: As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle. more…
fullText:
As previewed earlier this year, Google Chrome is now operating on a two-week release cycle.

Previously, Chrome received a major “milestone” update — like going from version 100 to 101 — every four weeks. Before 2021, Google had a six-week cycle.

The aim of releasing big updates every two weeks is to deliver “new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes faster.” Less is included with each update, but that will be paired with the increased frequency.

Meanwhile, Google says this “increased cadence is a win for the entire web.” Developers will be able to “ship modern web features with confidence, knowing that deployment windows are tighter, interoperability updates arrive quickly, and safety improvements reach users faster across platforms.” The fact that the “scope per release is smaller” will make “regression isolation faster.”

	

On the security front, Google says this change will “protect against fast-moving threats” given the rise of AI.

For enterprise customers, Chrome offers the “Extended Stable” channel that updates in eight-week increments: Chrome 156 followed by version 160. Google says most enterprise users should be on the two-week Stable option.

Chrome 153 is rolling out starting today for desktop, Android, and iOS. Meanwhile, version 154 will be available on September 22.

fullText:
Hey, happy Tuesday. How was your long weekend? I hope it involved a little Windows 98-style downtime, maybe some pickleball with Andre Agassi, a dive into the origins of the newly UN-endorsed Equal Earth map, and a few examples of GPT-6 Astra blowing some minds.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

In early September, Google DeepMind published a paper (via Import AI) that had a few parallels to the OpenAI-Hugging Face attack, though without the sandbox-escaping consequences. Instead, the company challenged 100 autonomous agents to solve 71 math problems. Though they could talk to one another and were allowed to share resources, they were explicitly warned not to cheat.

	

However, several minutes into the run, one of the agents found an exploit: “Over the following 27 minutes, the exploit spread virally through the swarm’s shared knowledge library, and the research collective unexpectedly ‘solved’ the remaining 34 problems.”

What’s really interesting about these findings is the percentage of agents complicit in the mischief: only 9% actively took advantage of the exploit; 5% were “converted” by the exploiters; 24% were considered “whistleblowers” and refused to cheat, attempting to contact the authorities instead; and 62% stayed unaware of the contagion and continued to operate as normal.

The paper ultimately argues that while some of the agents are prone to taking advantage of exploits, it’s largely a product of design and oversight more than inherent behavior. “Our findings show that the same infrastructure that allows the agents to coordinate and collaborate, if left unmanaged or poorly designed, also makes the system highly vulnerable to rapid pollution with specification gaming and reward hacks. Equipping agent collectives with the institutional infrastructure to translate emergent peer oversight into actionable self-governance offers a promising blueprint for scaling autonomous scientific discovery reliably.” 

In other words, they want to be good; they just need the right environment in which to do so. Sound familiar?

✉️ Inbox

A pile of MacBook Neo clones gives Googlebook all the more of an uphill battle. Ben’s Weekender essay dives into the miasma of what Google is jumping into with its Googlebook line.

Gemini Spark rolling out Google Photos control for automated editing, sharing, & more. I’m really curious about whether people will use this to batch-edit or better organize their libraries. I’m going to be testing it out.

Ugreen’s ‘HomeAgent’ is a local AI smart home ecosystem for its new line of cameras, more. This, along with Anker’s MindBase, is the beginning of what I think is a long road toward bringing local AI into the mainstream. Having a dedicated box with enough compute to control a smart home or NAS, and be a centralized hub for distributed private AI, is pretty compelling.

This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999. I hate how much I love this idea.

Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones. In a world where everything is getting more expensive, it’s a pretty good idea to relaunch a 6-year-old product at half its original price. Still nowhere near a bargain, though.

🤝 Cc: Will Sattelberg

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, 9to5Google’s superb podcast host and long-suffering Bills fan, Will Sattelberg.

Who are you?

Isn’t that the question we all ask ourselves in front of the mirror every morning? (I’m Will Sattelberg.)

What do you do for work?

I’m some combination of a writer and a podcaster. I guess I mostly make things online for people to enjoy, hopefully.

What do you do for fun?

Some combination of indoor kid hobbies (gaming, movies, cooking, D&D) and outdoor hobbies (running, long walks, traveling). We also have two cats in our house that we enjoy hanging out with, although only one of them is really playful in any sense of the word.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

In all honesty, not great — click on any random episode of The Sideload to hear my mental anguish on a near-weekly basis (Ed. Also listen to Pixelated, the other show he co-hosts.). I really fell in love with technology as an adolescent (I started listening to CNET’s Buzz Out Loud when I was 13) and getting to cover it professionally was sort of the end result of a dream I didn’t even realize I was chasing. But like lots of things that are in your life long enough, eventually your relationship with an interest begins to reshape itself.

Frankly, a lot of the elements of technology that first got me hooked on gadgets have been left in the rearview mirror by the most notable names in the industry — Google included — while the slow death of both traditional websites with front pages worth visiting and the feed-based social networks that originally killed them off has made it more difficult to really feel like you’re in the conversation to begin with. 

These days, the technology that makes me happiest tends to be single-purpose devices designed to accomplish a few things really well, rather than following through on the jack-of-all-trades, AI-will-fix-it routine. Mostly, I just hope brighter days are around the corner.

What are a few apps you can’t live without and why?

I’ll need to start by echoing David Imel on Pocket Casts. I haven’t used the app quite as long as him (mine says I’ve been listening since November 22nd, 2015), but my listening time is, no joke, just two days’ worth of playback away from hitting a full 365 days. Crazy stuff.

Letterboxd remains indispensable for movie fans, even if — like me — you mostly use it these days just to log whatever you’re watching to your diary. I have over a decade’s worth of movie-watching experiences logged on there with only a couple of gaps, and being able to look back at what I was watching 10 years ago is a genuinely cool feat. I just hope the app doesn’t sell.

Finally, this one’s actually fairly new to my app drawer, but I’ve been using Rise to get my sleep schedule back under control, and even after just a few weeks of use, I have been going to bed at a more regular (and reasonable) time, and I’m already noticing an overall difference in my energy levels.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Technically it started shipping to early adopters late last year, but the AYN Thor is by far my contender for favorite gadget of 2026. It’s an Android-powered emulation handheld designed to mirror Nintendo’s 3DS family, but with all sorts of modern touches. I’d love to tell you I’ve finally filled in my DS and 3DS gaps, but truth be told, I mostly use it to play all sorts of weird and wild Pokémon ROM hacks, like — most recently — the Creepypasta-inspired entry Pokémon: Ghost Grey.

What’s a recent TV show you loved?

My fiancée and I, frustrated as ever with the current slate of streaming shows, have mostly been diving into the archives to fill in some backlog gaps (most recently Sex and the City, which I enjoyed far more than I thought I would. Carrie Bradshaw deserves as much credit for the antihero trend as Tony Soprano and I’ll die on this hill), but I will shout out two fairly different shows as recommendations. 

First, Widow’s Bay really is as good as everyone is saying. Blew me away in pretty much every way it could, from the acting to the writing to the cinematography. A really fresh spin on “horror-comedy,” a genre I think can get old fast.

I’ll also shout out Taskmaster, which, full disclosure, my friend and former boss James Peckham recommended to me in 2023 at a cafe in Barcelona and I still dragged my feet for two additional years until Jason Mantzoukas showed up. Anyway, the entire 21-season (series, Jason) run is officially available on YouTube, and series 22 just started airing, so it’s a great time to check it out. If you have any love or fondness for classic Whose Line is it Anyway?, I think you’ll get a huge kick out of it.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

I’ll be honest, I’ve been slacking on my new release movies this year, but I’ll echo David’s shoutout of The Drama as a film I both liked more than I thought I would and one that has stayed with me longer than I anticipated. My favorite Zendaya performance so far, and it’s not even close.

What’s a recent game you loved?

As for games, “recent” gets complicated (I’ve been trying to clear out some of my backlog), but I’ll shout out the 2019 Resident Evil 2 remake as something that I really fell in love with over the summer. I’m also really excited about Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, set to launch in about two weeks. That game looks to be, um, about one million hours long.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I don’t run every day, but I do love to run as a way to clear my mind, and we’re entering my favorite season to run in. And you know what? Maybe I should run every day.

Thank you, Will, for being the best co-host a boy could ask for. And for not writing about Lost.

Even the Trumps can’t escape RAMageddon.﻿

by  Dominic Preston

Sep 10, 2026, 9:13 AM UTC

Dominic Preston

 

is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Bad news if you didn’t lock in a Trump phone at launch: It now costs $749, a $250 increase on its price at launch. The T1 Phone itself hasn’t changed.

Trump Mobile didn’t announce the price increase, instead quietly changing its website overnight. This wasn’t a total surprise though, especially given the phone ships with an unexpectedly generous 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. When I spoke to two Trump Mobile executives earlier this year, they called the $499 launch pricing “introductory,” and a few months later, the website itself was changed to reflect that, calling it a “promotional price.” That wording is now gone.

When I reviewed the Trump phone in July, I wasn’t especially impressed, even at $499. At $749 there is absolutely no reason recommend it. You could buy an iPhone 17E or Galaxy S26 FE and have $50 left over to buy a gold case; $50 more would net you an older flagship like the iPhone 16 or Pixel 10. Any one of these phones would blow the T1 Phone out of the water.

To my surprise, my Trump phone has received some support since it launched. There’s been exactly one software update, moving it from Android’s February 2026 security patch to the May 2026 version. It’s still running Android 15 though, which is now two years old.

While the Trump phone officially started shipping in May, almost a year after it was announced, it remains unclear just how many customers have received their phones. A report from the BBC last month found that at least some buyers still say their phones never arrived.

title: How do Apple Refurbished products compare with Amazon and Walmart?
snippet: If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website. Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply … more…
fullText:
If you’re willing to exercise a little patience rather than rushing out to buy a shiny new Apple product on launch day, then Apple’s refurbished store has always been an excellent option. Typically, there will be around a three-month wait between a product launch and the first refurbished models appearing on Apple’s website.

Other companies offers their own alternatives, like Amazon Renewed and Walmart Restored, but it’s important to understand the different standards and warranties that apply …

Apple Certified Refurbished

Buying from Apple’s Certified Refurbished store gets you a typical discount of 15% on a product that will be indistinguishable from new. Specifically, Apple guarantees all of the following:

Full inspection and testing by Apple

A brand new outer shell, so there will never be any marks or scratches

A brand new battery, so you’ll get the same battery life as usual

All original accessories and cables are included

Apple’s standard one-year warranty applies in exactly the same way as a new product

The same eligibility for AppleCare+

Literally the only difference you’ll see is that products are supplied in a plain white box rather than the original packaging.

Amazon Renewed

Amazon Renewed can offer more competitive pricing, but it’s worth being aware that you’re not getting the same guarantees as to condition:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

Used outer shell, so expect marks and scratches (see below)

Used battery, only guaranteed to exceed 80% of the original capacity

Accessories may not be genuine Apple ones

90-day Amazon warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

As for marks and scratches, Amazon offers three tier quality tiers:

Premium/Excellent: No signs of cosmetic damage when held 12 inches away

Good: Light scratches, barely visible when holding the device 12 inches away

Acceptable: Scratches that are easily seen and felt

Walmart Restored

Walmart Restored is a lot vaguer than Amazon on what you’re getting for your money:

Inspection and testing by the seller, not by Apple

No promises as to cosmetic condition, only “like-new performance and reliability”

No specifics on the battery condition beyond the above

No information on accessories

Seller warranty, instead of 1-year Apple one

The seller warranty is for one year on the Restored Premium tier, and 90 days on Like New, Good, and Fair tiers. The company isn’t specific about its definitions for each tier.

9to5Mac’s Take

If you want a product indistinguishable from new in terms of both condition and Apple warranty, then it’s clear that Apple’s refurbished store is the place to go.

Amazon Renewed can, however, offer significantly better pricing, so if you’re willing to accept the compromises listed above, you may consider this a decent deal. In particular, if you’re opting to take our advice to save money by upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro instead of this year’s model (when the only accessory you’re sacrificing is the cable), there are some attractive deals here:

1TB iPhone 17 Pro Cosmic Orange $1,214 (Reg. $1,499 new) – all-time low

1TB iPhone 17 Pro Deep Blue $1,215 (Reg. $1,499 new) – all-time low

1TB iPhone 17 Pro Silver $1,208 (Reg. $1,499 new) – all-time low

512GB iPhone 17 Pro Cosmic Orange $1,164 (Reg. $1,299 new) – all-time low

512GB iPhone 17 Pro Deep Blue $1,170 (Reg. $1,299 new) – all-time low

512GB iPhone 17 Pro Silver $1,171 (Reg. $1,299 new) – within $1 of all-time low

As for Walmart Restored, I’d worry about the extreme vagueness of the promises, but you do have the option of returning them if you aren’t happy.

title: Sorry, Apple, but the iPhone Duo Isn’t the Smart Display I’m Waiting For
snippet: Reports keep saying Apple is releasing a home smart display. It still hasn’t happened, and here’s why that’s a problem.
fullText:
Apple’s “Surprise and shine” on Wednesday featured plenty of callouts to AI, with Apple envisioning its iPhone and the new foldable iPhone Duo as “personal hubs” where artificial intelligence is everywhere, especially the new Siri AI. But one major announcement was notably missing, and it’s especially frustrating for smart home fans.

Throughout 2026, I’ve heard reports from publications citing Apple insiders that the delayed Apple smart home push was finally — no, really this time — coming during the Apple fall event. Most importantly, the rumors said Apple was ready to unleash a smart home display, similar to Amazon Echo Shows but with a unique, versatile design and updated features like facial recognition. Reports mentioned several installation options, including wall mounting or a pivoting smart display that could let Siri watch different faces in turn.

With Siri AI early access debuting throughout this year, and Apple talking about new Apple Home features like video descriptions for security cameras, the smart display seemed like a done deal for this fall. But no. Apple didn’t show a hint of any Siri home display. I don’t think the Apple Home app got even a second of screen time for this event.

The closest we’ll get to any kind of Apple display is the new iPhone Duo, which can be tented to resemble something sort of like a smart display, showing calendars or an alarm clock, but it’s a far cry from a fully independent device made to take up permanent residence in a kitchen, shelf or bedside table. And while it may be the “largest iPhone display we’ve ever designed,” according to Apple, at $1,999, the Duo is exponentially more expensive than today’s smart displays.

Ginormous pricing aside, the foldable Duo isn’t big enough to take over my favorite roles for a smart display, like serving as a second TV screen while you’re busy, and its speakers certainly can’t compare with the room-filling options most home displays come with these days. Siri AI also doesn’t appear set up to display conversations, food orders and video at a command like Alexa Plus can — although that remains to be tested.

Read more: iPhone 18 Preorders Are Coming. Everything You Need to Know

Why didn’t we see Apple’s home display device?

Apple faces home-screen competition from Amazon and others, which could be one reason it’s delaying plans here.Amazon

My first thought is that the iPhone Duo already took enough work to prep for this event, and Siri AI (available in beta when OS 27 drops on Monday) may not be quite ready for a home screen the way Alexa Plus is. With the Duo playing so many different roles, Apple may be watching its performance and popularity carefully before deciding if and how to move into smart displays. Ditto for Siri AI, which, as I mentioned, may not be ready for the many integrations other AI voice assistants currently offer.

Since RAMageddon and other trends are pushing device prices higher and higher right now, Apple may also be leery of releasing a new device at a price that almost surely wouldn’t compete with top-rated competitor models. Remember, that was one complaint people had about the original Apple HomePod smart speaker, which launched at $349, way above the smart speakers of the day, and eventually led to the more reasonably priced HomePod mini.

Apple’s reaping some advantages by waiting so long to get into the AI game, but those delays also invite risk. A smart space occupied by Echo Shows, Nest Hubs and smart calendars for years could be challenging to enter, which may be another reason Apple is weighing its options here.

But Apple may also be saving its home display for a different reveal. We are expecting more news about the iPad mini, potentially in October. I don’t think this is likely, especially since a standalone display would be a new category for Apple, and it would prefer to announce that with more fanfare.

As for me, I can’t wait for an Apple smart display to finally — if ever — launch. Not only are these some of my favorite devices to test, but I think Apple could make its display refreshing and useful, including connections to Apple TV shows, an easy FaceTime experience and easy handoffs when switching from iPhone or iPad to a more central display. But time will, once again, have to tell on those specifics.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

With degrees in Business Management, Literature and Technical Writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. title: Reports describe two ways for Apple to make more money; only one is good
snippet: There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree … more…
fullText:
There were two reports in the last few days indicating different routes for Apple to make more money by boosting Services revenue. 

In my view, it should absolutely do the first of these, but not the second – and it appears Phil Schiller may agree …

Let’s start by summarizing the two reports.

Home security & monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg suggested that Apple may be planning a new home security and monitoring service to sit alongside some of the new home hardware we’re expecting.

Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

A second report from the same source on Sunday said that the company is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Ternus and services chief Eddy Cue want to make even more money from the App Store and figure out ways to raise margins and squeeze additional recurring revenue from the platform.

Apple should not take the latter approach

Tackling these in reverse order, I think the second approach would be a very big mistake. 

Apple’s effective monopoly on the sale of iPhone apps has come under fire from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you are forced to do so through the official App Store, and that leaves you with no choice but to accept the company’s terms on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

I understand a common view is that nobody forces anyone to buy an iPhone or make apps for it, but that is not the reality of how even the most laissez-faire forms of capitalism work: even the US has had antitrust legislation in place since 1890. When you achieve a certain level of market dominance, then constraints are imposed on how you need to behave in order to ensure you don’t abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze even more money from the App Store is very much the antithesis of skating to where the puck is headed, and Phil Schiller reportedly shares this view as Bloomberg suggests it’s one of the reasons he’s stepped down now.

Schiller, on the other hand, seems to believe that such moves will only further irk developers and governments. While there was no internal blowup or anything like that, it’s something he wanted no part of.

Innovative services are the way to go

Introducing new innovative services that people will want to buy, in contrast, is absolutely the right thing for Apple to do. I can easily see value in the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that making its own smart home camera would be one of the … smartest things the company could do. I said the same again about rumours of an Apple smart doorbell. Adding an optional Services component to security products makes perfect sense for two reasons.

First, there are all the privacy arguments I’ve made before. HomeKit Secure Video has already made a major contribution to ensuring the privacy of security camera feeds. If there is one company I’d trust to perform AI analysis of security camera footage, it’s Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within a HomeKit environment. I’m sure there will be many other areas where Apple can offer similar benefits.

To me, the key is that Apple needs to adopt the same approach to services it does to hardware. Make great products that lead to people willingly parting with their money and doing so with a smile on their face. Not squeezing money in a way that irritates customers, developers, and regulators alike.

What’s your take on this? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: It’s iPhone Duo Users Who Will Want a Stylus
snippet: Apple’s first foldable phone is also its first with pen support.
fullText:
“Who wants a stylus?” 

Steve Jobs famously posed this question when he introduced the first iPhone in 2007. It was a jab at the other smartphones of the era with small screens that were better navigated with a skinny stylus than with a fat finger. 

Jobs quickly answered his own question. “You have to get ’em and put ’em away, and you lose ’em. Yuck! Nobody wants a stylus.” The iPhone’s giant-for-the-time display was best navigated with nature’s stylus, Jobs argued, your finger.

Fast forward two decades, and we’ve come full circle with Apple announcing the iPhone Duo, which is not only the company’s first foldable phone but also its first phone to support – gasp! – a stylus. 

iPhone Duo users, that’s who.

In the case of the Duo, it’s not about the display being too small, but about having a display so large when unfolded that it rivals an iPad’s. The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, which is within an inch of the 8.3-inch iPad Mini. And on that giant iPhone screen (as well as the Duo’s smaller 5.4-inch outer display), you will soon be able to draw, sketch, tap, write and swipe with an Apple Pencil. 

In introducing the iPhone Duo at its fall event, Apple said that its new foldable will support Apple Pencil (with USB-C) later this year. A software update is needed to add pen support to iOS.

With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, perhaps the iPad-like pen support will help people justify the high price by viewing the Duo as two devices in one, acting as both a phone and tablet.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Matt Elliott
						

						

							Senior Editor

title: Google Home update fixes alarms, improves media & smart home voice controls
snippet: The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home update is fixing issues with alarms that some users were experiencing while also improving media and smart home voice controls in Google’s continued effort to address pain points in Gemini for Home.

The most noticeable upgrade in the latest Google Home update should be around voice commands. On smart speakers and displays, Gemini “now understands a broader range” of commands regarding media and smart home devices. You can also chain commands in the same sentence. 

Google explains:

Expanded capabilities and understanding for media controls: Gemini on speakers and displays now understands a broader range of voice commands across media and home device controls. And, you can now combine media commands with other commands to get things done faster.

Try saying:

“Turn off the lights and stop the music.”

“Skip this song and turn on the backyard lights.”

“Stop captions on this video.”

This update should also fix an issue with Google Keep integration as well as an issue that was preventing users from creating or editing alarms and lists. Seeing as smart speakers and display are very often used as an alarm clock, that’s welcome news.

	

Rounding out this update, the Google Home app should clean up any rogue automations from third-party apps. The automations editor should also be a lot easier to use now, as starters, conditions, and actions are now listed in alphabetical order automatically.

title: Apple Watch’s new feature listens to your chats and recaps them
snippet: The Siri Recap feature is similar to other note-taking apps like Granola.
fullText:
At its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, Apple launched a meeting notetaker for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, one of a series of new audio intelligence features that can listen to sounds through your Apple Watch.

The feature, called Siri Recap, uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, according to the company. Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points from the conversation, which can then be reviewed in the Siri app. 

Apple said that you can choose to keep this feature always on, set up a schedule, or turn off completely.

The notetaker wasn’t the only audio-focused feature introduced for the Watch during the event. Apple’s new audio intelligence features also include Shazam, which can identify songs instantly. This means Apple has finally caught up to Google’s Now Playing feature. The Watch can recognize loud sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying and notify users.

Apple also introduced a feature called Live Rewind, which lets users recap 15 seconds of conversation when they double-press the Digital Crown.

Apple emphasized that the features don’t store recordings and that raw audio is inaccessible. The Siri Recap feature doesn’t identify speakers either. Users can access Live Rewind recaps, which are end-to-end encrypted. Despite these guardrails, an always-listening feature will likely raise privacy concerns because Siri Recap may still capture sensitive information in its summaries.

Besides some of the privacy features, Siri Recap sounds similar to other notetakers like Granola and Circleback, which also have Apple Watch apps.

title: The iPhone Air 2 Wasn’t Announced. Here’s Why That’s Bad for Apple Buyers
snippet: The iPhone Air 2 was a no-show at Apple Park on Wednesday.
fullText:
Apple hosted its annual iPhone launch event on Wednesday, and something we didn’t see — along with base iPhone 18 models, as Apple focused purely on premium devices — was a second iteration of its lightweight iPhone Air.

At just 5.6mm thick and weighing only 165 grams, last year’s $999 iPhone 17 Air gave buyers a middle-ground option between the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17 Pro models, and for a pretty reasonable price. 

While sales of the iPhone Air were reportedly disappointing, it was arguably a first step toward launching the iPhone Duo — a demonstration that a slim, lightweight phone could be just as durable and high-functioning as a fully specced-out one. It came with just one rear 48-megapixel wide-angle camera, a smaller battery and a single speaker.

The Air’s pared-back features and slim profile would have been pivotal to designing Apple’s new folding phone, since foldables must be both slim and make similar compromises on specs — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 only has two rear lenses, compared with the three that come on other Galaxy models, and the iPhone Duo likewise has just two rear cameras.

We were hoping Apple would release another version of the Air with improved cameras and battery life, especially since that middle ground still exists. Some people just want a phone that’s slightly better than the base iPhone, and many people want a capable phone without having to spend upward of $1,199 — the cheapest phone Apple announced on Wednesday as it took the wraps off premium handsets like the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

	

			

	

			

									

						iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max					

							

		

Many people also don’t want a phone that folds. CNET’s survey of more than 2,600 adults last month found that 75% were not interested in a foldable iPhone and that most would want to spend less than $1,000 if they did get one. But the Duo costs between $1,999 and $3,199 — far exceeding the iPhone Air’s original $999 price tag.

Apple also raised the prices on its iPhone 17 lineup on Wednesday as it announced its new high-end handsets, leaving the middle ground with fewer options, even in previously available models. The iPhone 17 Air now starts at $1,099, with the price increases coming amid RAMageddon, the global memory shortage caused by the spike in AI tools. Apple continues to whittle down options for more budget-conscious consumers in a difficult economy. 

We’re still holding out hope that the iPhone 18 Air has been pushed back until a rumored spring launch, where it could be unveiled alongside an iPhone 18 base model and a potential iPhone 18E, the budget follow-up to this year’s iPhone 17E. 

IDC Worldwide Device Trackers Senior Research Director Nabila Popal likewise believes Apple is strategically withholding the second iPhone Air until next year to bundle with the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18E — launching a trio of more affordable smartphones to contrast with the premium trio of the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo that were just announced.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said. “Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice.”

But for now, the lack of lower-end models means anyone wanting to upgrade their phone to a brand-new Apple handset will be stuck choosing between an $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro and up to an eye-watering $3,199 for a 2TB iPhone Duo.

title: Where’s the iPhone 18? Here’s Why Apple Didn’t Reveal a New Standard iPhone
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and iPhone Duo are coming soon, but the baseline model is presumably coming next year, likely for these reasons.
fullText:
Without a new iPhone 18, Apple has kept the iPhone 17 as its main baseline phone in its lineup — though with a price bump.

																			Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET
												
			
				

The Apple Sept. 9 event revealed a new lineup of devices, including new Apple Watches, the new iPhone 18 Pro and the first foldable iPhone Duo, with one glaring omission: The standard iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen. Apple didn’t comment on the absent phone, but rumors say it will come early in 2027 — and there are several reasons why the company would delay its entry-level model to next year.

It’s a pivotal moment for Apple. The event was the first for new CEO John Ternus, who started his role on Sept. 1, and we’re learning in real time whether he plans to stay the course his predecessor, Tim Cook, set or take Apple in a different direction. The foldable iPhone Duo is a bold foray into a niche subset of phones that sell a fraction of the flat iPhones that make up the bulk of Apple’s earnings every quarter. 

But Apple has masterfully navigated expanding its lineup with a product that fits between its existing devices. The iPad was introduced to fit the niche between phones and laptops, and the foldable iPhone seems aimed at the gap between smartphone and iPad. In the background is the RAM shortage, making memory and components pricier than ever — and indeed, the iPhone 18 Pro got a $100 price bump over its predecessors, and the current iPhone 17 got more expensive as well.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable, automatically adjusts its display to its orientation.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Amid those conditions, there are potential reasons for Apple to push its more basic phones to next year. The easiest assumption is that it will make the company more money, with the iPhone 18 Pro undoubtedly priced higher than the iPhone 18 — anyone eager to upgrade right now only has the more expensive phones to choose from. 

It’s possible that Apple wants to space out its different models to better meet demand, possibly accounting for the production complications that arise with parts getting pricier from the RAM shortage. Or maybe they just want to give the folding iPhone Ultra the limelight. Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, feels this move is brilliant strategy and surprisingly not spurred by the memory crises or supply side constraints.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said.

Releasing the iPhone 18 later may not dim the unit’s sales, either: In the first half of 2024 and 2025, the baseline iPhones released the fall before still made up 16% of Apple’s total shipments in those periods, Popal said.

One thing is for sure: Apple is making big shifts with its Sept. 9 event; its tagline, Surprise and Shine, is telling.

The iPhone Air (mostly) survived my unhinged screen time. 

Jesse Orrall/Zooey Liao/CNET

A lineup shakeup: Bumping the iPhone 18 to 2027 and no iPhone Air 2

Last year’s iPhone Air was a marvel of engineering, following what seemed to be a new trend of slim phones after the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge released earlier in 2025. But what had been a trend has disappeared in 2026, with no high-profile phones released whose main claim to fame is an extremely slender width.

Presumably, that’s because Apple and Samsung lost confidence after the very low sales for either slim phone. The IDC reported that the iPhone Air sold just 7.7 million units over four quarters, and the Galaxy S25 Edge sold 2.3 million over five quarters. Neither phone exceeded 1.8% of total phone sales for either brand across those time periods, IDC said. It’s always possible that Apple does release another iPhone Air later on.

But all the work to slim down conventional phones seemingly hasn’t gone to waste — it’s likely contributed to trimming the width on foldable phones. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5 millimeters when unfolded flat, but Samsung has gone even further, with the wide-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 down to 4.5mm and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra reaching 4.1mm when fully unfolded. Considering that the Galaxy S25 Edge was 5.8mm, the company’s best foldables reaching nearly 2mm thinner is an achievement.

So Apple is relegating its iPhone 18 to 2027, likely earlier in the year. That’s around when it launched the iPhone 17E (in March 2026), so the company could be bundling its baseline iPhone 18 and likely even cheaper iPhone 18E in the same event. This would set a new schedule for Apple: more affordable phones earlier in spring, and then the next generation of its top-tier premium iPhones in its typical September launch window. This gives each lineup its own well-deserved attention and spotlight, IDC’s Popal noted.

“Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice, which is always good for business,” Popal said.

The iPhone 18 could be accompanied by an iPhone 18E and even an iPhone Air 2, Popal predicts. Even if these will conceivably be cheaper than the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo models, they’ll still likely be pricier than their predecessors — because Apple’s already made its older iPhones more expensive.

Typically, when Apple announces a new standard iPhone, the previous version is discounted $100 and sold for another year or so. Instead, it’s raised iPhone 17‘s price at $900, ripping the band-aid off now before the next baseline iPhone launches at a higher price. This could better distinguish it from the traditionally cheaper E-series phones like the $600 iPhone 17E, which appeal to a different, more budget-conscious segment of the market, Popal believes. Apple knows consumers will feel the sticker shock of the price increases, which is why it’s retained the iPhone 16 in its current lineup — though it, too, has gotten a bump back up to its original $800 price, a change from the discounted $700 it had been up until this morning.

That twice-per-year release schedule matches what Samsung has done for years, with an event in January for its premium flat phones and then another in August for its foldables. We’ll have to see whether Apple turns its spring showcase into an announcement event — perhaps bundling it with the Macs and home accessories that have sometimes simply launched via press release. It’s a brand new day for Apple, and anything is possible under Ternus. We’ll just have to see what’s in store for iPhones, folding and flat.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max’s Battery Is a Beast, but Is the Battery Worth the Upgrade?
snippet: Do the math to make sure the upgrade makes sense.
fullText:
Apple just leveled up its battery on its new premium iPhone. Is it worth the leveled-up price tag?

As expected, Apple unveiled the pricier part of the iPhone 18 lineup at its “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday. The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have some serious upgrades, including faster performance from the A20 Pro processor, a new automatically adjustable camera aperture with built-in AI software, and a larger vapor chamber. 

But the big “wow” factor is the battery. We saw a big improvement in the iPhone 17 Pro Max, which holds the crown as our current best-tested phone battery. But the iPhone 18 Pro Max is a pretty sweet upgrade for $100 more than its predecessor’s original price.

During the event, Apple said you can get 45 hours of video playback and 30 hours of usage per charge with the new premium version. It’s also expected to have faster wireless charging, and 15 minutes of wired charging should put the phone at 50%. By comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro Max promises 39 hours of video playback. And based on our testing, the phone’s battery life reached 49% in 20 minutes.

The 18 Pro Max seems to pack a powerful punch with its battery. And surprisingly, Apple’s not raising the price too much. The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB, which is only $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro Max for the same storage. But are the battery upgrades worth the price? I don’t think so.

Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a better battery, but if you’re like me, you just want your phone to hold a battery for a day without rushing to a charger. If you’re not watching videos for days, you may not see much of a difference between the iPhone 17 Pro Max and the new model. Especially if you want a better battery on a budget. So if you have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it’s not worth upgrading for better battery life. However, if you have an earlier model, it may be worth considering one of the latest models.

A recent CNET survey highlighted what US adults really want in a phone upgrade. Most (55%) want a cheaper phone, and next to that is better battery life (52%). Truthfully, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max price increase seems small (especially given the RAM shortage), you may be able to get a solid battery for less. 

I have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and I’m not sold on the new model’s $1,299 price tag when its predecessor is still available at select retailers. Shortly after Apple’s event, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max disappeared from Apple’s site. But you still may be able to find the phones at other retailers and mobile carriers. We also noticed Apple quietly increased prices on other iPhone models, so it’s worth shopping around.

Apple’s Upgrade program and other mobile carrier trade-in programs may make the newer model cheaper. But if you’re buying outright or won’t get a deep discount, save yourself the money and look for the older model that still holds a charge for the day. And if you have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, don’t rush to upgrade for better battery life quite yet.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max vs iPhone 18 Pro: Two exclusive features
snippet: Today Apple introduced iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. While each Pro model is largely identical, there are two exclusive new advantages—one for each model. more…
fullText:
Today Apple introduced iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. While each Pro model is largely identical, there are two exclusive new advantages—one for each model.

#1: iPhone 18 Pro has C2 modem for cellular, while iPhone 18 Pro Max uses Qualcomm

Apple began transitioning its products to in-house cellular modems in early 2025 with the iPhone 16e. First it offered a C1 modem, then the C1X followed in the iPhone Air last fall.

Now Apple has introduced the next-generation C2 modem. It’s available in iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, but curiously is absent from the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Per Apple’s technical specs page, C2 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s Qualcomm modem offer comparable specs. They both support mmWave in the US, for example.

But Apple-designed modems do have the benefit of unlocking some exclusive benefits, which Pro Max users will miss out on.

#2: iPhone 18 Pro Max has much bigger battery gains than iPhone 18 Pro

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are both improving in the battery department this year. But as leaks previously indicated, Apple reserved much larger gains for the Pro Max model.

Here’s an overview of quoted battery life for this year’s models vs last year’s:

title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro: Here’s everything new
snippet: Today Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. Here’s everything new with iPhone 18 Pro vs last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, its latest flagship models. Here’s everything new with iPhone 18 Pro vs last year’s iPhone 17 Pro.

Cameras: New 48MP Main camera with variable aperture

Every year Apple makes the iPhone camera system better. But with four different cameras on the iPhone Pro models, sometimes changes are limited to one camera or another. Last year, for example, brought an all-new Center Stage front camera and Telephoto improvements.

With iPhone 18 Pro, the Main camera is the focus of Apple’s upgrades.

Apple says the 48MP Fusion Main camera is all-new, notably adding a variable aperture feature. Here are the details:

The new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture is the most advanced camera Apple has ever made, bringing aperture control to iPhone for the first time along with even more creative control. Six laser-cut blades smoothly transition between different apertures, making it incredibly easy to capture the best shot by automatically adjusting for depth of field and lighting. Combined with a new sensor that improves image quality, the result is better low-light photography, crisper detail in the back of group photos, and more unique shots. Variable aperture also provides more control for creative pros by giving them the ability to manually adjust any of the four aperture settings in the Camera app, and an API is available to developers for even more control across the aperture range in their apps.

Users will be able to switch between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, and ƒ/4.0 variable aperture options.

Apple also introduced a variety of new Camera app software features, including updated Photographic Styles and pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, white balance, and viewing histogram. Those are all exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro too, as are Smart focus tracking, Cinematic mode effects from video, and Apple Reference Image.

Performance: A20 Pro chip and thermal upgrades

The new A20 Pro chip is a big upgrade over last year’s A19 Pro. That’s partly thanks to the new 2nm process it was built on, which improves performance and efficiency.

A20 Pro has a 6-core CPU, with 2 new super cores that Apple says are the fastest in any smartphone, plus 4 new efficiency cores. There’s also a 7-core GPU with 40% faster graphics performance, increased bandwidth, and faster Neural Accelerators than A19 Pro.

iOS 27 is packed with major AI features, and A20 Pro is an especially big leap for AI. That’s thanks to a new Dual 16-core Neural Engine—that’s double the number of cores as A19 Pro.

Finally, A20 Pro has a 50% increase in memory bandwidth, and thermal performance is improved thanks to a second-generation vapor chamber. Ultimately, these changes lead to 40% improved sustained performance over iPhone 17 Pro.

Design: New colors, uniform rear design, redesigned Dynamic Island

iPhone 18 Pro largely retains the same design as iPhone 17 Pro, with a prominent camera plateau on the back.

The most notable design change involves color. iPhone 18 Pro comes in four new colors: Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. This gives it a fresh look versus the bold iPhone 17 Pro colors.

Apple has also updated the back of iPhone 18 Pro with a more unified blend of colors between the glass cutout and aluminum frame. Last year’s models had a two-tone design, but this year it’s a more uniform look.

Finally, there’s a redesigned Dynamic Island on the front of iPhone 18 Pro. Its smaller footprint enables up to three simultaneous Live Activities.

Battery: Best-ever battery life, faster charging

iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max offered the best-ever iPhone battery life. But this year Apple is upping battery life yet again, with big gains especially for iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Battery Life (video playback)

iPhone 18 Pro

up to 36 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max

up to 45 hours

iPhone 17 Pro

up to 33 hours

iPhone 17 Pro Max

up to 39 hours

Faster wired charging is included with iPhone 18 Pro too, which can get 50% charge in just 15 minutes.

Connectivity: Apple-designed C2 modem on at least 18 Pro

Apple has a new in-house C2 modem debuting in iPhone 18 Pro. It replaces the Qualcomm modem found in iPhone 17 Pro, while still including support for mmWave in the US.

Here are the details via Apple’s press release:

iPhone 18 Pro introduces C2, Apple’s next-generation cellular modem system, which brings AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability. C2 delivers meaningfully faster uploads when compared to C1X while consuming 15 percent less energy, and now supports mmWave in the U.S.

Interestingly, Apple’s tech specs page suggests that C2 might be exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro, with the Pro Max model sticking with Qualcomm.

iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro: wrap-up

	

iPhone 18 Pro starts at a higher $1,199 price, compared to $1,099 for iPhone 17 Pro. iPhone 18 Pro Max gets a similar $100 increase, starting at $1,299.

title: No iPhone 18 announced today: Here’s why
snippet: Today at its September event, Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but there was no base model iPhone 18 introduced. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Today at its September event, Apple unveiled iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, but there was no base model iPhone 18 introduced. Here’s why.

iPhone 18 base model expected to launch in early 2027, as Apple shifts release schedule

Normally, it might be common to refer to today’s Apple event as the “iPhone 18 event.”

But in a move that likely surprised many, Apple didn’t announce an iPhone 18 today—at least not the base model.

Instead, the company debuted three high-end new iPhones only: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo.

This flagship lineup differs significantly from Apple’s prior pattern of shipping a new base iPhone at the same time as Pro models. But reporting dating all the way back to May 2025 predicted such a change was coming.

Per widespread reports, Apple’s three new iPhone models introduced today will be joined by three more debuts in early 2027:

iPhone 18

iPhone 18e

iPhone Air 2

So the base iPhone 18 hasn’t been canceled, it’s just shipping later than usual.

Why the change?

One theory is that since Apple wants to expand the iPhone lineup more than ever, with new models like the foldable Duo, it didn’t want to overcrowd the fall. Thus, splitting major iPhone launches into fall and spring cycles might be advantageous.

Another possible reason is that Apple saw the current memory shortage coming, and knew it would be a struggle to meet demand if it launched the base iPhone 18 at the same time as Pro and Duo models.

In any case, the iPhone 18 is still coming—just not until the early months of 2027.
