title: The variable aperture isn’t the cool part of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro’s triple camera setup with a variable aperture in the main (bottom) camera. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Apple always makes a big show of the latest cameras in its phones, and the major talking point of the iPhone 18 Pro is about the new variable aperture. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an adjustable mechanical iris in their main camera modules to let more or less light into the sensor, allowing users to shoot at f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. You can, of course, let the camera select your aperture automatically, but the manual aperture control comes along with other new pro controls allowing you to dial in shutter speeds, manual white balance, and even manual focusing. As a whole, this is a wealth of new controls for an iPhone camera … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Apple always makes a big show of the latest cameras in its phones, and the major talking point of the iPhone 18 Pro is about the new variable aperture. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an adjustable mechanical iris in their main camera modules to let more or less light into the sensor, allowing users to shoot at f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. You can, of course, let the camera select your aperture automatically, but the manual aperture control comes along with other new pro controls allowing you to dial in shutter speeds, manual white balance, and even manual focusing.

As a whole, this is a wealth of new controls for an iPhone camera. You’d normally have to install a third-party camera app like Halide to do some of this, and now it’s all just baked into the 18 Pro’s native camera app. (It’s almost as if Apple poached a key person directly from Halide.) But I’d temper any expectations over the variable aperture being the standout feature. It’s going to be mid, at best.

1/348 megapixels. Four selectable apertures. Image: Apple

Why? Because smartphone sensors are still pretty dang tiny, and most subjects are in reasonable focus until you get really close. And stopping down to f/4 is unlikely to blow you away with much sharper results like it does in full-size cameras or any special qualities aside from some sunstar effects in very particular lighting scenarios. In fact, due to lens diffraction, your photos might be less sharp at f/4 than f/1.8 or f/2.8. What you’re most likely to benefit from by stopping down the lens is more depth of field with close-up subjects, getting more people in focus during big group shots with plenty of light (where people aren’t all lined up together), and more flexibility in shooting video in overly bright situations (like direct sunlight). That might prove useful for those particular situations, but they’re likely to be few and far between.

And smartphone sensors are small enough to already have plenty in focus at midrange and further distances, even when shot wide open. It’s probably why other brands like Samsung and Xiaomi have experimented with variable apertures but quietly ditched them.

I think the real star feature of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera is its f/1.48 maximum aperture. Fuck stopping down, man. People love bokeh.

1/2Selecting aperture in the iPhone Camera app. Image: Apple

Last year’s Pro iPhone cameras had an f/1.7 aperture, and now being at f/1.48, the 18 Pro camera should work better in low-light as well as have a slightly shallower depth of field. Will f/1.48 be a huge difference in bokeh from f/1.7? Probably not. It’s likely to have depth of field that’s just a smidge shallower — but that’s the look that people often like.

I speak from experience here, as I usually shoot on full-frame cameras and one of my go-to lenses is a 50mm with an f/1.2 maximum aperture. A lens that fast, with depth of field that shallow gives a unique look that’s easy to overuse, but it almost never fails that people swoon when I take their portrait using that lens — with that blurry, “dreamy” blur isolating them from the background. The f/1.48 of the iPhone 18 Pro is obviously not going to compare to an f/1.2 on full-frame, but f/1.2 and similarly wide apertures on big sensors is the look that people often want to emulate. It’s the whole reason Portrait Modes on smartphones came into being in the first place.

The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to have a very good camera just like most top-flight smartphones have very good cameras. The added controls are exciting and fun, even if I don’t always want to be bothered with manual controls when taking quick snapshots. It’ll be nice to have them right at your fingertips without having to install a more specialized app. Just don’t be surprised if you start ignoring that aperture setting after some initial tinkering in the new phone honeymoon phase. But even long after that, f/1.48 will be the gift that should keep on giving.

title: It’s not just you; ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok were all down in confirmed outages
snippet: A widespread outage has taken out popular AI platforms including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. more…
fullText:
A widespread outage has taken out popular AI platforms including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

Update 12:38pm PT: All services are back to normal across ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. 

Update 8:49am PT: Services appear to be coming back online, with user reports dropping. OpenAI says that a fix has been applied and services are recovering, Claude says that most models have recovered besides Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, while Grok still just says there is an outage.

Despite a spike in user reports which are now dropping, Google’s Gemini never reported an official outage during this event.

	

With a spike in reports on DownDetector as well as confirmed outages on their respective dashboards, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and X’s Grok are all down. While AI outages aren’t particularly uncommon, it’s interesting to see all three down at the same time. Cursor, an AI agent, has also confirmed an outage due to the Grok and Claude outages.

Google’s Gemini appears to be unaffected at this time. Despite a spike in user reports around the same time, Google has not confirmed an outage. 

The underlying problem might have something to do with Microsoft Azure, which is also seeing a spike in outage reports. All three platforms rely on Azure for cloud services, though there are other providers, including Google, in the mix. Microsoft says that this is not the case.

We’ll update this article as more information is available.

title: iPhone Ultra is coming, here’s what the final rumors say
snippet: Apple is expected to announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow, which rumors say could be called the iPhone Ultra. Here are some last-minute rumors about what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple is expected to announce its first-ever foldable iPhone tomorrow, which rumors say could be called the iPhone Ultra. Here are some last-minute rumors about what to expect.

Starting price

In a new report today, Bloomberg said Apple was initially targeting a $1,999 starting price for the iPhone Ultra. However, due to rising component costs, Apple has most recently discussed a $2,199 starting price. iPhone Ultra configurations with more storage could stretch to $3,000, according to the report.

Delayed launch in China

In a post on Weibo today, leaker Instant Digital said the foldable iPhone will likely launch later in China than the rest of the world. This is primarily due to the device being eSIM-only, and eSIM adoption and infrastructure in China lag behind that of other countries.

The iPhone Air also launched later in China than elsewhere due to regulatory issues surrounding its eSIM-only design.

More evidence of Touch ID

In a post on social media this week, developer Pdfu shared more evidence that the iPhone Ultra will use Touch ID instead of Face ID. This, of course, has been widely reported as one of the device’s limitations, so this is just another layer of corroboration.

iPhone Ultra display crease

Apple set out to make a foldable iPhone without a visible crease, unlike other foldable phones on the market. In a report today, Bloomberg said the company has ultimately created a “crease that is far less visible than on currently shipping foldables.” To accomplish this, Apple developed an “advanced titanium-and-aluminum hinge system paired with custom cover glass.”

So even though it’s not completely creaseless, this is still something Apple “plans to highlight as a major competitive advantage.”

MagSafe

One conflicting rumor has been whether the iPhone Ultra will feature support for MagSafe. Mark Gurman had good news on this front in a recent interview. “MagSafe is there. All indications that I’ve heard are that MagSafe is in for this foldable phone,” he said.

Wrap up

title: Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work
snippet: Sam Altman, chief executive officer of OpenAI, during a media tour of the Stargate AI data center. | Bloomberg via Getty Images Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. One of the … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. Just days after a bitter row erupted over whether the company’s models benefited from unpublished work, a second mathematician has come forward accusing the AI giant of unethical and “dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data.

In a series of posts on Mastodon, mathematician Andreas Thom raised concerns that interactions he and his colleagues had had with the ChatGPT chatbot before OpenAI’s triumphant announcement may have contributed to its success in the field. One of the 10 results OpenAI announced with great fanfare last month involved Thom’s area of expertise, so-called non-sofic groups, and OpenAI acknowledged that their result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun.

Thom said he began reflecting on his own interactions with OpenAI after Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University, publicly questioned whether the company’s AI models had benefited from his use of OpenAI’s Codex. After OpenAI announced its non-sofic groups result, it was widely criticized in mathematical circles for failing to acknowledge recent contributions from Thom and Kun and the company quietly amended its writeup. Non-sofic groups are, roughly speaking, infinite mathematical structures that cannot be approximated by finite ones.

Thom said he was also struck by “OpenAI’s detailed command of our techniques,” which he said were neither the most obvious nor the most promising routes to a solution at the time. He said he wrote emails to OpenAI researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Mark Sellke, also a statistician at Harvard, to ask whether his interactions with ChatGPT were “part of the training data or accessible to the reasoning process” and could therefore have contributed to the result.

But the answer did not satisfy Thom, who said it only addressed whether his conversations with the chatbot could be accessed directly, not whether they had entered into the vast pools of training data the company uses to improve its models. “No such qualification, explanation, or evidence was given,” he wrote. “I take this as dishonesty to say the least.”

Thom said researchers aren’t equipped to reverse-engineer OpenAI’s training pipeline to figure out whether their work has been used or not. “Only OpenAI has the relevant data for that.” If the company is going to deny doing this, he said the responsibility is on them to prove that by disclosing all necessary datasets and clarifying various settings and terms setting out how it uses data.

OpenAI’s reluctance to conclusively rule out any use of user data echoes the way it defended its recent Millennium Prize breakthrough, both in its public messaging and its communications with Buckmaster — who was working on the problems with Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge in a personal capacity. In the blog post announcing the Navier-Stokes solution, which concerns the movement of fluids, OpenAI flatly denied using any specific user data: “We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem.”

But it would not conclusively rule out an indirect influence: “While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠.” Thom said it is the same obfuscatory distinction the company drew in its communications with him. “De-identification may remove a name; it does not remove the intellectual content of a mathematical idea,” he said.

In light of recent events, Thom said “Sellke’s categorical answer was, at minimum, unjustifiably broad and materially misleading; looking back it was plainly dishonest.”

Thom said it “would be ethically indefensible” if nonpublic research supplied by users helped to improve models that the company then used to race those very same users to publication, without consent, proper disclosure, or credit.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

His comments add to mounting unease over OpenAI in mathematical circles at what should be a moment of triumph for the company. Its announced solution to one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems is an extraordinary achievement that, should it be verified, few would deny. But this was complicated by the unusual circumstances OpenAI said led it to pursue the problem in the first place: It heard rumors online that other researchers had made major progress and thought it would try too.

The ongoing incident has left a sour taste in mathematicians’ mouths. Numerous researchers told The Verge they worry behavior like this will push the field into a more secretive state if mathematicians know that even rumors they are close to a big breakthrough could ignite a race with a well-resourced tech giant eager for glory.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Robert Hart

title: LG Denies Its Televisions Record Ambient Conversations for Ad Targeting
snippet: Researchers say that they exploited the microphone and content recognition features of an LG TV to listen to user conversations.
fullText:
LG on Wednesday denied that its TVs eavesdrop on customers after a gaming site appeared to show that the TVs can be used to listen to conversations in real time.

Also read: You’ve Heard About Smart Home Hacking: Here’s How It Works and How Likely It Is

“The claims made in the recently published video are not true,” an LG representative said in a statement to CNET. The company said LG TVs process voice data only when the voice button on the remote control is pressed and held or the TV’s “wake word” is uttered by the customer.

“Other than these instances, the TVs do not collect or record ambient conversations,” the statement said.

The company said that if the device doesn’t recognize the wake word, no voice data is transmitted to the server, and that the wake word is detected locally and immediately deleted.

Gaming site GamersNexus reported earlier this week that LG TVs can be hacked by a third party to become listening devices, even if a user disables the onboard microphone.

GamersNexus says it used a man-in-the-middle attack on an LG G5 TV to enable it to listen to audio from a remote computer, and says the TV was able to record audio without the TV being connected to the internet. In a man-in-the-middle attack, the hacker intercepts sensitive data by putting itself in between two other entities, such as a user and a web application.

The 2-hour video, compiled with the help of the Level1Techs site, says that hackers could listen to a USB webcam or an HDMI input even when the physical switch located next to the mic was switched off. It said this alleged vulnerability was possible due to the TV’s Automatic Content Recognition feature, which transmits viewing habits and voice requests back to LG.

“LG TVs are able to be utilized as eavesdropping listening devices, in part because of the advertising functionality that’s built into them. We were able to retrieve plain text transcripts of a voice conversation and inputs from the TV,” the video says.

The video also reports that the researchers were able to see a list of the IP addresses of all the other devices on the network, even if those devices weren’t connected to the TV.

“LG TVs feature the ability to scan for and connect to nearby devices on the same network. This is a standard function commonly provided by smart TVs and smart home devices,” an LG statement said.

The LG TV microphone, like many smart devices, is designed to listen for a wake word or phrase such as “Hi TV” and then perform the requested task. 

Meanwhile, Apple says its new “always listening” Audio Intelligence feature doesn’t let the company access users’ raw audio. 

Almost all TVs and streaming devices use automatic content recognition to target ads to customers based on viewing habits, but users can usually disable this feature in the device’s settings.

It’s worth noting that any smart speaker will record audio for a limited time after hearing its wake word. If you somehow disclose your Social Security number during that time, for instance, it will be recorded and transmitted.

Smart-home attacks are rare, but the researchers recommend removing LG TVs from your network to prevent unauthorized data collection and privacy breaches. Unprotected computers and routers, not televisions, are the most likely targets for hackers.

title: How Tim Cook shaped Apple’s foldable iPhone, and what it may cost
snippet: On the eve of Apple’s special event, Bloomberg is out with a new report detailing the decade-long foldable iPhone development. The report highlights former Apple CEO Tim Cook’s involvement in the project. Plus, details on how much the foldable iPhone could cost. more…
fullText:
On the eve of Apple’s special event, Bloomberg is out with a new report detailing the decade-long foldable iPhone development. 

The report highlights former Apple CEO Tim Cook’s involvement in the project. Plus, details on how much the foldable iPhone could cost. 

Mark Gurman says Apple engineers started iPhone Fold development around 2016. In 2020, Cook returned home from a trip to China and was “unusually energized” about foldable phones. He reportedly pushed Apple’s hardware teams to accelerate work on the company’s first foldable. 

Typically, Cook “stayed away from the conception of new products.” Therefore, his involvement in the foldable iPhone’s development gave the project added weight:

Cook’s enthusiasm helped change the direction of the work to something that could be more mainstream. Rather than begin with a foldable iPad, Apple turned its focus to creating a foldable iPhone. “Tim was the earliest and biggest champion of this,” one of the people said. “He saw them everywhere in Asia and said Apple needed to play in this space.”

In terms of pricing for the foldable iPhone, which everyone inside Apple refers to as the iPhone Ultra, the company originally targeted an entry-level price of $1,999. Most recently, however, rising component costs have shifted that goal to $2,199. 

More recently, Apple has discussed pricing the foldable product as high as $2,199, according to one of the people, who said various options have been considered in recent weeks and that the memory shortage has led Apple to blow past its cost goals.

Some larger-storage configurations of the device could approach $3,000. Compare that with the standard iPhone, which currently starts at $799, or the iPhone 17 Pro, which begins at $1,099.

Apple is expected to debut the iPhone Ultra tomorrow. 9to5Mac will be inside Steve Jobs Theater to cover everything in depth.

The Apple Lakeside store, located in a large out-of-town shopping center in Essex, England, is set to reopen on Saturday after a major redesign.

There are a total of 39 Apple stores in the UK, with recent or current redesigns and relocations for six of them. Lakeside and Regent Street, London, have been upgraded; redesign work is currently underway at Birmingham and Southampton; whole Trafford and Touchwood were relocated. The Basingstoke store will close later this year.

title: iPhone Duo Memes: The Duolingo Owl Is Hooting Mad That Apple Stole His Name
snippet: The new phone will set you back some $1,999, but enjoying the memes is totally free.
fullText:
Apple announced its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, at Wednesday’s “Surprise and shine” event. It’s a huge product drop from an iconic tech company, so naturally, people have thoughts to share. The reactions are pretty funny.

Many tech observers thought Apple might name its folding phone the iPhone Ultra, but the company went with Duo instead. That ruffled the feathers of a certain fictional owl: Duo, the mascot of language app Duolingo. (Duo’s used to wading into newsy issues — he once pretended to be murdered by a Tesla Cybertruck.)

	

			

“What an exciting Apple event!” Duo snarked on X. “I sure hope my brand doesn’t get infringed upon.”

what an exciting Apple event! i sure hope my brand doesn’t get infringed upon 💚

— Duolingo (@duolingo) September 9, 2026

Welp, guess what, Duo?

The name news led to a witty monologue of Duo discovering the news. “it’s called the iPhone WHAT??? oh god oh god my SEO my SEO.” 

Duo even went the “Can I speak to your manager?” route, reaching out to new Apple CEO John Ternus to complain.

One X user suggested the app “just change your name to Foldlingo, since they should have just called it the iPhone Fold/iFold to begin with.”

Just change your name to Foldlingo, since they should have just called it the iPhone Fold/iFold to begin with.

— daytrailing (@daytrailing) September 9, 2026

Samsung: Apple’s reheating its leftovers

Apple rival Samsung, which released its first folding phone, the Galaxy Fold, in 2019, and has been bringing out new models ever since, commiserated with Duo, writing, “I’m so sorry, @DuoLingo. They copied us too #Solidarity.”

Samsung was a little more bitter than Duo, though. It also posted, with Apple unmentioned but clearly implied: “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”

Let us know when you're done reheating our leftovers 😉

— Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) September 9, 2026

While a folding phone is new to Apple, that’s not the case with phone-makers in general. Google, Motorola and Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei are already there. This led to jokes about Apple being late to the party.

“Excited for Apple to finally invent the folding smart phone today!” snarked one Bluesky user.

Wrote another: “Can’t WAIT for Apple to call their folding phone ‘revolutionary’ a DECADE into the folding phone market.”

‘We have a folding phone at home’

Shark researcher David Shiffman brought the Apple news back to his topic of interest, posting a photo of a small, curled-up shark with the dialogue: “Me: Can we get the new Apple Duo folding phone? Mom: We have a folding phone at home.”

‘Folds like we did on Lake Ontario’

More than one person used the iPhone Duo announcement to jab at Apple Maps for renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America. President Donald Trump signed an executive order last month to get US agencies to relabel the lake, which straddles the US-Canada border.

‘Cracking noises ensue’

Although folding phones aren’t new, some people joked about the sheer idea of folding up a phone. Wrote one, “Welp. Apple has normalized folding your phone. [cracking noises ensue].”

And another wrote, “just a reminder that apple CANNOT stop you from folding your current phone in half.”

Hand over $2,000, please

The iPhone Duo doesn’t come cheap: Its starting price is $1,999, and a fully tricked-out version soars to more than $3,000, which naturally led to more jokes.

“Wow, I could buy a PS5 and a Switch 2 and still have plenty of money left to not get an XBox,” wrote one Bluesky user.

And another Bluesky user offered a sarcastic solution to the price problem, writing, “buying the left half of an iphone duo until i can afford the right half of an iphone duo.”

title: Apple Reference Photo Lets iPhone Photographers Prove What’s Real
snippet: The new iPhone 18 Pro gets a photo-authentication feature to show that a photo hasn’t been altered with AI.
fullText:
Apple spent much of its “Surprise and shine” fall event breathlessly detailing the new AI capabilities of Apple Intelligence and the new Photographic Styles with the iPhone 18 Pro. The new features offer greater AI-assisted abilities to change the look of a photo. In the midst of all this, the company also introduced a defense against AI-generated and -altered images.

The iPhone 18 Pro adds a new Reference camera mode, which digitally authenticates that an image you took with the phone hasn’t been altered with AI. It creates an unalterable reference photo captured by the phone’s sensor. The phone sends sensor signatures and other identifiers to Private Cloud Compute to authenticate the reference photo.

Reference photos are saved in the Photos app next to the main image that can be edited so you can see the original and edited versions next to one another to compare the two. One note: you can’t create, say, a reference screenshot. It works only with images captured from the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera and not screenshots you take with the phone.

Apple also announced support for Google’s SynthID standard for authenticating images. Together, these tools give photographers and journalists ways to verify their work. And fishermen now have verifiable evidence that the fish they caught really was that big.

title: Apple made fun of Android apps on foldables, but iPhone Duo has the same problem [Gallery]
snippet: Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing. more…
fullText:
Apps have always been a problem for foldable displays and, while they’ve gotten a lot better, there’s always room for improvement. Apple was already going to hold an advantage here, as we’ve previously discussed, but a moment during the iPhone Duo’s unveiling sticks out – Apple made fun of how Android foldables sometimes letterbox apps on the inner display, but it turns out that iOS does exactly the same thing.

In the early moments of the iPhone Duo’s announcement, new Apple CEO John Ternus called out “others” who have already launched foldables, with a background video showing the age-old problem – letterboxed apps.

To quote new Apple CEO John Ternus:

Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together. This results in a square screen that’s poorly suited for the way people use them. Scrolling through vertical content feels compromised, and movies are boxed in by oversized black bars, making a larger screen feel much smaller.

Here’s the clip:

	

This was a pretty major problem in the early days of Android foldables. While Android apps have always been good at scaling, the unique form factors of those early days often found weird middle grounds or, even more frequently, apps just hadn’t been updated to be viewed on anything other than an ordinary smartphone display aspect ratio. At the time, it was a wise move on Google’s part, but the problem has been going away thanks to a push on Google’s part as well as the wider adoption of these form factors. Heck, Android foldables got a tablet layout for Instagram before the iPad did. 

So, while watching today’s event, my reaction to that little dig was that Apple is just finding old problems to make Android look bad, again – not exactly new behavior. 

But then our sister site 9to5Mac dug up Apple’s own documentation of how iOS 27.1 will handle apps on the foldable display and, lo and behold, Apple is doing the same thing.

If an app isn’t updated to support iOS 27, it gets boxed in with black bars on either side, showing a portrait view of the app instead. If it isn’t ready for iOS 27.1, it still can’t take up the display area off to the side where the sidebar is.

This was my actual reaction.

As mentioned, Apple has an app advantage in that iOS developers will likely be much quicker to adopt this new form factor. I’m already jealous of that Slack app Apple briefly showed; Slack, you literally had that on Android half a decade ago, bring it back.

Thoughts?

title: iPhone Duo hands-on videos reveal Android foldable pain points we know too well
snippet: Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease. more…
fullText:
via Brian Tong			
	

Apple has a track record of waiting until the kinks get worked out before it tries its own hand at new devices, but hands-on videos of the iPhone Duo are already starting to show that Apple suffers from some of the same pain points other manufacturers like Samsung do, like the beloved screen crease.

Samsung has faced some backlash over the years as its continued to develop the Galaxy Z Fold line, as it rightfully should. Flaws exist on these $1,800+ phones, like an ever-present visible crease down the hinge line on the inner display or a less-than-invisible under-display camera.

It turns out Apple hasn’t been entirely successful at perfecting those flaws in its own design. Early hands-on videos are already starting to go live after Apple’s event in Cupertino, and more are very much on the way. Videos like this one from Brian Tong show some interesting details Apple’s keynote left out.

For one, the iPhone Duo’s inner screen is anti-reflective, but it comes off as matte more than anything. It’s a massive contrast from the outer display, which is made from Ceramic Shield 2. Sitting in stark contrast to that matte inner display is the under-display camera, which Apple showed off several times during its keynote. It’s something Samsung dropped from the Galaxy Z Fold design when it launched the latest models, for one reason or another.

	

The iPhone Duo’s under-display camera has no matte finish, likely because it functions as a Face ID sensor. That change in finish only serves to highlight a camera that’s supposed to be hidden from view.

Of course, it was never going to be completely hidden, and Apple’s pre-release footage and renders rightfully showed off a camera that was clearly hiding under an area of fewer pixels. Samsung used the same approach in the Galaxy Z Fold 7, but it’s always been just as noticeable. In reality, the camera seems far more noticeable because of the differing reflectivity.

Beyond that, we get a good look at the iPhone Duo’s inner screen crease. It was expected Apple would refine its foldable’s inner display design so a crease would be far less visible than current Android options, but the crease looks just as visible as it does on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra. Apple is using a two-layer flexible glass, which helps prevent a buildup in tension that would cause materials to bind up in the middle.

Still, the crease is a factual aspect of the iPhone Duo. That isn’t to say Apple hasn’t done a good job of hiding it, but it’s an unfortunate aspect of foldable phones for the time being.

The new foldable’s specs also reveal its IP68 water and dust resistant rating is also expected to be temporary, similar to the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

If Apple excels anywhere with the iPhone Duo its in how it designed iOS 27 around the new phone. Compared to where Android and One UI are in their respective builds, Apple’s approach feels much more purposeful for a phone that forces you to look at it a different way. It’s only a matter of time before Android manufacturers begin to copy some of these UX design choices. It introduces welcome competition.

title: Hands-on with Siri Modular, watchOS 27’s new Apple Watch face
snippet: watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 includes one new watch face: Siri Modular. The new face is available on both Apple Watch Series and Ultra models. However, the version on Ultra has a few more customization options. Check it out.

Both versions of Siri Modular use the same layout. There’s a top center line complication, the time (centered), a wide Siri suggestion widget, and a row of three circular complications.

Apple Watch Ultra also supports bezel options, adding one more way to configure the new watch face. 

First, three style options let you adjust the height of the clock. The first option features the tallest clock and three circular complications. The second style is a compact clock with the wide Siri suggestion widget and three circular complications. The third style is a medium clock with a wide complication.

All three modes support displaying the top line complication. None of the modes support displaying the current seconds as part of the clock. 

Both Series and Ultra also include font options for the clock. However, Ultra is only an option on Apple Watch Ultra hardware. Series models only offer Modern, Classic, and Rounded.

Meanwhile, the Ultra includes those bezel options I mentioned. These are like other Ultra-exclusive watch faces.

Lastly, there’s the option to set the watch face color, including lots of new options like Dark Bronze, Radiant Gold, and other new choices.

Siri Modular is part of the new watchOS 27 update, included in today’s release candidate software.

title: iPhone Duo: Here are all the little details you might have missed
snippet: iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is the name of Apple’s new foldable model, and it’s perhaps the most fascinating new model since the original iPhone. Here are all the little iPhone Duo details you might have missed.

iPhone Duo tidbits from Apple’s announcement and website

Apple’s first foldable iPhone was unveiled today ahead of becoming available to order next month.

If you’re looking to buy a new iPhone, you might be very interested in the Duo, but are unsure if it’s right for you.

Read more: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference

The tentpole features of iPhone Duo are pretty clear: it’s a foldable, with two displays, great cameras and battery life, and plenty of unique form factor advantages.

But there were a variety of smaller iPhone Duo details revealed both in today’s announcement and on Apple’s website afterwards.

Camera features

Software exclusives: iPhone Duo has several exclusive camera features available in software, like Smart Take, Kid Cue, and Duo Preview. But most notably, its Main camera lacks the variable aperture feature of iPhone 18 Pro.

Under-display camera: A first in the iPhone, the folding display of iPhone Duo has an under-display camera for a cutout-free inner screen.

Selfie cameras are very different: That under-display camera isn’t nearly as capable as the Center Stage front camera on the outer display, so you’ll want to use the outer camera when possible.

Buttons

iPhone Duo has a Camera Control button, but is missing the Action button that’s been available on other iPhone models for several years now.

Displays

There’s a nano‑texture finish only on the folding iPhone Duo display. You won’t find nano-texture on the outer screen.

Apple Pencil

Apple says iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil later this year on both the inner and folding displays. However, currently only the USB-C Pencil model is supported, not the Apple Pencil Pro.

Release Date

Unlike iPhone 18 Pro, which goes on sale later this week, iPhone Duo won’t be available to order until October 16. It then ships to all users a week later on October 23.

iOS 27.1

It’s probably not surprising, since iPhone Duo doesn’t ship until late October, but Apple says the new model will run iOS 27.1 when it arrives.

eSIM only

	

You won’t be able to buy an iPhone Duo with physical SIM anywhere in the world. Even in China, where users largely prefer physical SIMs, the iPhone Duo will be eSIM-only.

title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone Duo: Here’s every key difference
snippet: Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model. more…
fullText:
Today Apple unveiled three flagship new iPhone models: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the foldable iPhone Duo. Here’s an overview of the key differences between each model.

Form factor and dimensions: Foldable vs traditional

It’s the most obvious difference, but should be stated regardless. With iPhone Duo you get a very different form factor: it’s a foldable device. With iPhone 18 Pro, you get a traditional iPhone experience.

If you’ve never used a foldable, it’s hard to explain the difference in how each model might feel in practice. But generally speaking, with iPhone Duo you get essentially an iPhone and iPad in one device. The displays are unique shapes and sizes compared to a traditional iPhone though, which may take some adjustment.

Here is how each model’s dimensions compare:

iPhone Duo might seem more sleek than iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it ultimately weighs slightly more.

Displays: Dual vs single in varying sizes

iPhone Duo has two displays: a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch folding display.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you can choose from the standard 6.3-inch size or 6.9-inch Pro Max model.

So with the Duo, you can enjoy a “small iPhone” experience while also having the option of a larger inner screen than what iPhone 18 Pro Max can offer.

iPhone Duo’s folding display comes with a nano-texture finish, a first in an iPhone.

Cameras: Clear advantage for iPhone 18 Pro

Cameras are one of the most important iPhone features. And in this department, iPhone 18 Pro is the clear winner.

iPhone 18 Pro has the new 48MP Main camera with variable aperture. iPhone Duo lacks the variable aperture feature, so its Main camera lags behind the Pro line.

With iPhone 18 Pro, you also get the Telephoto camera that’s missing from iPhone Duo.

In terms of software features, each model has its own unique exclusives:

iPhone Duo: Smart Take, Kid Cue, Duo Preview

iPhone 18 Pro: Smart focus tracking, Pro controls, Apple Reference Image

iPhone 18 Pro also exclusively supports ProRes video recording up to 4K at 60 fps with external recording, a “studio-quality four-mic array,” Spatial video recording at 1080p at 30 fps, Spatial photos, ProRes RAW, Genlock, and more.

Battery: Excellent battery life on all models

Because iPhone Duo has two displays, its quoted battery life varies depending on which display you’re using. But overall, Apple is promising strong battery life on both the Duo as well as iPhone 18 Pro.

Here are Apple’s quoted numbers:

iPhone Duo outer display: Up to 44 hours

iPhone Duo folding display: Up to 31 hours

iPhone 18 Pro: Up to 36 hours

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Up to 45 hours

Everyone’s use patterns will differ, but if you split the difference between the two iPhone Duo battery estimates, you’re looking at around 38 hours in average video playback.

All the other big and small differences: Face ID, buttons, software, Apple Pencil, more

Authentication differs between iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, with the former using Touch ID and the latter Face ID.

iPhone Duo does not have an Action button, but does offer Camera Control.

iPhone Duo comes with several multitasking advantages in iOS 27, like the ability to use apps in Split View and have unique landscape views. It also has other fun software additions like a partially-folded StandBy mode.

Apple Pencil (USB-C model) will be supported on iPhone Duo later this year, another advantage over iPhone 18 Pro.

A new C2 modem is included in both iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, but curiously not iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Colors for iPhone 18 Pro are Burgundy, Glacier, Black, and Silver. iPhone Duo only offers two colors: Star White and Night Sky.

Finally, design materials differ: iPhone 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design, while iPhone Duo uses titanium.

Pricing and availability: Big gaps in both

Pricing is another major difference between Apple’s new models. Here are starting prices for 256GB models:

iPhone Duo: $1,999

iPhone 18 Pro: $1,199

iPhone 18 Pro Max: $1,299

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available for pre-order this Saturday and ship next Friday, September 18. Meanwhile, iPhone Duo won’t be available for pre-order until October 16, and ships October 23.

title: iPhone 18 Pro battery life: how much better is the battery compared to iPhone Duo and iPhone 17 Pro
snippet: Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … more…
fullText:
Apple has just announced the new flagship iPhone lineup, featuring iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. One of the biggest improvements is battery life. 

In fact, Apple says this generation represents the biggest jump in battery life iPhone history ever. So let’s break down what’s changed … 

Apple says the boosts to battery life on the new iPhones is achieved through a combination of new physical internal battery designs, improved efficiency due to the new A20 Pro chip, and system software optimizations.

Obviously, real-world battery life will be put to the test when reviewers get their hands on the new iPhones. For now, we can go off the spec sheets which we can demonstrate the relative increases. 

Apple provides battery life stats in terms of hours of streaming video playback to compare with earlier models. 

iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro battery life

For reference, iPhone 17 Pro touts up to 30 hours streaming video playback and iPhone 17 Pro Max gets up to 35 hours streaming video playback. 

With iPhone 18 Pro, the claimed longevity is 33 hours streaming video playback. That’s a 10% improvement compared to iPhone 17 Pro.

For the Max size, battery life goes from 35 hours to a claimed 40 hours streaming video playback on iPhone 18 Pro Max. That’s an increase of about 14%. 

Apple also provided a new battery life metric for the 18 series that attempts to more closely represent real-world usage, than just video playback. This includes a variety of activities like messaging, taking photos, playing games, web browsing, and more, based on what it knows people actually use their iPhones for. 

On that benchmark, iPhone 18 Pro Max will apparently be able to last for 30 hours on a single charge. iPhone 18 Pro achieves 24 hours under the same conditions.

The above figures are based on the iPhone 18 Pro models with eSIM, such as those sold inside the United States. The models sold in many international markets still accommodate a physical SIM tray, which impinges on battery life a little: Apple says the non-eSIM versions get 2 hours less streaming video playback. 

iPhone Duo battery life

Obviously, a lot of attention today is on the shiny new iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone. The Duo actually incorporates two battery cells, one in each side of the device. But it also has to power two displays, including the inner 7.8-inch display that is the biggest ever in an iPhone by a significant margin.

However, its claimed battery life is still respectable. Apple claims users can expect 26 hours streaming video playback when using the large inner display, and up to 37 hours when using the outer display. Assuming heavy usage of the inner display, the Duo’s battery life is roughly equivalent to the iPhone 17 Pro — based on these published numbers.

We’ll know more exactly how the iPhone Duo fares in terms of all-day battery life when people start getting them in their hands. While the iPhone 18 Pro goes up for preorder this weekend, the Duo does not go on sale until October 23, so we’ve still got to wait a little bit for hands-on impressions.

title: watchOS 27 upgrade coming to Apple Watch this month
snippet: watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device. more…
fullText:
watchOS 27 is coming this month, and now we have an official release date. Apple says we can expect the Apple Watch software update on Monday, September 14. The Apple Watch software update brings Siri AI, new ways to launch apps, and more changes to the device.

Siri AI is the biggest addition, giving Apple Watch a dedicated Siri app and a more capable assistant for answering questions. Conversations also sync across supported Apple devices.

As I wrote last week, Siri AI had a rough summer in beta, but watchOS 27 beta 8 brought a major improvement in my testing. Everyday requests finally felt responsive again, while broader knowledge questions made the watch more useful without always requiring the iPhone.

However, watchOS 27 also removes some familiar features. Walkie-Talkie is gone, and double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer provides its previous multitasking shortcut.

Pressing the Digital Crown now opens a dynamic app grid with suggested apps and Siri. The full app launcher remains available, but takes another step to reach.

Other additions include a unified Find My app, expanded Smart Stack suggestions, and improvements to Workout Buddy.

watchOS 27 supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later, Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later, and Apple Watch SE 3.

title: No iPhone Ultra today? Three possible explanations …
snippet: It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo. If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … more…
fullText:
It was widely expected that the first foldable iPhone set to be launched later today would be named the iPhone Ultra. However, a report yesterday said that the device will instead be called the iPhone Duo.

If accurate, it’s an interesting development as it might potentially point to the company reserving the Ultra suffix for a completely different future model … 

Opinion pieces in which I muse about possible future developments are by their very nature speculative, and this one perhaps more than most. When it comes to hard facts, the only thing we can say for sure is that Apple has used the Ultra label to mean the top-level offering in three contexts:

Apple Watch Ultra

Apple Silicon chips (eg. M5 Ultra)

CarPlay Ultra

It’s been speculated that the company plans to expand the use of the Ultra moniker to a range of new products. This was expected to include the iPhone Ultra and the MacBook Ultra.

Specifically, the iPhone Ultra label was reportedly going to be used for the foldable phone being launched later today. As of yesterday, however, we are expecting this to be named the iPhone Duo – so what’s up? I can see three possibilities.

1. The least interesting reason

The least interesting explanation would be that Apple isn’t using the Ultra label because the foldable phone isn’t the ultimate iPhone. It’s a device with a unique feature, but it’s expected to be inferior to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in several ways. If all the reports pan out, it won’t have a variable aperture lens on the main camera, and will also lack a telephoto camera; it won’t have Face ID; and it won’t match the battery life of the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Logically then, it shouldn’t be called the iPhone Ultra. But Apple hasn’t always followed the logic when it comes to product names – for example, the MacBook Air weighing more than the 12-inch MacBook back in 2015, and the Mac Studio being more powerful than the Mac Pro in 2022. So while this is one possible explanation, it’s far from a definitive one.

2. The Ultra will be the 20th anniversary model

A related possibility is that the iPhone Ultra label is slated for the 20th anniversary model expected next year, taking a significant step closer to that long-term ‘single slab of glass’ vision. If that combined the slickest design with iPhone Pro capabilities, then that would indeed be worthy of the name.

3. There’s something even bigger in the works

The most exciting possibility is that Apple won’t be done with all-new additions to the iPhone range after the launch of the slab of glass (iPhone Glass?), and that the iPhone Ultra label is being reserved for a completely different model – one that really would sit at the top of the lineup in every respect.

I won’t get into speculation about what form that might take, though it will surprise nobody when I say my own hopes would center around significantly superior camera capabilities, starting with a much larger sensor. 

Where do you stand? Which of the three explanations do you think most likely? Or do you have a better idea of your own? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Motorola is finally making a new Wear OS watch and it’s not called the Moto 360
snippet: It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra. more…
fullText:
It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra.

Rewinding the clock, the Moto 360 is perhaps still the most iconic Android smartwatch of all time. It was the poster child for the early days of “Android Wear,” but Motorola threw in the towel after a couple of generations. There was a brief revival of the Moto 360 name in 2020, but even that faded away – and the licensing deal behind it is likely why Motorola isn’t using that name now.

Motorola hasn’t stopped making smartwatches in that time, but they’ve all been based on an RTOS, making them fall into the category of smartwatches that are focused on health tracking and battery life at the expense of more useful notifications and access to a proper app ecosystem. The most recent attempt ended up cloning Wear OS’ design, despite the limitations.

Now, Motorola has a new smartwatch – the Moto Watch Ultra.

	

The $349 smartwatch offers up a Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chipset, 2GB of RAM, and 32GB of storage, all used to power Wear OS 6. We’ll have to wait and see if Motorola has made any customizations to the UI here, but re-entering the Wear OS ecosystem is a pretty big deal. Motorola does note that its Qira AI assistant is on board.

The Ultra has a 1.5-inch pOLED display in a 46mm chassis that’s 12.1mm thick – though Motorola’s images make it seem a lot thicker. The display is covered in Gorilla Glass 3 and the body is stainless steel with a brushed finish in silver or gunmetal finishes. There are four strap options, including both silicone and leather, but you can use any 22mm band as there are no fancy connectors, just a traditional spring pin. There’s NFC support for Google Wallet, IP68 + 5ATM dust/water resistance, and LTE support too. Motorola claims 2 days of use from the 550 mAh battery inside – Pixel Watch 5 (45mm) has a 465 mAh battery, for comparison. Charging is handled by a magnetic dock that connects over USB-C.

On the fitness side, Motorola is working with Polar – another brand that tried and has since left the Wear OS market – with features including activity goals, scores, and intensity zones, as well as inactivity alerts, energy sources, and wellness features around breathing and sleep. 

The Moto Watch Ultra will be available unlocked starting on September 10 for $349, with a debut on Verizon on September 24. Other carriers including T-Mobile, Metro, and AT&T will follow later on. 

Beyond the Watch Ultra, Motorola is today also launching a Swarovski version of the base Razr (2026). This special release has the same specs, but with a new dark grey case that has Crystals by Swarovski embedded in the back. It also costs $100 more at $899 and is also launching on September 10.

title: Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy
snippet: Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand. more…
fullText:
Decked out with a gimbal and shockingly good camera, the Robot Phone is one of the weirdest devices to come out of Honor. Even if you ignore the fact that it’s limited to China, Honor can’t keep up with demand.

When Honor began teasing a device that hid a fully functional gimbal and a 200MP camera tucked away in its camera bar, it truly seemed like an AI-driven fever dream of what future phones might look like.

Having played around with one this past week, I’m not distancing myself from that thought. Still, I can’t deny it’s a ridiculously cool idea, and a now fully functional Android phone the company launched last month.

Honor’s Robot Phone is aimed at creators more than anyone, for obvious reasons. The 200MP camera sits inside the device’s camera bar, which shouldn’t get you any weird looks if you use it in its retracted form. But as soon as you hit a certain dedicated camera app button and move the physical protective cover, that massive camera rises out of the Robot Phone’s rear panel as if it belonged in a horror movie.

	

The additional 50MP ultrawide and 200MP periscope camera do not move.

The camera app leaves controls up to the user, with full pan/tilt controls and a wide range to cover just about anything in view. It can be flipped 180 degrees for selfie capture, or used outward to record or capture the world in front of you.

Beyond that, Honor has packed some really cool film tools and recording formats. There are panning options and automatic spin controls to get neat shots you’d need to be really skilled to get with your regular old phone. The phone, being a product of Honor’s focus on AI, has object and person tracking. It works better than I anticipated during my short time with the phone, and stabilization was shockingly good for what is, again, a gimbal attached to a phone.

Its bag of tricks is huge, and it was a ton of fun to play around with. Honor pushes a little beyond simple camera tools with the AI-assisted mode, which is what some of the earliest teasers for the phone showcased. MagicOS has an AI assistant named “YOYO,” and it charges it with the ability to look around and gather digital information like a pair of smart glasses would.

It has its struggles when asking it questions in English instead of Chinese, but it’s a neat concept if a little unsettling.

Beyond the camera tools and mechanical gimbal, the Robot Phone brings many of the standard feature sets MagicOS 10 builds out for the manufacturer’s other devices. Overall, it’s a fun and interesting concept that deserves a ton of credit in what can often be a monotonous phone landscape.

At RMB 9,999 – nearly $1,500 – Honor’s Robot Phone is priced well, all things considered. That’s the running price for the 12/512GB configuration. The 16GB/1TB model nears $2,000.

But you probably couldn’t buy it if you wanted to. On top of being launched for the Chinese market with no global launch expected, Honor shared that the device reached sales targets almost immediately. It seemingly kept expectations low, and now has to catch up with demand while supplies are difficult to get a hand on for reasonable prices.

Again, I only messed around with the Robot Phone for a short time, but it ended up being one of those hands-on sessions that reminded me phones can be exceptionally fun. I’m not saying every phone should have an extending gimbal and overkill camera setup, but it’s kind of cool that the option exists – even if heavily limited.

title: Where Google Wallet state IDs are available on Android
snippet: States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android. more…
fullText:
States across the US are slowly rolling out support for adding your driver’s license or ID to the Google Wallet app on Android.

Update 9/5

How to add your state ID on Android

Open the Google Wallet app on Android 9+

Tap the “plus” button next to “View more” at the bottom

Choose “ID & personal info” and then “Driver’s license or state ID” 

Select your state and follow the instructions

The process involves taking a picture of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of yourself for verification: a “photo from this video will be submitted to your ID issuer.” 

Once approved, the ID will appear below the carousel of payment methods alongside other passes. The order can be rearranged, while you can remotely remove the ID online if your phone is missing: myaccount.google.com > Personal Info > Manage IDs.

	

What Google Wallet state IDs are supported

Arizona (Rolled out October 2023)

Arkansas (Rolled out October 2025)

California (Rolled out August 2024)

Colorado (Rolled out October 2023)

Georgia (Rolled out October 2023)

Iowa (Rolled out June 2025)

Maryland (Rolled out December 2022)

Montana (Rolled out August 2025)

New Mexico (Rolled out December 2024)

North Dakota (Rolled out October 2025)

[New] Ohio (Rolled out September 2026)

Puerto Rico (Rolled out October 2025)

Where state IDs are coming next

Google previously said to expect support in the following places:

West Virginia (Upcoming availability announced April 2025)

Where you can use state IDs

The primary place you can use this digital ID is at TSA checkpoints in some US airports. There are two ways to do so, starting with tapping your phone at the NFC terminal. You then review the information that will be shared with the TSA and authenticate with device unlock. There’s also a QR code method that requires opening the ID in Google Wallet. 

Officially, you still have to carry the physical ID card at all times.

Some apps, like from car rental services, are beginning to accept digital IDs for identity and age verification. On mobile, if an app or website requests your age, it’s as simple as confirming (and authenticating) that you want to share this information with a system-level prompt/sheet. On desktop web, the experience involves scanning a QR code. 

Google wants to make it possible to do that “without any possibility to link back to a user’s personal identity” through what it calls Zero-Knowledge Proof. This technology will be open-sourced for anyone to use. 

Looking ahead, the IDs can be used at DMVs in Arizona, Georgia, Maryland, and New Mexico as part of “improved and streamlined customer experiences.”

	

Google is also working on letting you use digital IDs to “recover Amazon accounts, access online health services with CVS and MyChart by Epic, verify profiles on platforms like Uber and more.”

Using passport as REAL ID

Google in April pointed out how you can “use your ID pass created from a U.S. passport with TSA security for domestic travel at supported airports, even if you do not have a REAL ID driver’s license or state-issued ID.” This comes ahead of the May 7, 2025 deadline. 

To do so, open Google Wallet > Add to Wallet > ID pass. This three-step process involves taking a picture of your passport’s info page, and then scanning the security chip found inside the back cover of your passport. You also have to record a video of your face that Google will review “to make sure you’re a real person, and compare the video to your passport photo to make sure you’re the owner of the passport.”

The NFC and QR code instructions for using this digital passport ID are unchanged from above. You also have to keep the physical version on you when traveling. As a reminder, this won’t work internationally.

title: iPhone Handoff Will Let You Use One Number on Two Phones
snippet: The feature will be available with iOS 27, but will be limited to specific cellular carriers for now.
fullText:
Soon iPhone owners will be able to split their phone numbers between devices.

When iOS 27 launches next week, it will include a new feature called iPhone Handoff, which allows you to use the same number on two different phones, Apple said at Wednesday’s Surprise and Shine event. The announcement came alongside the reveals of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and the long-rumored, foldable iPhone Duo.

The feature was first mentioned briefly in June on a slide at the Worldwide Developers Conference, but the company didn’t give many details at the time. Reddit users reported seeing the feature on their devices last month, and a MacRumors user shared a video last week showing how the feature works. Apple says the feature will be available with the iOS 27, which will be released on Sept. 14. 

“iOS 27 improves connectivity with smarter transitions between cellular and Wi-Fi networks, and introduces iPhone Handoff that lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones,” an Apple speaker said. “The number is instantly active on whichever iPhone you pick up.”

But there is a catch: Apple says the iPhone Handoff feature will only be available initially with T-Mobile and Telecom Germany. Verizon and EE will get support by the end of the year, with “more carriers to follow.”

Once it’s available, you’ll be able to set up the Handoff feature in the Cellular section of the iPhone’s settings, according to the video posted to MacRumors. You’ll be prompted to hold the phones close to each other and pick which one keeps the main eSIM and which one gets the companion eSIM. Only the phone with the main eSIM will be allowed to change the Cellular Settings after that.

title: Apple’s Redesigned Health App Brings a Slew of New Features
snippet: Whether you want to know more about your longevity or how prepared your body is for the day ahead, Apple wants to be the one to tell you.
fullText:
Alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12, which have new health sensors called the Health Sensing System, Apple unveiled a revamped Health app with Apple Intelligence at its core during its “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday. It includes lab tests in partnership with Quest Diagnostics, movement assessments and new Insights and Longevity tabs. Plus, a readiness score on the Apple Watch to prepare you for the day ahead.

On the iPhone

On Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhones and iPads running the latest software, with certain features available only on iPhones, the redesigned Health app will be available later this year in US English, though no specific date was announced. Other languages will follow. 

The revamped Health app will have a new Longevity tab that includes a “health age” showing how your metrics compare to your actual, chronological age. This health age will take into account Apple Watch metrics, including resting heart rate, sleep, VO2 max and HRV (heart-rate variability), as well as any information from blood tests.

Health age will show your biological age versus your chronological age. Apple

Based on data from the iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods, clinical health records and third-party apps and devices, the Longevity tab will have a visualization showing seven areas of your health: heart health, sleep, mental well-being, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition. It will also show what’s affecting your long-term health.

The Longevity tab visualization. Apple

There will be another new tab, Insights, that uses Apple Intelligence to provide you with a timely summary of your health across vitals, fitness, heart, readiness, sleep and cycle tracking. This summary will update throughout the day. Under this tab, there will also be a For You section with personalized recommendations and relevant articles that appear based on your health data.

In addition to articles, there will be videos from Apple Health clinical experts offering insights into various aspects of health, such as what LDL cholesterol is and how to improve it, or how to improve balance. 

Using vision-based AI models on the iPhone and heart-rate data from the Apple Watch, the Health app will also have new movement tests that measure strength, balance, flexibility, movement mechanics and VO2 max. The latter test will require an Apple Watch, AirPods Pro 3 or a third-party heart-rate-sensing device. These tests are entirely on device, according to Apple, so no video is ever recorded, stored or shared. 

A person using their iPhone’s camera to complete a movement assessment.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Designed to provide preventive health information, a $119 Quest laboratory test panel including over 50 biomarkers is available for purchase directly through the Health app. Testing can then be completed at US Quest Diagnostics locations and includes measurements for height, weight, waist and hip circumferences, and blood pressure.

According to Quest Diagnostics, the company works with third-party providers that review and approve all lab test orders. At the user’s request and for no extra charge, these providers can discuss test results, which will be available in the Health app.

	

			

On the Apple Watch

On the Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, there’s the new readiness feature, which looks at your sleep score, recent activity, vitals and training load to provide a score from 0 to 10. This gives you one of four recommendations — recover, pace yourself, ready or go for it — to help you decide whether you should push yourself or take it easy during the day ahead. This score will update throughout the day, showing you which metrics are driving the chosen number.

How ready is your body for the day you currently have planned? That’s your readiness score.Apple/CNET Screenshot

This comes with the Watch Series 12’s new S11 chip and Health Sensing System, which Apple calls the most accurate heart-rate sensing in a wearable. This is based on a study involving over 1,000 people that compared the Apple Watch’s new heart-rate sensors with those of leading wearables. The new, larger, power-efficient green LEDs on the optical heart sensor will passively measure your heart rate every 5 seconds.

Heart-rate variability will also be measured up to 24 times more often and will be available to view in the Vitals overview and Heart Rate app. There will be two different HRVs shown: the “recovery HRV” for identifying stress and recovery, and the “overall HRV” for your broader health. Overnight vitals will also show recovery HRV measurements relative to your baseline.

Speaking of overnight vitals, there will be a new view focusing on daytime vitals. To spot changes between the two, you can toggle between overnight and daytime metrics.

Toggle between overnight and daytime vitals to compare the two.Apple/CNET Screenshot

Along with its heart-rate sensing, the smartwatch’s pedometer has been redesigned with new machine learning algorithms, so the Apple Watch Series 12, according to Apple, offers the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch. This is based on a 1,000-step accuracy test conducted by Apple and validated using video step counting. It compared the Series 12 with industry-leading smartwatches available as of July 2026.

Final thoughts

While similar features, including readiness scores and longevity insights, have already been launched by competitors like Oura Ring, Whoop and Fitbit, Apple’s are available without the extra charge. Unless you choose to pay for its new lab tests feature, which will cost you at least $119. 

What further sets Apple’s revamped Health app and accompanying features apart is that they’re backed by its sensors. According to CNET’s own testing earlier this year, the Apple Watch Series 11 was the most accurate heart-rate monitor during workouts.

title: BASF subsidiary sues Apple over alleged Face ID patent infringement
snippet: TrinamiX, a subsidiary of BASF, says Apple’s current implementation of Face ID is infringing on several of its patents. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TrinamiX, a subsidiary of BASF, says Apple’s current implementation of Face ID is infringing on several of its patents. Here are the details.

trinamiX says Face ID infringes seven patents

As first spotted by Reuters, trinamiX says newer versions of Apple’s Face ID, used in iPhones and iPad Pro models, infringe on seven of its patents.

In the lawsuit, trinamiX describes itself as a BASF spin-off that “has grown from a startup into an operating company that designs, develops, and commercializes advanced sensing technologies, including biometric imaging, three-dimensional vision, and near-infrared spectroscopy solutions for consumer and industrial applications.”

The patents trinamiX alleges Apple is infringing cover technology that can detect human skin during facial authentication, addressing an issue that, according to the lawsuit, allowed researchers to bypass the original version of Face ID using specially constructed 3D masks.

TrinamiX says its technology works by projecting a pattern of light onto a face and analyzing how that light reflects back to determine properties of the surface. Combined with 3D depth information, the company says this can distinguish human skin from materials used in photographs, masks, and other attempts to spoof facial authentication systems.

The seven patents listed in the lawsuit belong to two families:

Optical skin detection for face unlock (US Patents no. 12,530,925; 12,288,421; 12,456,334; 12,361,760)

Detector for identifying at least one material property (US Patents no. 12,298,394; 12,332,352; 12,461,238)

The lawsuit lists the following Apple devices among the “Accused Products”:

iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max

iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max

iPhone Air

11-inch iPad Pro (4th generation)

12.9-inch iPad Pro (6th generation)

11-inch iPad Pro M4 and M5

13-inch iPad Pro M4 and M5

TrinamiX also mentions unspecified “other infringing iPhone and iPad models,” although it is not immediately clear which products it refers to.

After presenting its case, trinamiX asks the court to find that Apple infringed its patents, block Apple from making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the accused products, and award the company damages and attorneys’ fees.

The company is requesting a jury trial in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max melds a classic ARRI camera with an iPhone-like look, launches this month
snippet: Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially shown off its next flagship, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, which has a pretty familiar-looking design, a massive camera powered by ARRI, and a release date that’s mere weeks away.

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is a new entry to the company’s flagship lineup, arriving on top of the Pro that was at the top of the list in prior years – “Pro Max” is a whole trend this year, it seems.

There’s still a ton we don’t know about this new device, but it’s clear that the camera is right at the center of the conversation.

A huge camera lens on the back takes up over half of the phone’s width, with two other cameras flanking it. They all sit on an iPhone-like camera island with an accent color on the bottom half of the device – this is a very obvious case of “inspiration” drawn from Apple’s latest, though Honor argues the arrangement “draws inspiration from the design language of one of ARRI’s most iconic cinema cameras.” 

	

Honor explains:

The design journey of the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max began with a simple question: How can a device inspire the same sense of creative possibility as cinema? For nearly a century, ARRI has helped filmmakers turn imagination into moving images. In 1937, the iconic ARRIFLEX cinema camera revolutionized professional filmmaking with its legendary “three-lens turret”—a design that brought function, precision, and industrial beauty into one form. Today, HONOR joins hands with ARRI to bring that timeless inspiration to the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max through an all-new camera architecture. (Image attached)

There’s clear inspiration in the camera design, but the phone as a whole certainly brings in some iPhone vibes, and it’s a wild change of pace from last year’s Honor Magic 8.

Specs on the cameras and the phone as a whole aren’t official yet, but ARRI is a part of the processing pipeline, just like on Honor’s Robot Phone. 

Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy

The signature color here is “Moss Green” and Honor says it will fully unveil the Magic 9 Pro Max on September 28. That’s only in China, though, with a global release presumably following later on.

snippet: Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. The firm says it expects Apple to take 25% of the entire market this year – and it may be the biggest player by the same time next year. fullText:
Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. The firm says it expects Apple to take 25% of the entire market this year – and it may be the biggest player by the same time next year.

In timing unlikely to be coincidental, the Xiaomi 18 Fold, leaked last month, is officially launching in China the day before Apple’s event …

iPhone Ultra set to have a major impact

While folding smartphones get a lot of attention, Counterpoint says that they currently only account for about 2% of the total market. This is expected to change significantly in the next 12 months, with 24% growth expected this year and a further 37% next.

The report says the market will see new products from Samsung, Apple, Huawei, Motorola, Honor, Google, Vivo, Oppo, and Xiaomi. The firm says Apple will be entering the market with a bang.

Apple’s entry will likely make an immediate impact. Counterpoint forecasts up to 6 million foldable iPhone shipments in 2026, giving Apple a 25% share of the global market and the No. 2 position, behind Samsung at 38% and ahead of Huawei at 22%.

It will be significant for Apple to achieve this ranking so quickly after entering the category, particularly given the relatively short selling window expected this year […] A full year of Apple sales will be a major driver, with Apple shipments expected to more than double and its share set to reach 40%.

That would exceed Samsung’s current 38% share.

Xiaomi launches 18 Fold on eve of Apple event

Xiaomi, which has made a name for itself by cloning many Apple products, appears to be seeking to do the same with its 18 Fold. 

The upcoming model, which shares the book format of the iPhone Ultra, which was leaked toward the end of last month before being shown off at IFA, has now officially launched on the eve of Apple’s Surprise and Shine event.

title: WhatsApp doubles music clip length for status updates
snippet: Users who post status updates on WhatsApp can now publish longer music clips, with the length limit doubled to 30 seconds. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Users who post status updates on WhatsApp can now publish longer music clips, with the length limit doubled to 30 seconds. Here are the details.

WhatsApp status gets a 30-second music clip limit

WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out support for music clips up to 30 seconds long in status updates.

Status updates are WhatsApp’s equivalent to Instagram Stories, and previously, posts containing music were limited to 15 seconds.

Now, users can select up to 30 seconds of a song to publish alongside a photo or share a music clip directly as a status update.

Here’s WABetaInfo on how to choose the music clip duration under the new 30-second limit:

After selecting a song from the music catalog, users can now see a clip duration picker in the music editor. The picker shows multiple options, up to 30 seconds. In this screen, users can scroll through them to select how many seconds of the song they want to include in the status. Although the maximum duration is 30 seconds, users can also choose a shorter clip if they prefer. Once they choose its duration, WhatsApp adds the music to the status update.

As is usually the case with WhatsApp’s server-side rollouts of new features, the new 30-second limit is still not available to everyone. However, WABetaInfo notes that some users on both iOS and Android are already seeing the new length limit. On iOS, the site lists WhatsApp version 26.35.72 as a compatible update.
