title: This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999
snippet: IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly. more…
fullText:
IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly.

The RugOne XSnap 7 Pro first appeared earlier this year, but is now making a splash with official pricing and release information at IFA. The device is landing on Kickstarter next week and will cost $999 when it arrives in the US in October – €1,099 in Europe.

This rugged device comes from Ulephone, a known brand for these ruggedized Android smartphones, with “RugOne” being a new sub-brand under the company. And, as per usual, it’s a chonky device with a 19.1mm profile, IP68/IP69K/MIL-STD-810H certifications, and no need for a case with its rugged, drop-resistant design. It has a 6.67-inch FHD+ display using Gorilla Glass Victus on top, runs on a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 chip with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, and has a massive 9,300 mAh battery. It even has a 64MP night vision camera to back up its 50MP main sensor. 

But the claim to fame here is a built-in, detachable action camera.

	

The camera attaches to the phone magnetically with a 133-degree field-of-view and 2.7K (1440p) recording. It can record for 40 minutes on its built-in battery and has 64GB of storage for up to eight hours of storage, but a built-in app on the phone can let the camera use the phone’s storage to offload that footage, and the phone also recharges the camera. The app can let you stream from the camera from up to 50 meters away and the action camera is waterproof up to 5 meters with no additional equipment.

It’s a wild idea, and one that actually seems more compelling than most of these rugged devices. A clear bit of utility, decent specs, and even a promise of software support – it XSnap 7 Pro ships with Android 16 and is promised updates through Android 20. 

What do you think?

title: Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker
snippet: If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in. more…
fullText:
If you happen to walk past the Orbitkey’s setup at IFA in Berlin, you might have seen what the company is known for — key organizers. You’d be forgiven for not thinking these new key organizers had Google Find Hub trackers built in.

Orbitkey isn’t new to Google Find Hub trackers, and certainly not key organizers. But its brand-new Key Organizer Tracker is the culmination of both, blending the visual design of what makes the company’s popular key holders so popular with more utility. I spent some time during IFA with the new key tool, and it’s already part of my EDC going forward.

The Key Organizer Tracker works with both Google Find Hub and Apple Find My networks by keeping a built-in tracker tucked in one of the sides. It looks thick at first glance, but I found that the new tracker/organizer is no thicker than some key-keepers, like the Ridge version I was lugging around. If your key organizer has a belt clip, Orbitkey’s Key Organizer Tracker will take up just as much space.

I’ve been using it for a few days during my IFA trip, and even though I don’t need to pull out my keys while on the go, I’ve toyed around with it enough to appreciate the design. Keys stay tucked and don’t spin, and the post has a semi-locking mechanism that prevents the keeper from loosening unnecessarily. Instead of a piece of spring steel sticking out to keep friction on your keys, Orbitkey uses a patented pressure ring that provides the perfect amount of pushback to keep them from spinning or locking in place.

	

Even the bottom key ring made for accompanying car keys is designed well. It’s fixed at the bottom, where the leather and plastic bend around. It doesn’t slide up into the space where keys sit, which makes pulling it out and grabbing the right key easier.

The tracker itself is no-nonsense, which is perfect. There’s a button for pairing and an LED to indicate status. It has a speaker to play loud chirps through the Google Find Hub app, and it charges via a magnetic pin charger included with the organizer. Orbitkey says the new Key Organizer Tracker lasts for 3-5 months, depending on your use. With how easy it is to charge, even with keys on it, that’s a respectable length of time.

Fit and finish feel great, as well. It has a faux-leather outer layer in tons of color options, and the rest of the keyboard’s build is made of sturdy, quality plastic.

Orbitkey also announced a new standalone tracker to complement the key holder. It’s shaped like a small popsicle stick, so it might not fit in your AirTag-branded accessories. Still, I’ve found it sort of slips into just about any bag. In Orbitkey’s new tech pouches, it fits into a dedicated pocket, so it won’t get lost in the clutter.

It has the same specs as the key tracker, with 3-5 months of battery and the same charging method.

Both the Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker and the standalone Tracker come in a bunch of colors. Even though my pictures only show the black colorway, the rest of the company’s color options are vibrant. The key organizer comes in Black, Blush, Cobalt, Citrus, and Orange leather-free options. Leather versions come in Black, Tan, and Forest.

The Orbitkey Key Organizer Tracker starts at $69.90, and the Universal Tracker starts at $34.90. Both are on sale now, and the Key Organizer Tracker is currently available for pre-order.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 display corners can bend inward on purpose, Samsung says [Gallery]
snippet: The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design. more…
fullText:
The internet is mad. Shocking statement, I know, but this time it’s about a perceived quality control issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 that sees the display corners able to bend or flex inward, but that Samsung says is part of the design.

On Reddit, Samsung’s forums, and endless social media posts – as well as a heaping pile of clickbaity headlines – a “flaw” with the Fold 8 is being criticized. Some have noticed that when you apply pressure to the corner of the inner display on Samsung’s new foldable, the corner flexes inward, leaving a small gap between the display and the bezel until the pressure is released. It seems to be more pronounced on some devices rather than others – on my personal Fold 8, it’s barely noticeable.

Reactions have varied, with one thread calling on Samsung to recall the device due to this.

Via @TheGalox_
Via Samsung forums

Samsung says, though, that this is normal behavior.

	

In a statement to Business Post as well as a reply apparently through its forums, Samsung explains that the corners of the display flex to protect the display in the case that something is trapped within the folded display, as well as to “reduce the impact of interference or pressure between internal components of the display.” The statement explains:

If something like sand adheres to the top surface of the internal display, the screen could get scratched when the Fold is folded. We designed it so the display indents slightly to provide a cushioning effect and prevent damage. Since this feature was prepared to ensure consumers do not experience inconvenience, we have not provided a separate official explanation.

One of the main concerns here was in regards to water resistance, with many assuming that this gap would let water get into the internals of the device. This was tested directly by one user, who applied pressure to the display corners while the Fold 8 was entirely submerged in water, with the foldable coming out unscathed. 

What do you think?

title: Samsung ‘advice’ to Apple suggests it fears the build quality of the iPhone Duo
snippet: Samsung says it welcomes Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market, although the company appears to feel threatened by the likely build quality of the iPhone Duo/Ultra. A Samsung exec said he sees Apple’s launch as “acknowledging and recognizing” the Korean company’s “pioneering” lead … more…
fullText:
Samsung says it welcomes Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market, although the company appears to feel threatened by the likely build quality of the iPhone Duo/Ultra.

A Samsung exec said he sees Apple’s launch as “acknowledging and recognizing” the Korean company’s “pioneering” lead …

Samsung currently dominates the folding smartphone market, but a report yesterday suggests that’s likely to change within the next twelve months. A leading market intelligence company predicted that Apple will own 40% of the market by this time next year; Samsung currently has a 38% share.

Hee-Cheul Moon, one of Samsung’s R&D leads, spoke to Wired.

On the eve of Apple’s highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung […] says the competition is “absolutely welcome” […]

“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says.

Samsung has suffered major problems with the build quality of its foldables, while Apple is believed to have waited so long precisely because it wanted to ensure it could overcome the quality issues that have plagued competing devices. Specifically, Apple wanted to ensure the crease was almost invisible when unfolded, and that the device would be robust enough to withstand constant folding and unfolding without issue.

Apple reportedly put a huge amount of engineering work into the quality of the hinge, and its robustness seems likely to carry a weight penalty – and it’s this which Samsung is seizing upon as an implied criticism.

Moon said, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it’s not easy.”

Wired reports that Apple’s foldable is expected to weigh around 235g, while Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 weighs 201g.

snippet: As the debut of Googlebook quietly approaches, a week full of new laptop launches at IFA continues to make me wonder why literally anyone should be even a tiny bit interested in Google’s new platform. fullText:
As the debut of Googlebook quietly approaches, a week full of new laptop launches at IFA continues to make me wonder why literally anyone should be even a tiny bit interested in Google’s new platform.

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Googlebook made its debut earlier this year as the company’s Android-based desktop platform that will replace ChromeOS and, frankly, I’ve spent the last couple of months just sitting here stewing over the complete lack of information on what this platform is supposed to do and why anyone should care. Truly, I cannot remember the last time I was this skeptical about a Google product – is this how other people felt about Stadia?

At this point, not much has changed.

	

We’ve seen leaks of some of the first Googlebook laptops from Asus and Lenovo, while Acer was spotted teasing its Googlebook at IFA in Berlin. Some early apps have shown up too, including “Magic Pointer” which is the one new feature Google has actually shown off from this platform, a “Desktop Camera” app, and “Look up” which is in fact not a reference to that DiCaprio movie but instead an AI-powered experience that lets you interact with text to find relevant information such as definitions, flight tracking, and more. That one works on some Android phones, too. 

Yet, I still cannot fathom where Googlebooks fit into the larger market. ChromeOS had a clear selling point – stable and usable software on low-cost hardware, with later generations adding in some clever AI features and using more capable hardware. But where Googlebook might have been interesting from a cost perspective, a focus on “premium” hardware combined with RAMageddon and a sea of MacBook Neo competitors… I just don’t get it folks. 

The new IdeaPad Vibe from Lenovo and the Dell 14S were both announced this week as direct answers to Apple’s hit budget-conscious laptop, and Google is literally going in the opposite direction.

Damien laid out some potential ideas back in June, such as a focus on AI-aided vibe coding, but it’s still hard to imagine Google’s pitch at this point. Windows laptops are getting more affordable in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and is anyone looking to spend money on tech they don’t need to right now? Maybe I’m just having trouble seeing the potential or the positives here, but I can’t remember the last time I was so sour on a potential new Google launch. 

What do you think?

title: Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones
snippet: Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year. more…
fullText:
Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year.

Confirmed in Galaxy Store listings for both the “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” apps, Samsung will be shutting down these AR experiences on December 31, 2026. Samsung explains that both will be “returning with improved services in the future.”

“Quick Measure” is an AR app that lets you get measurements of real-world distance from your phone, while “AR Doodle” lets you “draw” on real-world locations through the camera app.

The shutdown will block new downloads of both apps, while also pulling the plug on any future updates. The app won’t just stop working immediately, but any OS updates will break the apps in time. Notably, Samsung seems to have hidden both app listings on the latest One UI versions, making them inivisible in the Galaxy Store.

	

Samsung says:

Please be advised that service for the Quick measure app is scheduled to be terminated on 31 December 2026.

After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly.

Additionally, compatibility support for the Quick measure app will no longer be provided for future OS updates.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and thank all our customers for their loyal use of the Quick measure app. We are committed to returning with improved services in the future.

It’s unclear when these replacement apps might arrive, but it’s certainly a shame to see these going away.

title: Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people
snippet: A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way. more…
fullText:
A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way.

The issue at play here sees Google Messages reviving old messages that were sent to a contact and sending those alongside another new message to a different contact. You can see the problem, right? A message meant for your significant other could theoretically be sent to your parents, for example. It’s been reported by many users in recent weeks, with the problem even visible in real time; some have tested sending themselves messages only to see old messages randomly inserted into the same thread.

Highlighted by Droid-Life, there are still reports of this behavior popping up right now, with some reports popping up just in the past day.

It’s not happening for everyone, but it’s obviously a major issue for those affected. Sending old messages to random people could, at the very least, result in confusion, but could go as far as revealing private information. 

	

In a statement, Google confirmed that it is aware of the issue and has a fix, but it’s not rolling out quickly. Google said:

We’re currently rolling out a fix that will reach everyone over the coming weeks. Please ensure you stay up to date with the most recent version of Google Messages.

That was on September 2, and reports continue to pop up now, the better part of a week later. Updates continue to land on Google Play, so go check for a patch if you’re affected. Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into this bug.

title: Apple faces new UK rules over nude images on children’s iPhones
snippet: Bloomberg reports that the UK intends to introduce legislation that would require Apple and Google to “stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that the UK intends to introduce legislation that would require Apple and Google to “stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets.” Here are the details.

Apple says it plans to strengthen Communication Safety

The UK’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said in a statement to Parliament today that the government plans to introduce new legislation requiring major tech platforms, including Apple and Google, to build “device-level protections” meant to prevent children from “taking, sharing, or viewing nude images on their devices.”

The move, which she says will be brought to Parliament “as soon as we can,” follows a three-month deadline given to tech companies in June to introduce such protections voluntarily.

In her speech to the House of Commons, Nandy acknowledged that Apple and Google have made “meaningful changes” since then, but said those changes “do not meet the scale of this crisis.”

From her statement:

Children are facing unacceptable levels of sexual harm online. They are being groomed, coerced, and manipulated into creating and sharing intimate images across online services.

The Internet Watch Foundation believes that 91% of these images are self-generated by children themselves. They are used for blackmail and sexual extortion.

Each year, around 9,000 child sexual abuse offences involve an online element, with under 18s the subject of almost a quarter of online blackmail.

Nandy added that device-level protections are just one of two measures the government plans to pursue, the second being requirements for apps used by children “to prevent them from accessing or sharing nudity”:

We will explore what legislation is needed to implement this commitment, with a view to moving as quickly as possible. This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.

In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said that it shares “the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

Apple also said that it introduced in 2021, “a feature that prevents children from viewing or sharing photos or videos that contain nudity,” adding that “it now includes support for third-party apps.”

title: European founders and VCs urge lawmakers ‘to get EU Inc right’
snippet: Amid negotiations for a new EU-wide corporate status, an open letter signed by unicorn founders and investors warns that 'EU Inc' shouldn’t be watered down.
fullText:
Europe could soon have its own equivalent of the Delaware C Corp, but its advocates aren’t releasing the pressure on lawmakers. In an open letter released on Thursday, a who’s who of Europe’s startup scene stressed that this new corporate status shouldn’t be watered down.

The letter is the latest step of the EU Inc campaign, a movement calling for an EU-wide company statute that would let companies incorporate under a common framework and operate across the bloc. Its promoters have secured endorsements from the European Union’s top authorities, but now are expressing concern that the final legislation could become “unusable if its central features are weakened.” 

As usual with European lawmaking, various national lobbies have entered the chat, including Germany’s notaries, whose association has criticized aspects of the European Commission’s proposal. But negotiations are still ongoing for the European Parliament and Council to settle on a final text, and EU Inc’s promoters are pointing out what’s at stake.

With some 100 days left before European institutions shut down for winter recess, the letter calls on policymakers to preserve the proposal, saying it the potential to “remove much of the friction and fragmentation that continue to throttle European companies, unlock investment and spur a new wave of entrepreneurship.” 

Taking a page from older lobbies, the letter highlights points that “may seem like technical details, but […] separate a company form founders use from one they ignore.” In particular, they insist on one central registry; and that employees should be taxed only when they actually dispose of their stock options.

This need to get into the weeds isn’t new. In 2024, when original petition was gaining steam, Index Ventures partner and EU Inc supporter Martin Mignot told TechCrunch that “the devil is in the details, and that’s going to be where we’re going to be very, very watchful.” 

EU Inc has also stepped up its namedropping game. On the investor side, EU Inc’s new letter has been signed by VCs including Accel partner Sonali De Rycker, Sequoia partner Michael Moritz, and Atomico founder Niklas Zennström — one of many tech figures who’s been supporting the campaign by sporting its cap.

To add gravitas on the entrepreneur side, promoters also highlighted endorsements from founders behind unicorns including Alan, ElevenLabs, Lovable, Mistral, and Synthesia. Some of these have their HQs in the United States; reading between the lines, the message to lawmakers is also that if EU Inc has its way, this could be a thing of the past.

Anna has moderated panels and conducted onstage interviews at industry events of all sizes, including major tech conferences such as TechCrunch Disrupt, 4YFN, South Summit, TNW Conference, VivaTech, and many more.

title: Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it
snippet: Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. fullText:
Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it.

The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima himself. Sony, which published both of Kojima Productions’ previous Death Stranding games, framed it as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” but insisted their “relationship remains strong.”

Kojima put things more bluntly on his personal X account, claiming that Sony gave the studio an unexpected cancellation notice in June, and that it has spent the last three months “searching tirelessly” for a new publishing partner. He called Xbox “a partner with whom we share a common vision for the future.” It might have helped that the two companies are already working together, with Xbox lined up to publish the studio’s next game, OD.

“Creators have choices about where and how they bring their ideas to life,” said Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in a statement. “We’re honored that Kojima-san has chosen Xbox to work with Kojima Productions on Physint. His ambition to challenge conventions reflects the kind of creativity we want to support at Xbox.” Securing a title of Physint’s stature reflects the priorities Sharma laid out in a memo to Xbox staff this summer, promising a focus on “our strongest franchises and biggest new ideas.”

The Xbox announcement also notes that the relationship between the two companies will “extend beyond games,” with plans in the works across film and television, though no further details were given. Kojima Productions first announced plans for TV and film projects back in 2021, so far resulting in two upcoming Death Stranding adaptations: an animated spinoff called Mosquito and a live action adaptation from the director of Pig.

Kojima calls Physint a “genre-defining action-espionage title,” prompting hopes that it will serve as a spiritual successor to his Metal Gear series, though it’s not expected to launch until at least 2030. OD also has no release date, but should arrive sooner — the horror title was announced in 2022, and a first trailer dropped this time last year.

title: I Tried the iPhone 18 Pro’s New Deluxe Camera and Shot Photos With Starbursts
snippet: Hands-on: At Apple’s Sept. 9 event, I tried the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The standout feature is the new variable aperture on the main camera.
fullText:
While the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are among Apple’s newest phones, they are the ones that don’t fold. Thankfully, a handful of upgrades, like a fancy new camera tool, will make photographers rejoice!

I tried the iPhone 18 Pro in a packed demo area in the Steve Jobs Theater at Apple Park right after the company’s “Surprise and shine” event. Admittedly, it wasn’t the ideal environment for photographic testing. But I was later able to take some photos and videos using the new variable aperture, in a calmer setting that showed off its potential. I now understand what the “shine” in the event’s name referred to.

Think of a camera’s aperture like your eyelids. When your eyes are wide open, they let in more light. Under the bright sun, you squint to reduce the glare and see better. A variable aperture does the same for a camera lens. There are tiny blades that open and close to let more light onto the image sensor, or to reduce exposure in a bright scene.

Most phone cameras have a fixed aperture that can’t be adjusted. But the iPhone 18 Pro acts more like a dedicated camera, letting you stop it down for sharper images or, in dark environments, open the aperture wide to capture a brighter scene.

I was even able to achieve starbursts, thanks to the physical aperture blades. If there’s a bright light source in your shot, like string lights, you can stop the aperture down to add light peaks. The effect is caused by the way the aperture blades meet. 

In terms of how it works, there’s an auto setting that lets the phone pick the best aperture. But you can also set it manually, choosing between four f-stops, which determine how wide the aperture’s opening is set.

The iPhone 18 Pro isn’t the first phone with a mechanical aperture. I remember shooting photos in 2018 with the Galaxy S9, which had a dual-aperture camera. Xiaomi’s 14 Ultra had a stepless aperture that let you stop anywhere between f/1.63 and f/4.0. The iPhone 18 Pro has fours stops: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0.

While I think professional photographers, filmmakers and other creative types will enjoy it most, a variable aperture isn’t enough of a reason for most people to buy an iPhone 18 Pro, especially if you’re just posting pics on social media. Just get the iPhone 17, especially since the iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,199 and the 18 Pro Max at $1,299, a $100 more than the 17 Pro and Pro Max from last year.

So what else did I think from my hands-on time with the new Apple phones?

The burgundy color looks magnificent in-person. It has a rich and sophisticated charm, forgoing the iPhone 17 Pro’s bold construction vest orange.

The iPhone 18 Pro in silver (left), burgundy, glacier and black.

The Dynamic Island is slimmer, thanks to a wildly clever implementation of putting the FaceTime camera under the display. We’re still not at a full circle for the Dynamic Island, but it’s now closer in size to an ibuprofen tablet than the 17 Pro’s longer, slender oval.

The batteries on both Pro models are larger, with the SIM card tray models of the iPhone 18 Pro at 4,056 mAh and the 18 Pro Max at 5,391 mAh, according to Apple’s site in Ireland. (Thanks, EU, for Apple requiring energy labels!). While US models are only eSIM, Apple fills the space normally used by a SIM card tray with more battery. By contrast, SIM card tray versions of the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max have 3,988 mAh and 4,823 mAh, respectively.

It will be curious to see how those increased capacities offset power-hungry Siri AI features and operating that variable aperture. The 18 Pro and Pro Max are powered by a new A20 Pro chip, which Apple says brings efficiency gains to offset battery drain.

I look forward to testing the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, once I can get them. You can preorder the new Pro iPhones starting Saturday, Sept. 12 and they’ll be in stores starting Friday, Sept. 18.

Admittedly, it wasn’t the ideal environment for photographic testing. But I was later able to take some photos and videos using the new variable aperture, in a calmer setting that showed off its potential. I now understand what the “shine” in the event’s name referred to.

title: Automattic’s board forces CEO Matt Mullenweg into leave of absence
snippet: Mullenweg said in a company Slack message that it was against his will.
fullText:
Matt Mullenweg, the founder and CEO of Automattic, best known as the parent company of WordPress.com, has been put on a leave of absence by his board against his will, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.

Earlier Wednesday, Mullenweg posted in a Slack channel visible to all employees that the company’s Chief Financial Officer, Mark Davies, had “conspired” with other board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker to vote to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence.

The message read:

And the biggest news: I won’t be able to make the [meeting] tomorrow. @Mark Davies has conspired with @Ann Dunwoody, @Toni, and @Sue Decker behind my back and they voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that. Wishing Mark and all of you the very best.

To clarify @Mark Davies was voted as interim CEO. I received the resolution 50 minutes before the meeting start, and requested repeatedly for time to have it reviewed by independent legal counsel, even a few hours, which was denied.

A Slack message to the open-source WordPress.org community from the project’s executive director, Mary Hubbard, also confirmed Mullenweg’s change of status at the commercial company. However, Hubbard said that WordPress.org was not impacted. “Matt remains the leader of the WordPress project and I remain Executive Director of WordPress. Our teams, priorities, and work continue as planned,” she wrote.

Mullenweg’s Slack message did not make clear why Automattic’s board took this action. Sources told 404 Media, which was the first to report the news, that Schneider — the former CEO of Automattic from 2006 to 2014 — confirmed that the action was initiated by the board. Davies also told employees in the Slack channel that Mullenweg remained on the board of directors.

In an emailed statement to TechCrunch, Automattic confirmed Mullenweg was on leave.

“Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” the email read. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.”

Automattic, which owns other brands including Tumblr, WooCommerce, and Pocket Casts, was founded by Mullenweg in 2003 after he co-created the popular open-source content management system WordPress.

Over the past few years, Mullenweg and the company have been mired in lawsuits and controversy. The company is in a protracted legal battle with WP Engine, a WordPress web hosting competitor. The lawsuit followed allegations from Mullenweg that WP Engine was profiting from the open-source WordPress project without contributing back to the community, and he demanded it pay 8% of its monthly gross revenue as a royalty fee for using the WordPress brand.

WP Engine sued in October 2024, and accused Automattic and Mullenweg of defamation and abuse of power. Automattic filed counterclaims last year. In February, WP Engine claimed that Automattic intended to target 10 more competitors with royalty claims. 

Tensions became so high under Mullenweg’s leadership that he told employees in 2024 to quit, with severance, if they disagreed with him and 159 did so.

Last year, Mullenweg also threatened to deactivate the accounts of several members of the open-source WordPress.org community, after two of them said they planned to spearhead a new forked version of the open source WordPress project.

In April 2025, the company laid off 16% of its staff. The cuts included some longtime employees who had been with the company for more than a decade, sources told TechCrunch.

Some alumni have been asking current employees how they feel about the news, a source told TechCrunch. Some employees said they were “ecstatic” or “relieved” but others had mixed emotions because the move creates more instability.

It isn’t clear why the company’s board made this decision now. One person speculated that the timing may have something to do with Mullenweg’s annual trip to the Burning Man festival, after which he tends to return “with ideas.” This year’s festival ended on September 7.

Mullenweg did not immediately respond to our request for comment.

fullText:
Jay Peters

 

is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Apple has seen reason: It has a black model in the iPhone Pro lineup again.

Last year, Apple went bold with its colors for the iPhone 17 Pro, offering a flashy orange, a shiny silver, and a dark blue. Don’t get me wrong, they looked nice. But there was no black (or dark gray) for the first time since the start of the iPhone Pro lineup, which Apple first introduced in September 2019 with the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max.

I care about this because I always buy the black phone. I learned my lesson with the iPhone 6: I got it in gold to mix things up and came to regret it. I don’t need something flashy — I need a phone that blends into the background and looks decent in whatever case I throw it into. After the iPhone 6, my next phone was the iPhone 7 in the excellent matte black (I wasn’t brave enough to endure the jet black model’s potential scratches), and I’ve only ever gotten the black or gray phones since.

My black titanium iPhone 16 Pro in a black Torras case (with a mostly black homescreen) still works very well, thank you very much, and I’m not in the market for a new phone. But when I make my annual mid-September visit to the local Apple Store to look at all the new iPhones, I won’t be rushing to see the iPhone 18 Pro in burgundy, blue, or silver. I’ll be beelining for the model in black.

title: The iPhone Duo is Apple at its absolute best (and a little bit at its worst)
snippet: Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo! It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer … more…
fullText:
Wow. After Samsung had a seven-year head start on Apple in the foldables market, the company really had to live up to its ethos of waiting until it could do a far better job than everyone else, and boy did it deliver with the iPhone Duo!

It was abundantly clear that Apple had thought through every detail of what a foldable iPhone needed to be, and has taken advantage of every benefit the form factor has to offer …

It starts with the basics. Prior reports talked about Apple waiting until it could make the crease virtually invisible and ensure the hinge design would be robust enough to survive endless cycles of folding and unfolding, and while the latter remains to be seen, we can already see the work that went into that hinge design.

There’s the under-screen front-facing camera that’s visible when you need it and almost invisible when you don’t.

Apple also thought about all of the different ways in which the device could be held or positioned, and how the software could best take advantage of that.

I’m not sure who first said it, but I think it’s absolutely true that great design is something no-one else thought of, yet looks blindingly obvious in hindsight. The OG iPhone was a great example of this. Other smartphones had physical keyboards and required* a stylus to use them, while the iPhone is used with your finger and a keyboard only appears when it’s required. It was obvious afterwards that of course smartphones should work this way.

*Yes, the Duo supports the Apple Pencil, but it doesn’t require one.

For me, there were plenty of examples of this in the Duo presentation. Why should we need to first isolate a subject in a photo and then copy it into another app when we could simply drag it there directly from the original photo? That’s completely obvious after the fact.

Replacing a camera self-timer with the device simply waiting until everyone stops moving and then taking the photo automatically. Obvious!

Then there were the UI features that have no reason to exist but simply look beautiful, like that blurring effect as you fold the phone.

I could go on at some length, but the bottom line is that I had extremely high expectations for this device yet was still blown away by just how good it appears to be. I’m British; the only time we ever use the word “wow” is sarcastically – but I still had to open this piece with it, without a trace of sarcasm.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo. 

And that brings me to that “little bit the worst of Apple” remark in the headline. The company has the ability to create product videos that make us feel we can reach out through the screen and touch the device. Apple can create strong desire for a product we have absolutely no business buying. I’m not the target market for the iPhone Duo, but I do, absolutely, unquestionably want one. How about you?

title: Google Pixel Tablet has been discontinued, out of stock everywhere
snippet: The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store. more…
fullText:
The Pixel Tablet is done, as Google has officially pulled the plug on the slate by entirely deleting the listing on its store.

Google launched the Pixel Tablet in 2023 as a hybrid of a typical Android tablet and a Nest Hub smart display. It was met with mixed reactions, but still serves as the only tablet in Google’s lineup. 

And now it’s done.

While updates are set to continue through 2028, Google has quietly removed the Pixel Tablet from its Store. A direct link to the listing now redirects to the homepage, while there’s also no mention of the Pixel Tablet anywhere on the Google Store besides a few accessories that remain. The change was spotted by Jetstream earlier today. 

	

Sales of the Pixel Tablet closed up in late August (thanks Noah!), but the listing was still working roughly a week ago – we checked it when Nest prices went up, and the Tablet was still listed as out of stock at the time (August 31).

Google never did ship a Pixel Tablet sequel, with rumors of some big upgrades being canceled over profitability concerns. Had a sequel continued on, it allegedly would have arrived in 2025, with a third-gen release in 2027 that was also shelved.

	

While third-party retailers often have stock left over when Google ends its own sales of a product, Pixel Tablet is out of stock everywhere we’ve looked. Amazon doesn’t even have any third-party sellers with stock left.

RIP.

title: Motorola teases wide Razr Fold as its ‘next move’ in response to iPhone Duo debut
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo announcement has triggered a couple of companies, and it’s apparently warranted at least one teaser for even more foldables. This one seems to be a wide version of the Motorola Razr Fold.

After years of watching manufacturers improve on the concept of a foldable phone, Apple has a genuine answer – the iPhone Duo. In a lot of respects, it looks like the original Pixel Fold. But software seems to be a heavy selling point, with plenty of tricks and touches that sell the idea of an iOS-powered foldable.

The fallout has been interesting. Samsung’s team took to Twitter/X to acknowledge Apple’s release, with a slew of posts that almost seem clingy. They didn’t have anything solid to offer, though. But Motorola did.

The mobile company responsible for the Razr of years past and the Razr foldables current posted a snarky little video on Instagram in response to the iPhone Duo’s existence. A series of shots shows Razr phones spanning back a few generations snapping shut. The iconic pink Motorola Razr flip phone starts it off. The last recognizable phone in the video is a Motorola Razr Fold, which launched earlier this year.

	

Right after that, the video ends with a blacked-out foldable that resembles the iPhone Duo’s short and stout nature. It’s not Apple’s new release, but it’s possible it could be a wide Razr Fold from Motorola. In the post, Motorola calls it its “next move,” which seems telling enough.

If our eyes can be trusted, there are a couple of details to pick out for what could be a wide Motorola Razr Fold. The camera bar spans the entire width of the phone’s rear panel. A button can also be seen on the top left of the inner display view. The iPhone Duo has two volume rockers on the right side.

It’s just a silhouette, and those little details could prove to be completely off. But Motorola isn’t ready to say what the device is, or when it will launch. It simply wants users to know it exists since the hype for short and wide foldables seems to be growing, thanks to Samsung and now Apple.

title: Samsung reacts to Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo; ‘reheating our leftovers’
snippet: Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.” more…
fullText:
Samsung is apparently of two minds when it comes to reacting to Apple’s first foldable device, with some interesting reactions to the iPhone Duo’s unveiling, calling the device “a Sims sequel” and “reheating our leftovers.”

Apple’s first foldable is official, with the iPhone Duo sharing a form factor similar to that of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8. Samsung’s device has been very well received since its debut in July, though one could argue that the new shape was somewhat of a reaction to Apple’s imminent arrival on the scene. Chicken or egg, your choice, but Samsung’s public reaction has been quite something to watch.

The foldable pioneer was welcoming to Apple ahead of the launch, but the Twitter/X feed tells another story. Samsung called the iPhone Duo a “Sim sequel” and “So far, so same,” referring to how much of what the iPhone Duo can do has been seen on existing Android foldables, including Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

Samsung further poked fun at Apple only having one foldable form factor and, for whatever reason, took issue with the idea of using the Duo as a clock, but also called the iPhone Duo a case of “reheating our leftovers.” 

	

Let us know when you're done reheating our leftovers 😉

— Samsung Mobile US (@SamsungMobileUS) September 9, 2026

Bold statement given the complete 180-degree turn the Fold 8’s design is compared to Samsung’s long history of book-style foldables. Surely a coincidence, but I digress. 

Samsung even pulled Duolingo into the conversation to poke fun at Apple’s branding – Duolingo itself had already done – with Duolingo replying to call Samsung an “ugly stranger” in reference to a viral meme.

Apple’s iPhone Duo launches in October for $1,999.

title: Boox Picco is exceptionally tiny for an e-reader, but it parts ways with Android and third-party apps
snippet: Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere. more…
fullText:
Boox offered some wandering the halls of Messe Berlin at IFA 2026 the opportunity to check out its most exciting upcoming release – a tiny e-reader called the “Picco” that you could probably pocket and take anywhere.

Boox laid out a product trajectory over the last few years that builds on Android to offer an e-reader experience open to third-party apps. That includes Google Play Books, Kindle, and so much more.

The Boox Picco, which is slated for a November release, won’t offer that experience.

Instead, this e-reader experience hinges on a “take anywhere” design coming in at somewhere just under 4 inches. At that size, it’s the ultimate travel e-reader if you’re ok with a rather small viewing area.

	

It’s garnered a lot of hype for an e-reader, and it deserves a lot of it. It’s small, thin, and has some of Boox’s best features, like an adjustable front light for reading at any time of the day. It even has a set of custom buttons and page rockers built specifically for an easy experience.

Related: The Boox Go 10.3 Gen II is as massive as it is minimal, and I love that for it

But the Boox Picco won’t run Android, and that feels like a big loss. Android e-readers, like much of the company’s backlog, allow users to install third-party apps beyond what the OS offers. In essence, it opens the doors to your existing libraries you’ve built over time from apps like Kindle or Google Play Books. Without those apps, you’re left with the Boox store and epub files.

The Picco will come with a companion app that lets users transfer files to the reader, and even though what we got hands-on time with was an early unit, it seemed like a solid system. But this leaves you limited on options, and you’ll have to find epub versions of your favorite stories and publications.

You might also be disappointed if you were expecting MagSafe compatibility or Qi2.2 support to get it to stick to the back of your phone.

I can’t let that entirely detract from the absolutely adorable e-reader. The early unit we played around with felt great in hand, and even with a tiny screen, I can see plenty of uses for such a small device. It’s essentially the size of a mini field journal, and carrying it on you in your bag or even pocket all day is a no-brainer if you know you’ll get some downtime to catch up on a book or two.

The lack of Android probably also facilitates a more compelling price. Boox says the device will be listed for somewhere around $100, though no details are final. If the Boox Picco hits that price tag and the experience is as easy as it seems it will be, the Picco might deserve every bit of praise it’s getting before it’s even released.

Boox plans to launch the Picco sometime in November.

title: Google Photos trash bin now deletes media after 30 days, down from 60 days
snippet: Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026. more…
fullText:
Google Photos has updated its trash bin timeline, cutting the time from 60 days to 30 days as of September 2026.

The trash bin in Google Photos gives users a chance to recover deleted photos and videos for a limited period of time. That period was 60 days for the longest time, effectively giving users about two months to recover anything that might have been deleted by accident or simply needed to be recovered. 

Google has now cut that to 30 days.

The change is rolling out now, as noticed in an app pop-up by the folks over at Android Authority earlier this week. It’s also live on a Google support page where the company explains:

	

Photos and videos that you delete will stay in your trash for 30 days before they are permanently deleted. Photos and videos that were permanently deleted can’t be restored.

That previously read as 60 days, with the change apparently being effective as of September 4, 2026, according to archived versions of that page. Just a day prior, it still read as 60 days.

title: Camera app in iOS 27 reportedly includes four major pro photography features
snippet: Code reportedly found in the Camera app in the latest iOS 27 beta appears to point to the introduction of some major pro photography and videography features. While the stock camera app has grown in power over time, the reported discoveries seem surprising for an app primarily geared to point-and-shoot usage … more…
fullText:
Code reportedly found in the Camera app in the latest iOS 27 beta appears to point to the introduction of some major pro photography and videography features.

While the stock camera app has grown in power over time, the reported discoveries seem surprising for an app primarily geared to point-and-shoot usage …

Apple has historically tried to walk a tightrope between making its own Camera app extremely easy to use for snapshots while also giving some degree of creative control to those who like to use it as a more serious camera. Despite the gradual evolution of the app, however, most keen photographers and videographers tend to use third-party apps instead.

The reported introduction of some powerful features normally associated with professional cameras may well change this, if the discoveries do indeed turn out to be accurate. Developer pdfu says they discovered code supporting four main features not currently enabled in any of the betas. 

Exposure scopes

Judging exposure visually can be extremely unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in bright sunlight. Most dedicated cameras support a histogram feature intended to provide an accurate depiction of the exposure, while video editing software tends to use a waveform as another way of viewing the same information. Pdfu says they have found code for both features within the beta.

1. Exposure scopes

The Camera app adds a complete implementation of waveform and histogram views. These can help users judge exposure in different formats.

There is no consumer within the Camera app, but you can see a demo of all graphs against stock photos below. pic.twitter.com/0UBdKJtbMc

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 7, 2026

Focus peaking

How much of a photo will be in focus between immediate foreground and far background depends on a number of factors, but for some shots only part of the scene will be in focus. Again, judging what is and isn’t in focus visually can be unreliable, so professional video cameras in particular use an approach known as focus peaking.

With this, you can enable an overlay where the parts of the photo in focus will be highlighted, typically in a red colour – though the example shown on the left uses yellow.

2. Focus peaking and highlight-clipping overlays

Focus peaking emphasizes edges with strong local contrast. Highlight-clipping can warn users about highlights that are becoming too bright.

Once enabled in iOS 27, they can be rendered individually or together in the preview. pic.twitter.com/PLjalPkKJB

— pdfu (@itspdfu) September 7, 2026

Highlight clipping

The biggest danger with getting the exposure wrong is overexposing. In general, if you underexpose the shadow areas, these can be recovered in post-processing – you’d have to get it very wrong for dark areas to turn completely black (an RGB value of zero). Overexposure is a much bigger issue as it’s very easy to blow the highlights completely – that is, the bright areas exceed an RGB value of 255 and cannot be recovered.

Many dedicated cameras use what’s known as zebra indicators, red stripes indicating areas that are completely blown. In some cases, you can manually set the value for these so you are warned when you are approaching blown highlights (eg. 90%) rather than when you actually hit them.

This feature too is shown above, on the right.

Manual focus

The camera app does currently allow you to lock the focus on a particular element in the scene, but you can only do this in conjunction with locking the exposure on the same point via the AE/AF lock (auto-exposure/auto-focus). 

The report says that Apple has tested true manual focus in the camera app via a slider. Pdfu says this may be limited to one or more of the upcoming new iPhones.

Other features

In addition to the Pro features, there will reportedly be an option to take a series of self-timed photos. It’s common for people to want to take several when shooting photos of a group, so this feature could enable you to simply put the iPhone on a tripod or position it somewhere, and then take a series of photos to then choose the one everyone is happy with.

Finally, there’s an indication of a new image processing approach to adapt to the variable aperture we’re expecting to see in the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac’s Take

None of the features described are enabled in any of the iOS 27 betas, and I’d be surprised by Apple putting them into the stock camera app instead of limiting them to Final Cut Camera, but the report does appear credible.

What are your reactions to this report? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Xbox Cloud Gaming will limit players to 15 hours per month before they have to pay more
snippet: Microsoft is making a change to Xbox Cloud Gaming that will place a limit of 15 hours a month or less on players before they have to pay more for cloud gaming. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is making a change to Xbox Cloud Gaming that will place a limit of 15 hours a month or less on players before they have to pay more for cloud gaming.

In a post today, Microsoft details that Xbox Game Pass subscribers will now be limited to a set number of hours per month, a restriction that does not exist today. Limits depend on the Game Pass subscription tier, ranging from 5-15 hours per month.

Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours

Game Pass Premium: 10 hours

Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Microsoft says that the change will impact “4% of Game Pass subscribers.”

Once someone uses up their allotted hours, more hours will be available for purchase through the Xbox Store. Pricing has not been announced, with more details to come in November when the change actually kicks in. Players will also be able to directly purchase cloud gaming hours even if they are not active Game Pass subscribers. 

	

Why the change? The company explains it is “because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer,” presumably all the more so in the midst of RAMageddon.

title: Google rolling out Gmail Live, Docs Live, and Keep Live
snippet: Following the announcement at I/O 2026, Google is rolling out Gmail Live, Docs Live, and Keep Live this week. After testing in recent months, these voice capabilities are now generally available. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at I/O 2026, Google is rolling out Gmail Live, Docs Live, and Keep Live this week. After testing in recent months, these voice capabilities are now generally available.

Gmail Live lets you talk to your inbox. Instead of manually searching for information and reading through threads, Gemini lets you have a “natural, spoken conversation with your inbox to pull precise information.”

You can ask follow-up questions without repeating the context, and Gmail Live can be interrupted at any time to switch topics without starting a new session. The fullscreen interface shows a transcript and links to the source emails. To launch, tap the new Live icon in the Gmail search bar.

Gmail Live is available with Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra on Android and iOS in English worldwide.

	

Google positions Docs Live as a “hands-free thought partner and co-writer” that helps you quickly create a first draft for summaries, proposals, and more. Gemini can draw from information in your Gmail, Drive, Chat, and the web. 

It will show a recap of the information before proceeding to generate the document. You can ask Docs Live to add specific information and format as needed. In the Google Docs app, tapping the FAB (floating action button) reveals a new “Create with voice” option to launch the experience.

Docs Live is available with AI Pro and Ultra on Android and iOS.

Finally, Keep Live listens to “audio brain dumps and processes them” to generate notes and lists. Gemini “understands your stream of consciousness,” with Google Keep showing an inline preview of what it generated after a few seconds. 

You can tell Google Keep to put “ingredients for pesto pasta” in your shopping list, and “Gemini understands your intent and reflects it in the note.” Multiple notes can be generated in the same session, while you can use your voice to edit, like telling Keep Live to check off items.

Additionally, Keep Live isn’t limited to new notes and can add information to existing ones:

For example, if you already have a grocery list and you tell it you need to remember to get bananas, Keep will just add bananas to your existing list.

Keep Live is available on Android and requires AI Plus (updated), Pro, and Ultra. These three features are “coming soon” to Google Workspace business customers.

title: The XGIMI Aura 3 lineup brings Google TV to 4K 120Hz capable short-throw laser projectors
snippet: XGIMI has officially unveiled its new ultra-short-throw (UST) projector lineup at IFA 2026 with the debut of the Aura 3 Series, consisting of the AURA 3 Pro and Aura 3 Max. more…
fullText:
XGIMI has officially unveiled its new ultra-short-throw (UST) projector lineup at IFA 2026 with the debut of the Aura 3 Series, consisting of the AURA 3 Pro and Aura 3 Max. 

Positioned as the world’s first 4K UST projectors to offer 4K 120Hz output, the series targets both high-end home theater setups and high-refresh-rate gaming on massive displays.

Both models in the Aura 3 lineup feature an RGB Triple Laser light engine paired with XGIMI’s Dynamic Dual Iris optical system. The dual-iris system regulates light output to achieve a native contrast ratio of up to 8,000:1 alongside Dynamic Black Enhancement. 

The top-tier Aura 3 Max delivers up to insane 5,700 ISO lumens of brightness and covers 110% of the BT.2020 color gamut. With an ultra-short throw ratio of 0.163:1, the projector can project a 120-inch picture when placed roughly eight inches away from a wall, with supported screen sizes reaching up to 200 inches. That’s more than big enough for any home entertainment system no matter where you’re planning on making a home theater upgrade.

	

HDR standards supported across the lineup include Dolby Vision, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG, and IMAX Enhanced, along with Filmmaker Mode, dynamic tone mapping, and Anti-Rainbow Effect (Anti-RBE) technology. The system also includes support for 3D content – yes 3D content in the big ’26 – and even ships with two pairs of 3D glasses.

To handle 4K resolution at 120Hz, XGIMI uses two DLPC 8545 display controllers operating in parallel. This is really good news for gamers because high-frame-rate gaming features are enabled via HDMI 2.1 inputs, including Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), AMD FreeSync Premium, and Dolby Vision Gaming, with claimed input latency dropping as low as 1ms depending on the mode.

On the software side, the Aura 3 Series runs Google TV out of the box and, unlike some options, provides native access to all the major streaming services such as Netflix, Prime Video, and YouTube, as well as Google Cast integration. Audio is handled by an integrated 80-watt Harman Kardon speaker setup supporting Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X. When the projector is idle, an “XGIMI WALL” ambient feature allows it to display curated wallpapers and digital art.

Pre-orders for the AURA 3 Series are open now on XGIMI’s official store. Buyers can reserve a unit ahead of time with a $50 / £50 deposit to lock in an additional $200 discount.

One of the only frustrations is that the lineup will officially launch via Kickstarter on October 20, 2026. Kickstarter exclusive pricing starts at $2,199 for the Aura 3 Pro and $2,399 for the flagship Aura 3 Max. Not cheap, but certainly one of the most space-conscious ways to refresh your home entertainment setup.

Following an appearance at IFA 2026 last week, Xiaomi has posted the full details of its new wide Fold, while it’s also been directly compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

The triple camera array around back includes a 200MP main sensor, 50MP 3.5x telephoto, and a 50MP ultrawide too. 

Colors include “Warm Gold,” “White,” “Black,” and “Nishino Red” (translated).

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is available for purchase now in China starting at ¥10,999. Directly converted, that’s just shy of $1,640 USD. It’s still unclear if or when this foldable might make its way to global markets, but it’s certainly an intriguing release.

title: Google Clock rolls out redesign of Timers with presets on Android
snippet: Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app. more…
fullText:
Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app.

The big change is that Google has introduced presets for 1, 5, 10, and 15 minutes that immediately start counting down once tapped. Google has tweaked the numbers at the top with Hours, Minutes, and Seconds replacing h, m, and s.

A big green “Start” pill replaces the previous icon at the bottom of the screen. Finally, the number pad no longer uses circular backgrounds. This tweak makes the screen feel flatter, with the interface now much busier but more efficient.

Old vs. new

	

If you have multiple timers, Google has shrunk down the cards and now offers a grid instead of the previous scrollable list. This is a much better use of screen real estate, while there are no changes to the single-timer look. The pause button is now inside the circular countdown, while reset is outside. 

This Timers redesign is rolling out as part of a server-side update with version 9.1 of Google Clock. If you’re not seeing it yet, Force stop from App info.

title: How to check if Motion Assist has rolled out to your Android 17 phone
snippet: Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17.

Once rolled out, you can search for “motion assist” in the Settings app. The long way is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Appearing alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection, this new feature is part of Google Play services.

The preference menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding the Quick Settings Tile. This lets you manually enable and disable “from any screen.” You can add it from this page or the usual edit screen under “From system apps.” Once active, there’s also a system notification that lets you disable with a tap.

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

	

Color: Based on system, Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

The moving shapes adjust to the device’s motion and “may help reduce motion sickness when you’re in a moving vehicle.” On the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you get three columns of shapes on the left and right edges, while Google’s phone example shows two.

Motion Assist is not yet widely rolled out. We’re seeing it with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services, but there’s a server-side component. As of today, it’s only appearing on one of our devices.

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Matt Mullenweg, the CEO of WordPress.com owner Automattic, has been placed on a paid leave of absence, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In an internal message by the outlet, Mullenweg claims Automattic chief financial officer Mark Davies “conspired” with board members to place him on leave.

“They voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that,” Mullenweg wrote, referring to Davies, along with Automattic board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker, 404 Media reports.

Mullenweg, who also co-founded WordPress.org, has headed up Automattic since 2014. In 2024, Mullenweg waged a public pressure campaign against a prominent WordPress host, a move that divided the open-source community and ignited a legal battle that’s still going on today.

Automattic spokesperson Megan Fox confirmed the company’s decision in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” Fox writes. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.” Mullenweg will remain on Automattic’s board, 404 Media reports.

“Automattic’s board has decided to ask Matt to step away from his CEO role and take a leave of absence,” Schneider said on the company’s internal message board, according to 404 Media. “We have asked Mark Davies to assume the interim CEO role while Matt is out. We’ve worked closely with Mark over the years and we’re confident he will steer the ship well while Matt is away.”

Update, September 9th: Added Automattic’s statement.

title: Annoyingly, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the best advert for an iPhone Fold yet
snippet: Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold. more…
fullText:
Samsung has beaten Apple to the punch, but I’m annoyed that while it’s, in fact, a fantastic device, it’ll only help bolster the sales of the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

It is a really ironic position for Samsung to find itself in. They have spent years flexing their engineering muscle, burning through iterations, and pushing folding display technology to its absolute limit to lead this space. Although I would argue that some others are doing the “traditional” foldable better now.

Yet despite all the leading, innovating, and market domination, Samsung’s latest flagship wide-body foldable might just end up courting buyers right into Apple’s hands with its iPhone Fold.

The cynic in me sort of feels that, like the Galaxy S25 Edge, getting ahead of Apple was a calculated play to try and court those who are intrigued by the form factor, but maybe not ready to commit to the very compromised 1:1 aspect-ratio’d Z Folds. It’s hard to argue that most folding phones are narrow devices that feel like holding a thick TV remote when closed.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is refreshing compared to Samsung’s previous folding phones because it’s leaning into the entertainment strengths that are supposedly why folding phones are so popular. As with any tech product, there are always going to be compromises, especially when it’s a 2-in-1 experience. Foldables are mature, but the wide body feels like it’s ready to be fully explored. In my mind, a wide-body folding phone is the optimal design. The final form is the tri-fold, which, coincidentally, Samsung has managed to ship to those with deep enough pockets.

Back to the Fold 8: for the most part, many reviews have pointed out how refreshing the Z Fold 8 is despite the fact that Oppo and Google did it first. Samsung has just done it better than anyone thus far. In fact, the Z Fold 8 is easily one of my favorite smartphones of the last few years. As soon as I picked it up, it made sense. I carry it as a secondary phone with a backup SIM. It is my Balatro-playing, web-scrolling, book-reading, movie-watching phone. It’s a small tablet, but also a small phone; there’s literally nothing to hate in my mind.

It probably doesn’t help that Samsung grapples with a fundamentally different challenge than Apple. Samsung is forced to lead the space, combat a wave of aggressive Chinese competitors, and constantly prove why it deserves to be the king of Android hardware. It has to innovate in public, iterate openly, and deal with the early design missteps that come with pioneering new categories.

When everyday people see the Z Fold 8 in public or read reviews praising its new wide-body format, they don’t necessarily think about switching to Android. Instead, they think, “If a folding phone can finally look and feel this good, I can’t wait to see what Apple does with an iPhone Fold.” Samsung is doing all the heavy lifting of educating the public and legitimizing the form factor, only for Apple to potentially reap the rewards.

Cards on the table, I do not like iOS, but I’m under no illusions that Apple will have optimized every single aspect of the experience to maximize the experience on the inner and outer screen. Android’s foldable software has improved significantly over the years, but app optimization across varying aspect ratios on Android remains a hit-or-miss affair depending on whether developers care to update their apps. I’m having a great time, but some things could be better. Apple doesn’t have that problem—when Apple drops a new form factor, developers fall in line almost immediately.

We might have differing opinions on our mobile OS of choice, but 9to5Mac’s own Fernando Silva had some very positive things to say about the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8. While we’ve had folding devices for almost a decade, it’s interesting to see the critiques from an Apple-centric position. I implore you to go check it out.

In hindsight, the iPad Mini was the very first step ahead of a potential iPhone Fold. It’s a compact tablet running iPadOS with multi-window capabilities tailored for small-format tablet displays. The second step was the ultra-thin design language introduced with the iPhone Air. Apple’s undoubted prowess in the tablet space has likely held back some internal ambitions to ship a folding phone. They didn’t want to cannibalize their own iPad Mini sales until the market was mature enough to justify merging those two product lines. The tech market is mature now, so for Apple, it’s clearly time to enter the space.

When an iPhone user looks at a Galaxy Z Fold 8, they see an incredible piece of engineering, but they also see One UI, a different app ecosystem, and a departure from their comfort zone. Instead of acting as a gateway to convert those users to Samsung, the Z Fold 8 serves as a proof of concept.

It proves to the “average user” – a phrase I’m not all that fond of – that folding phones are no longer delicate, awkward experiments with annoying aspect ratios. It reassures them that the hardware is ready, leaving them content to simply wait for Apple to drop its own version. Samsung has built a fantastic device that, annoyingly, has accidentally become the ultimate marketing campaign for Apple’s next big thing.

title: IPhone Duo’s Under-Screen Camera: Invisible, but at What Cost?
snippet: A camera hiding under Apple’s new folding phone sounds like the future, but comes with compromises too.
fullText:
I love the idea of a phone or tablet with no camera cutout or bezel at all, where everything would be screen… and a camera hidden under the screen would handle the magic for you.

That’s exactly what Apple did with the inner camera on its new iPhone Duo, coming later in October. It’s a phone full of new tech specs to catch up on, but that new bonus camera (to go with the front-facing camera and dual rear cameras the Duo also has) fascinates me. And, based on the reported specs, concerns me.

Masked under layers of OLED pixels, the new camera has a much smaller spec list than the other three on the Duo. No megapixel count is listed. Apple promises 1080p video recording and FaceTime compatibility. It has Center Stage for auto-centering video calls, a feature I’ve found essential on iPads. It also has an f/1.8 aperture.

What it seems to lack are higher-res 4K recording features, an extra cinematic mode, slow-mo or time-lapse features, LED flash or portrait modes. It’s a more bare-bones camera, likely intended for use mainly for FaceTime and video chats.

Can you see the camera? Hint: it’s right above the left corner of the Find My widget. (Credit: Apple)Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Sure, if I were taking selfies on the Duo, I’d use the higher-end front-facing one (or the dual rear cameras flipped around to selfie orientation, something folding phones can do). Would that hidden camera step in well enough to be the FaceTime/Zoom/chat camera I need? If so, would that make it a great candidate for an under-the-screen camera on future MacBooks or iPads? Or…even an Apple Watch?

The compromise at play seems like a lot now, but it’s something the Duo can afford, since it has other cameras on other surfaces that can be invoked if needed. I’m glad Apple avoided camera notches or cut-outs on the inside, although I wonder how invisible the camera truly is when gaming or watching movies (or anything else).

It seems like an interesting experiment by Apple to slide its camera tech into smaller places. I want to try it. But I wonder if it’s ever going to replace cameras that are visible…and probably better.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large

Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. My background includes an MFA in theater which I apply to thinking about immersive experiences of the future.
