title: Already Appled Out? Here Are All the Tech Trends We Found at IFA 2026 in Berlin
snippet: Here are eight of the top trends I spotted while roaming the IFA floor.
fullText:
IFA Berlin has often been a place to see cutting-edge tech, cool concepts, and interesting prototypes (or should we say weird?). While there certainly have been some of those this year, like iRobot’s Roomba Duo, various humanoid demos, and a flying car concept, 2026 has felt more muted than last year. We’re still seeing the same demos of things like the Saros Rover and the Dreame Cyber X concept. Instead, what I’ve seen is companies really trying to drill down on perfecting the products and product lines that work for them. 

Here are the trends I saw at IFA Berlin 2026 that drew my attention and are worth watching for next year. 

Dust mites and allergies are the new target for robot vacuums 

The Eufy E35 Omni was at IFA, but they didn’t run it.Ajay Kumar/CNET

Robot vacuums have become good maintenance tools for cleaning up dust and pet hair, but if you’re someone with asthma or serious allergies, you likely still need a good HEPA-certified vacuum and air purifier to keep things manageable. Well, that’s the new target of companies like Anker with the Eufy Omni E35 and Ecovacs with the Deebot X12S Omnicyclone. Both are certified by different organizations to prove they work as claimed. The X12S was tested by the SGS Testing & Control Services Singapore and, in testing, removed an average of 97.44% of dust mite allergens and 95.45% of dust mites from carpet. The Omni E35 also claims the ability to remove a slightly higher 99% of dust mites and has Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America certification.

Realistically, the percentage difference isn’t particularly significant. What’s notable here is that companies are actively seeking out certifications that prove their robot vacuums are capable of robust levels of cleaning and sterilization, that it’s suitable for maternal health, newborns and allergy sufferers. This might sound niche, but as someone who has three asthmatic cats and occasionally seasonal allergies, I’m interested to see if it lives up to the testing claims.

This is something we’re likely to see more of as robot vacuums become established not just for cleaning but for sanitizing as well, with models that can deploy steam, UV light, and sprays. In the same way air purifiers became increasingly common over the past decade as an easy way to cleanse your air and reduce allergies, we may see certified, high-quality robot vacuums take on the same role. 

Deep cleaning is the new challenge to overcome 

If you’ve been following robot vacuums at all, one thing you’ve probably noticed is that they’ve gotten pretty good at vacuuming, but mopping can still be a challenge with older and dried-on stains. An old spill of tomato sauce, red wine or ketchup on tile is still going to require you to use elbow grease to remove it — I speak from experience. 

“One side is suction power, on the other side is mopping itself,” said Frank Wu, Roborock’s vice president for Europe, speaking with me at the company’s IFA booth. “At the end of the day, the target is to bring a better cleaning power to every corner of the home.”

Pretty much every company is trying to address this cleaning gap by using different mopping options, ranging from roller mops that self-clean with more downward pressure measured in newtons, as with iRobot and Eufy’s new lineup, which increases the pressure to 14N or 18N, depending on the model. That’s a simple and theoretically easy solution, just give the robot vacuum the elbow grease it’s missing, and iRobot has tried to do that for the vacuuming side of things too by adding a “skirt” that drops down on the Roomba 875 Combo that significantly increases suction strength on the already substantial 35,000 pascals.

 The key problem with this strategy, though, is that robot vacuums are size-constrained, and unless you try something like iRobot’s Duo, which incorporates a floor washing unit combined with a mobile docking station, you’re never going to get the power of a real wet and dry mop, let alone an upright or canister vacuum.

Another way companies at IFA have tried to address this is Ecovacs Deebot X12S Omnicyclone, which incorporates high-pressure water sprayers to saturate old stains and help work them out of hard surfaces. Clever idea, but questionable implementation with the X12S. As I watched, I completely missed its ketchup-stain target and instead doused the floor, but it still managed to remove the mess. The 875 Combo uses a hot steam spray from the bottom of the unit to help loosen the stain, but no demos were offered, so I can’t know how it works in practice until we lab test it.

The humanoid robots were a big yawn this year 

Ajay Kumar/CNET

I’m sorry to say that humanoid robot demos were just plain boring this year. Yeah, there are dancing robots and robots that can do backflips, like the PrimeBot T1 and Q1, and ones that can sort laundry or pick things like Dreame’s robot butler and SwitchBot’s Onero H1. Yawn. The real issue is that these things still don’t do anything more than what they did last year, and as I wrote in my cover story, the timeline for these robots is a lot further away than we’d hope and a lot more expensive. With a realistic timeline ranging from five to 10 years for partially functional home assistants that can do things like fold laundry and prices that will be closer to $100,000 than $10,000, I expect us to get many more years of IFA humanoid demos without actually getting a humanoid robot that you can buy and use in your home.

Part of why I’m not particularly impressed by any of these humanoid demonstrations is that robot vacuums have gotten so good. We’ve stopped talking about whether they can clean well or avoid objects easily. The newest models we’ve tested at CNET lab do an amazing job of it, and IFA demonstrations reinforced it for me as I watched Dreame’s X60 Ultra Complete Pro perfectly weave through obstacles with remarkable speed and responsiveness that I don’t typically associate with robot vacuums. The downside is that a Dreame representative confirmed to me that currently there are no confirmed plans for the model to come to the US, and with the added complication around the FCC ban and uncertainity around waivers, many of the more interesting new models may be delayed, though most companies have told me that they plan to move ahead with their launch plans.

This also affects humanoids, since a large share of the parts required for these advanced robots is sourced from Chinese supply chains. If the FCC ruling remains in effect without waivers, expect progress on US humanoids to freeze for the next decade as domestic supply chains are painstakingly built, while China races ahead with its already advanced models.  

Balcony solar is a great idea whose time has come 

For those who aren’t familiar with it, balcony solar is simply putting a plug-in solar panel on a balcony or other outdoor space and using it to store solar power and use it to power your appliances and devices when energy prices are high. It’s really intended for people who live in apartments or other homes where you might be a renter or don’t have the option of putting solar panels on the roof for a full system. Bluetti’s Balco 260 and Balco 500, Jackery’s Solar Vault 3 Series and EcoFlow’s Stream plug-in solar are all examples of this, which I saw at their booths, though it’s hard to really give impressions for a stationary battery that’s not in use.

Some of these weren’t necessarily IFA releases either and have been launched earlier in the year, such as the Solar Vault 3 Series. What I will say is that all of these systems are scalable, meaning you can add additional batteries based on your needs, connect more solar panels and use smart transfer switches or other power management.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

With New Jersey becoming the 10th US state to legalize the use of balcony solar power (something that’s already quite popular in Germany and the European market), I do expect to start seeing these being used in the US to help defray our ever-increasing energy costs. New Jersey’s law is particularly beneficial since it restricts the ability of property management or HOAs to stop you from using balcony solar, though you’re going to want to dig into the laws for your state before installing it. In most cases, it should work with a standard AC outlet, but if you want to feed power back to the grid, things get a little more complicated and may require an electrician’s installation. 

With nearly every major power station company releasing its own version, I expect adoption to start in the US, especially in New Jersey and New York, where people typically don’t have the option to install a solar panel on their roofs but face high energy costs. However, a Bluetti representative at the company’s IFA booth told me that they’ve currently paused their rollout due to uncertainty around — you guessed it — FCC regulations.  So while I do think adoption will happen regardless, since, by all indications, Jackery and EcoFlow are moving ahead, US supplies of home batteries and solar panels may be affected. 

Dyson had one of the strongest showings this year as a tech company 

At IFA 2026, we’re seeing all the upgraded, AI-powered, repairable, camera-equipped tech. And then some.Tara Brown/CNET

Dyson hasn’t really been just about vacuums for a long time, even though it still has that perception when I mention it to people like my parents. Dyson was off-site at IFA this year, but it still drew tons of attention because its releases entered brand-new product categories, including the famous $500 Dyson CameraJet, which integrates a water flosser into an AI-optimized electric toothbrush to clean interdental gaps. It’s Dyson’s first entry into the category, and unlike vacuums and air purifiers, it’s not necessarily a natural fit where there’s a lot of overlapping tech and development that can be carried over.

Dyson’s new HushJet air purifiers are a total redesign.Tara Brown/CNET

However, Dyson didn’t rest on its laurels, with a total of 11 new products, something smart home managing editor David Watsky noted as being a much faster pace than what the company has released in the past. This includes multiple robot vacuum models with cutting-edge capabilities across price points, redesigned HushJet air purifiers, and new beauty products such as its first dryer brush and next-gen hair straightener. With competitors like Roborock, iRobot, Dreame, Narwal, Mova, Shark and others all coming out with a vast array of products and models on a yearly basis, I can’t help but wonder if Dyson is feeling the pressure to keep up in the pace and frequency of its releases.

Definitely a space worth watching if you’re a Dyson fan. 

As usual, some of the best products at IFA can’t actually be purchased by Americans

Robot lawnmowers doing a synchronized fan dance isn’t something I knew I needed.Dillon Lopez/CNET

I’m talking about Dreame and Mova specifically here, though there are other examples like Anker and Ecovacs, with the latter having Tineco and Yeedi as sub-brands. Walking through their booths, I was struck by the sheer number of products they cover. You have the robot vacuums, cordless vacuums, wet and dry vacuums, robot lawn mowers, pool robots, window cleaning robots, air purifiers, smart pet tech like feeders and litter boxes, beauty tech like hair dryers and smart mirrors, humidifiers, fans and cooling, home battery backups, automotive, home security, home appliances, smart lighting, and other product categories I’m surely forgetting.

It’s an incredible, overwhelming number of products that make Dreame and Mova jacks-of-all-trades and almost overwhelming to cover. According to the hefty product brochure a Dreame representative handed me, the company had over 40 product releases for IFA, and I’d estimate a similar number for Mova. Many of these are products that won’t be sold in the US, which was the case for nearly the entire lineup of both companies, so that means we don’t cover them very much at CNET. 

Ajay Kumar/CNET

But walking into their booth at IFA always reminds me that there’s an entire universe of excellent, quality product options out there that American consumers don’t have access. It’s tragic, and with the current uncertainity about what you can actually sell in the American market and regulations and tariffs that can change overnight, I don’t expect that to change soon.

Every home will have a wet and dry vacuum to go along with their robot

You’d be forgiven for thinking Roborock, Dreame, Narwal, iRobot and others are primarily robot vacuum manufacturers. They certainly all have an extensive lineup of robot cleaners, but one of the biggest product lines we’ve seen grow is wet-and-dry cleaners. 

While Roborock didn’t share its sales with me directly, it said the Roborock F25 Ultra, which I tested and enjoyed using to keep my hardwood floors clean from my horribly messy cats, was one of its most successful new releases. I was able to see its Gen 2 model at the Roborock booth, as well as its integration into a unique five-in-one model (which may or may not come to the US) that combines a cordless vacuum and wet-and-dry vacuum into a base station unit.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

“We see a very, very typical scenario that some of the consumer they buy both a robotic vacuum cleaner and wet and dry,” said Wu. “The robots take care of the routine basis of cleaning, while when something urgent happens, something we just need to clean one certain spot, you can use wet and dry to take care of it.” 

This applies to traditional cordless vacuums as well, which are only capable of dry cleaning. Wu gave me an example for where a wet and dry model would excel. “If you are having some gravy or dirt on the floor, you just cooked, your baby just dropped some milk or whatever on the floor. That’s not some kind of scenario traditional vacuum could take care of, that’s the scenario for wet and dry.” 

Appliances are getting smart enough to run only during off-peak energy hours

One thing that kept coming up as we walked the showroom floor was energy efficiency. Appliance manufacturers have found a new way to cut electricity costs: large appliances that run when grid energy prices are lowest.

The technology itself isn’t new, but we’re starting to see it built consistently across product lines — not just reserved for premium brands such as LG and Samsung.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it pick the perfect cycle.David Watsky/CNET

For context, electricity prices fluctuate throughout the day, with “peak” hours typically falling from roughly 4 p.m. to 9 p.m., the late afternoon into evening. Many of the smart appliances we saw at IFA include settings that restrict cycles to off-peak hours only.

Miele’s Diamond G8 dishwasher was one example, letting you program the machine to run exclusively during off-peak hours — though you can still override the energy-saving mode if you need clean dishes right away. The G8 also has an AI-powered camera that identifies the dishes loaded in the rack, runs an optimized cycle, and reduces hot water waste.

China-based appliance brand Midea unveiled its AI Ecomaster system at its sprawling booth this year. The smart, coordinated home network similarly taps into local energy pricing data and triggers washing machine and dishwasher cycles when grid prices drop. For homes with solar power, the Ecomaster can draw from stored solar energy whenever grid prices spike.

Midea’s new voice-controlled air conditioner follows you around the room with a stream of cool.David Watsky/CNET

This technology is currently limited to dishwashers and washing machines, but because large appliances use so much energy, the savings can add up meaningfully over a year.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Watsky
						

						

							Managing Editor / Home and Kitchen						
					

											

								

											David lives in Brooklyn where he's spent more than a decade covering all things edible, including meal kit services, food subscriptions, kitchen tools and cooking tips. 
David earned his BA from Northeastern and has toiled in nearly every aspect of the food business, including as a line cook in Rhode Island where he once made a steak sandwich for Lamar Odom. 
Right now he's likely somewhere stress-testing a blender or tinkering with a toaster. Anything with sesame is his all-time favorite food this week.

title: Report: Apple Watch shipments rise 14% in Q2 as overall market drops
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report shows Apple, Garmin, and Huawei bucking a market-wide decline in smartwatch shipments in Q2 2026, with Huawei reaching a record share of global shipments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report shows Apple, Garmin, and Huawei bucking a market-wide decline in smartwatch shipments in Q2 2026, with Huawei reaching a record share of global shipments. Here are the details.

Apple records growth across all regions

In a new report published yesterday, Counterpoint Research says the smartwatch market saw a 4% year-over-year decline in global shipments in the second quarter of 2026.

According to the report, Apple saw the biggest jump, with shipments up 14% year over year and accounting for 20.1% of global smartwatch shipments. This kept Apple in second place, behind Huawei, which saw shipments grow 1% year over year and held a 21.8% share.

The ranking continues with Imoo, which held a 7.8% share despite a 3% year-over-year drop in shipments, followed by Xiaomi at 6.1% with a whopping 38% decline. Garmin held a 5.6% share after shipments grew 11%, while other brands collectively accounted for the remaining 38.5%, with shipments down 8% year over year.

Here’s Anshika Jain, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research, on Apple’s performance for the quarter, compared with its closest competitors:

“Huawei led the market shipments in Q2 2026, while Apple recorded the fastest YoY growth among the top five brands. Apple recorded growth across all regions, driven by the continued adoption of its refreshed late-2025 lineup. The Apple Watch Series 11 and Watch SE 3 together accounted for over 80% of Apple’s global shipments in Q2 2026. China was the primary driver of Huawei’s growth, accounting for approximately 80% of its global shipments.”

The report also noted that Apple recorded the fastest growth among the top five brands in China for the quarter, “signaling its recovery following the decline seen in the same quarter of 2025,” with the country’s consumer electronics subsidy program also helping boost smartwatch sales.

title: Pixel 11 lets you make any Camera Look default with this buried setting
snippet: The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too. more…
fullText:
The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too.

This tip-slash-correction comes via Google’s PR team, which reached out to me last night to let me know that, despite what I found during my hands-on time with Camera Looks, you actually aren’t limited to Google’s four “default” looks as, you know, your default. While Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla are all available under a “Default Look” dropdown menu, if you prefer some of the Pixel 11’s more unique styles — Velvet, Classic, Digi, etc. — those can be saved as your standard preset option.

If you’d rather have complete control over your default, grab your Pixel 11, tap the settings icon in the lower-left corner of the camera app, then tap the triple-dot overflow menu icon in the upper-right. Towards the bottom of the list, look for the Photo menu options, then toggle “Always use selected look” on.

Now, if you return to the Looks menu, selecting any of Google’s non-default options will still be saved as your preference when you leave the app. Whenever one of these more stylized options is selected as your main shooting mode, you’ll see its name briefly appear in the lower-right corner when opening the app, along with a purple Looks icon that sticks around indefinitely. Unlike with one of Google’s four standard processing modes, that permanent Looks icon drops you directly into this menu; you’ll have to hit Back from here to return to other settings like exposure and white balance.

	

It’s honestly great to see that Google does allow Pixel 11 users to save any of these shooting modes  as what’s available immediately upon launching the camera, though I won’t pretend it’s not a bit convoluted to split default preferences into two completely different experiences. But hey, it’s early days for Camera Looks — maybe the Pixel 12 will launch with a more refined UX that unifies this into one slightly-more organized package.

title: Disney+ loses Google Cast support in some countries
snippet: Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries. more…
fullText:
Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries.

Disney has been battling, and losing, in a patent battle with “InterDigital” in recent months. This previously caused the app to lose support for 4K HDR playback in Dolby Vision and 3D content in some regions, which has come and gone in the time since. 

The latest impact is around Google Cast functionality, which is actively being disabled in some regions. BroadcastNow and T3N reported on the dispute, which has led to an injunction against Disney+ in Germany and The Netherlands. While Disney can (and almost certainly will) appeal, the app is currently barred from supporting Cast in these regions.

title: Sony WH-1000XM4C launch for $299 alongside two more affordable headphones
snippet: As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship. more…
fullText:
As rumored, Sony is reviving its WH-1000XM4 headphones with a new WH-1000XM4C reboot, bringing some new colors to a much more affordable entry to the market compared to the company’s flagship.

Sony’s flagship headphones are very good, but they’re also pricey. The current WH-1000XM6 retails for $460, though you can often save when buying on deals. But, now, Sony has a more affordable entry in this lineup with the new WH-1000XM4C.

This is a reboot of Sony’s 2020 flagship, which was equipped with USB-C and all of the sound and ANC you’d expect from a high-end pair of over-ear headphones. 

What’s new? Not a whole lot. Sony says to expect the same overall ANC and audio performance, but with the “latest sound tuning.” The hardware is mostly identical, though with new colors including Lavender, Black, and Platinum Silver.

	

They’re available for $299, well below Sony’s current flagship and in line with competitors such as Nothing Headphone (1). It’s borderline impossible to get a brand new pair of WH-1000XM4 nowadays, and even on the used market, you’re still spending around $250 or so in some cases. You might be able to find WH-1000XM5 for less – Amazon has frequent sales – but it’s likely these will see discounts in time too.

Beyond this, Sony is also introducing WH-CH730N and WH-CH530N as even more affordable over-ear headphones. At $179 and $69, they won’t deliver quite the same sound or ANC, but the value is there for certain. 

All three pairs support Fast Pair on Android. WH-1000XM4C will be later this month, with current shipping estimates on pre-orders landing around September 30, while the other two are launching this month.

title: Report: Apple TV working on spin-off to its hit series Silo
snippet: Apple TV just wrapped up the third season of its hit sci-fi series Silo, with a fourth and final season already dated for summer next year. But it seems the streamer has more ambitious plans yet. According to reliable Apple TV reporter Sigmund Judge, Apple is working on a spin-off show that could go into pre-production later in the year. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just wrapped up the third season of its hit sci-fi series Silo, with a fourth and final season already dated for summer next year.

But it seems the streamer has more ambitious plans yet. According to reliable Apple TV reporter Sigmund Judge, Apple is working on a spin-off show that could go into pre-production later in the year.

Apparently, the spinoff will be based on an upcoming Hugh Howey novel, centered on the happenings in Silo 40.

While Apple has not confirmed the plans, and although Howey is publicly denying it, there is one little detail that makes this seem very plausible: the Silo sets have not yet been deconstructed. 

Typically, a show with no planned future (either ended or cancelled) will quickly tear down and sell off sets in order to make room for something else on the production lots. However, Judge reports that filming on Silo season four ended in March, almost six months ago, and yet the sets remain standing. 

This is very good evidence that Apple plans to re-use them in the future, probably for the spin-off reportedly currently in development. 

We have already seen Apple invest heavily in its science fiction franchises with spin-off series like Star City (from the world of For All Mankind) and an announced upcoming series set in the Monarch universe. 

And Silo has clearly been a big viewership hit for the streamer, so it makes sense to keep the content coming.

title: A foldable Mac is years away, but Apple is still working on it
snippet: There have long been reports and rumours about Apple working on a foldable clamshell device that is either an iPad, a Mac, one of each, or a hybrid of the two. A recent report said that although this was once a priority for new CEO John Ternus, the project had been cancelled – but I don’t think that’s entirely accurate … more…
fullText:
There have long been reports and rumours about Apple working on a foldable clamshell device that is either an iPad, a Mac, one of each, or a hybrid of the two.

A recent report said that although this was once a priority for new CEO John Ternus, the project had been cancelled – but I don’t think that’s entirely accurate …

Personally, I think the concept of a hybrid Mac and iPad has essentially been superseded by events. There are iPhone and iPad apps that will run on today’s Macs, and for many of us, iPhone mirroring is another tool we can use to achieve the same thing. We’re also seeing increasing convergence between the operating systems, and I’m sure that will continue: we’re now long past the point where Apple was arguing that we would be converging a toaster and a fridge.

But I do think we will eventually end up with an all-screen foldable Mac once the technology exists to make a soft keyboard a viable replacement for a hard one. That isn’t going to happen anytime soon, but it will happen.

The reason I think it is still a long way off is my belief that there will be an interim step in the form of dynamic hardware keyboards. It’s literally a decade since I talked about why I think these are the future, and while this type of tech is in use today for niche applications, they still haven’t yet hit the mainstream.

The Sonder Keyboard was one early attempt, using miniature e-ink displays to remap the labels and functions of the keys.

For example, a QWERTY keyboard is almost irrelevant to someone who spends all day video editing in Final Cut Pro, which is why there’s a market for both physical keyboards and overlays.

How much smarter would it be if our MacBook keyboard or desktop Magic keyboard could adapt its labels to match the app we are using at the time?

Soft keyboards that feel like hard ones

The longer term goal, however, is entirely soft keyboards. I said back in 2016 that the very same argument Steve Jobs laid out then for virtual keys on a smartphone when introducing the iPhone could be applied equally to a Mac keyboard.

What’s wrong with their user interfaces? They all have these keyboards that are there whether you need them or not. And they all have these control buttons that are fixed in plastic and are the same for every application. Well, every application wants a slightly different user interface, a slightly optimized set of buttons, just for it.

 There are, of course, three problems with a soft keyboard:

Glass keyboards are uncomfortable to type on

We rely on key movement for feedback as well as comfort

Touch typists need to be able to feel the keys before pressing them

Apple already has patents to address each of these. First, using a flexible display rather than conventional glass can allow for deformation when a virtual key is pressed. The second problem can be solved using a combination of this movement and haptic motors. Finally, there are two ways of addressing the issue of being able to feel physical keys beneath our fingers.

Apple’s patent was for an electrostatic charge that is perceived as a change in surface texture. In other words, charges can be applied to the surface of the display to make it feel like physical keys are present even though the surface remains flat. And in 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University came up with another approach.

The FIG researchers have succeeded in creating embedded electroosmotic pumps (EEOPs)—capable of moving liquids by applying electrical fields instead of using moving parts—that measure just 1.5 millimeters thick. They can be paired with an equally thin liquid reservoir beneath them, and a flexible surface structure on top, to almost instantaneously create pop-up buttons (the process takes about a second) measuring almost five millimeters in height with enough pressure and rigidity to make them feel solid when pressed.

It’s ‘when’ not ‘if’

Of course, all of this tech is still at a very early stage, but we have only to look at Mac trackpads for precedent. These still sound and feel like they are mechanical devices, but they have for years been solid-state devices that use haptics to simulate physical clicks – and they are incredibly convincing.

Soft keyboards will eventually reach that same level of sophistication. They will solve all three of the issues listed above, whether using the approaches Apple has postulated so far or new technologies that have yet to emerge.

When that happens, Steve’s arguments will apply equally to the Mac. In clamshell form, the keyboard will take whatever form makes sense for the task we are carrying out at the time. When all we need is a single giant display, be that for viewing movies or sketching using an Apple Pencil, then we will simply unfold it into a screen that is twice the size.

So I fully accept that the first generation product may have been put on the back burner for now, but that is absolutely not the same as saying it has been cancelled. This is technology whose time will come.

Those are my thoughts; what about yours? Please share in the comments.

title: iPhone 18 Pro appears to show new colors in a retail store, but likely fake
snippet: A video shared by a leaker with some track record appears to show two of the new iPhone 18 Pro colors as part of a display at a retail store. The brief video clip shows both the dark cherry and blue colors we’re expecting, but it is almost certainly fake … more…
fullText:
A video shared by a leaker with some track record appears to show two of the new iPhone 18 Pro colors as part of a display at a retail store.

The brief video clip shows both the dark cherry and blue colors we’re expecting, but it is almost certainly fake …

The video is just 14 seconds long and shows someone holding a dark cherry iPhone 18 Pro Max, placing a dark blue iPhone 17 Pro Max next to it for comparison. We also see a light blue model on a stand.

The environment appears to be a retail store. Macworld suggests it’s possible that it’s genuine.

Given how soon they will need to appear in stores, it’s plausible that outlets will have already received demo units, although it’s obviously risky for one to allow footage to leak online before the announcements.

I’m very much more sceptical, however.

My colleague Fernando Silva recently attended the IFA trade show, and said that every single case company had dummy units that looked and felt real, so it’s trivial to obtain these. Additionally, the store environment looks sketchy to me. The display table is extremely small for a store, and the product tags appear to simply be unattached and sitting at a random angle. We also see very little in the way of a convincing store background.

Finally, while the leaker has had a track record in the past, they have more recently simply been aggregating posts from Chinese social media.

title: Upgrade paths: Should Pixel 9 owners upgrade to Pixel 11? [Video]
snippet: We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here. Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video] more…
fullText:
We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]

Your 24-month cell plan might be coming to an end, so it’s timely to talk about this switch now, and we’ll do our best to help you decide which phone is right, which phone is wrong, and ultimately whether an upgrade is worthwhile.

An unchanged design

Let’s get the obvious out of the way at the start: the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are very, very similar. You could be forgiven for thinking they are the same. For anyone with a non-Pro phone, you’ll see more pronounced changes, but for all intents and purposes, the designs are almost identical across the entire device lineup.

Let’s get into the actual improvements. No matter what Pixel 9 phone you have, all Pixel 11 displays are better. Maybe not drastically so, but you get a jump up in maximum brightness of around 10% on the Pixel 9 to 11. The Pros get a 20% brightness jump at peak. This is something you probably would notice, but still not a major change. All the screens are well tuned, there’s no bezel reduction, just the same great experience, but brighter.

	

We know the design is the same, the core frame dimensions are identical, the same height, width, and thickness. The only visible change is in the camera bar shape and size. You can’t use your old cases on the new phone, so that is an annoyance. The Pixel 9 and 11 are within 1g, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are almost 10 grams heavier than the 9 Pro and Pro XL. 

That could be due to the marginal battery size increases and maybe even the addition of Pixelsnap magnets, but it’s likely some internal changes that add a little extra mass, and better thermals too. Pixelsnap is great for connectivity, but a good case can mimic it pretty closely on the Pixel 9.

Similar software experience

One of the key differences between the Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 is Gemini Intelligence. It’s emblazoned all over the latest phone and adds some functionality that likely won’t come to the older devices unless Google has a change of heart.

You need to figure out if you care enough about some of the AI tools like App Automation, Rambler, the enhanced Proactive Assistant responses and replies for messaging, plus some of the other enhancements that the Pixel 10 added last year.

Some of this is merely fluff. Some are great features. Do they drastically improve your life? That remains to be seen.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Where are the upgrades? [Video]

Even the move from Tensor G4 up to the G6 chip might not be a big enough leap for lots of people. Neither is an amazing performance beast, but they’re competent chips that handle most things you’ll throw at either phone.

Faster storage is arguably a bigger ingredient in the equation because apps will load faster, and you also get the benefit of a 256GB base model now. It was a long-overdue quality of life change that will make a bigger difference in the long term.

Frustratingly, getting less RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro or Pro XL versus the Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL feels like a slap in the face. It’s not necessarily noticeable right now, save that you can have more apps in memory. Some of the RAM is wired for AI task control, so you’ll lose out here unless you pay more to get 16GB RAM.

The fact is, though, that the performance gap is not exactly a chasm, and Android 17 is identical here. Unless Google specifies otherwise, you’ll get all the same updates in the future too.

Quality cameras continue to impress

If you want a telephoto lens and have the Pixel 9, then yes, you might want to upgrade. The digital zoom is not as good on the base 9. It’s capped and isn’t going to get close to the action.

The other lenses are fairly similar, but know that the main sensor is slightly larger on the Pixel 11. With the default settings, it’s a toss-up.

Camera Looks are where we get some notable improvements. These are sensor-level filters that you can customize to tune your Pixel 11 camera output. No Pixel 9 will get these tools. It’s arguably the biggest change on a Pixel camera since the addition of a triple camera setup.

If you have a Pro phone, there is a better telephoto lens that lets you zoom up to 120X. Video modes get some upgrades, AI-powered Magic Capture, plus a new Creator Mode is here too.

Like basically every other head-to-head comparison, the camera improvements are more about refinement than redefining, which makes a Pixel camera so reliable.

I don’t think someone would be disappointed at what has changed, maybe underwhelmed given the two-year leap. The reality is that a Pixel camera has mostly been about consistency, which hasn’t changed.

Is now the time to upgrade from the Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

You don’t need us to tell you that the generational “leaps” are becoming less and less pronounced, even if you skip a few new releases.

Whether brands are holding certain functions back or other factors are at play is a topic rife among practically any industry observer right now. AI is playing a big role in the physical hardware you will buy now and for years to come.

In our eyes, there is only one key reason you should consider making the switch from a Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11, and that is if your phone is on its last legs or if you have the base 9 and want a telephoto lens. Those are the only two major reasons someone should consider the jump.

The Pixel 9 Pro and Pro XL are still fine phones. There seems to be no major or widespread issues that might cause people to be desperate to upgrade or switch away. It wasn’t the best phone on the market at launch, but, like any Pixel before, these devices tend to age better than others thanks to updates and enhancements courtesy of Google’s now-extensive support window.

	

If you’re even considering ditching a Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL for the Pixel 11 lineup, think hard about what you’re actually getting. There isn’t anything on the software front that really warrants the substantial price increase. The new modem is good, but not a quantum leap. The camera improvements don’t provide exponential gains for photography or videography.

This is also true of most other pieces of tech right now. If your cell plan or contract is coming to an end imminently, maybe a cheap SIM plan could be a way to save cash at a time when smartphones are ballooning in price thanks to the constant march of AI development and the costs associated with the expansion.

The truth is that a two-generation upgrade cycle makes little sense today. You will simply get more bang for your buck by hanging on for another year. A battery replacement or repair would likely provide more value in most cases, given how little has truly changed over the past couple of years.

title: Gemini overlay gets bubble minimization and multitasking on Android
snippet: The Gemini overlay on Android now has a multitasking option that gives you a floating bubble shortcut when you Minimize. more…
fullText:
The Gemini overlay on Android now has a multitasking option that gives you a floating bubble shortcut when you Minimize.

The Gemini overlay now shows a “Minimize” button above the container. It’s centered immediately after you enter a prompt, while the pill-shaped container appears at the right after the response.

This collapses the overlay into a bubble with the spark logo. Google explains how: “Gemini is still available while you multitask. Tap to expand. Drag to move or dismiss.”

That said, the Gemini bubble is fixed to one of six positions and cannot be placed anywhere. Additionally, a bug appears to reset the bubble to the bottom-right corner after every minimization.

	

After the response has loaded, you can tap outside the sheet to get back the bubble. Using the system back gesture will close the entire overlay, while you can also drag to dismiss.

This shortcut is a bit faster than opening the Gemini app and then the side panel to return to a conversation. Another way to use it is asking a question and then minimizing to do something else instead of having to wait for the response. 

Alternatively, you could use Android 17’s system Bubble option with the Gemini app for a richer experience.

The Minimize button and Gemini bubble are widely rolling out on Android today.

title: Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is a MacBook Neo competitor starting at $699
snippet: Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe. more…
fullText:
Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe.

Announced at Lenovo Innovation World ahead of IFA, the Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is squarely aimed at Apple’s most affordable and incredibly popular MacBook Neo, and it puts up a good fight on paper. The laptop can be outfitted with either a 14-inch or 15-inch OLED display and measures in at 14.9mm thick and from 2.87lbs. Thicker and bigger than Apple’s laptop, but not all that much heavier, at least in its starting weight. Lenovo says the Vibe will be available in both plastic and metal variations.

Metal
Plastic

It sure looks the part, though, with Lenovo teaming up with Pantone to offer 7 different color options for the IdeaPad Vibe including:

Dreamy Violet: a muted violet shade layered with inviting depth that inspires serenity, bringing a sense of comfort wherever it goes.

Spicy Gold: A rich golden yellow that blends warmth and energy, creating a confident, welcoming feeling.

Zen Green: A nature inspired green hue that evokes a sense of balance, harmony, and encourages a slower pace.

Chill Blue: An icy blue with a crisp modern vibe that stimulates refreshing clarity and an effortless fresh start energy.

Radiant Coral: Warm and uplifting with an optimistic orange boost that brings friendliness and positivity wherever it goes.

Moody Blue: Expressing credibility and confidence, a deep blue hue conveying refined elegance.

Lowkey Grey: A timeless grey projecting strength, stability, and understated sophistication.

The keyboard also features interchangeable keycaps so you can customize the look with some fun color combinations.

	

These are all metal versions

Pretty colors only matter so much, though, and Lenovo has stacked this laptop with a pretty enticing setup. You get a pair of USB-A ports, an HDMI port, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and even a microSD card reader. There’s a 5MP webcam (with physical privacy cover), an optional keyboard backlight, and an optional touchscreen on the 15-inch size.

But what’s under the hood?

You can pick between an AMD Ryzen AI 400 chip or a Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip. The AMD model supports up to 32GB of RAM which can be upgraded by the end user. Configurations also include up to 1TB of storage, also upgradable and featuring dual slots. The Snapdragon version supports up to 24GB of RAM and, while the storage is still upgradable, the RAM is not. Lenovo says to also expect an Intel version in the future.

The Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is launching in two initial waves. AMD models will be available in October, with Snapdragon to follow in November. Both will start at $699.99, matching the price of the MacBook Neo since Apple’s RAM-induced price hike. 

Meanwhile, Lenovo is also introducing the IdeaCentre AIO I which is an all-in-one desktop computer with a 24-inch or 27-inch display, similar colors to the Vibe, and a price starting at $939. It will also be available starting in November.

fullText:
September Apple events are always a swirl of information and new, exciting products, and today’s was no different. Apple announced its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max; active noise cancellation (ANC) is now on the cheapest AirPods model, the AirPods 5; and a Siri Recap feature comes to the Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4. But missing were the AirPods Pro with cameras that have been rumored throughout the year and, according to Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, are delayed until 2027. I’m happy about that and I hope we never get them.

I have too many concerns about a company — any company — putting cameras anywhere, especially in devices like earbuds that are now so ubiquitous in our daily lives. LED lights on glasses or earbuds do little to ease people’s minds when someone is recording them. And some Meta smart glasses users have shown people will hide their recording intentions. While recording in public in the US is generally legal, it can be very creepy. And with earbuds as common as they are, someone could wear them into sensitive situations unnoticed.

Rumors say that the cameras on the potential AirPods will be low-resolution and “aren’t designed” to take images or video, but instead use what they see to inform Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. That information could be used to help with turn-by-turn directions or identify writing and objects like books. Even with a low-resolution camera, it’s still potentially always gathering information about the world (and people!) around you. That invasion of privacy is something I cannot get past.

During today’s event, Apple introduced Audio Intelligence with the Apple Watch, which sounds like a precursor to the Visual Intelligence we’re expecting on the rumored AirPods Pro 4. In its support documentation, Apple points out that audio is not stored and there’s no way to access a recording, which could be the same for video data with Visual Intelligence, and that for its Siri Recap feature, any data used to create a summary is not even accessible by Apple. Any stored data — such as a Siri Recap or a bit of text the user can save with Live Rewind — is also end-to-end encrypted. People are not identified in the Siri Recap, either. Of course, none of this is live yet, so we’ll have to wait and see how well Audio Intelligence works once it’s released.

Functionally, a camera will only gather information if it can see things. What if you have thick, long hair? Or like to wear hoodie sweatshirts? Or fancy, elaborate jewelry? The AirPods would just turn into what they should be — earbuds. It’s possible the reason the AirPods with cameras have been pushed into 2027 is to find solutions to these problems. Or maybe part of the delay is Apple separating itself from the current public climate around cameras thanks to Meta and Flock.

The one immediate benefit of the AirPods with cameras could be accessibility. They could improve situational awareness for people with visual limitations or help hard-of-hearing users read lips. They could even figure out the person you’re speaking to and focus the AirPods’ mics on them for increased intelligibility.

When you take out privacy concerns or the fact that lots of people — and companies — look for opportunities to exploit people, there’s good that can be done. But it involves a lot of trust to be put in untrustworthy hands. I’m not sure I’m ready for that. Or if I ever will be. Whether any of us are ready or not, though, it seems the cameras are coming. The introduction of Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watch is evidence enough that the company is going all in on using sensors to analyze the world around us.

title: Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo foldable and more announcements
snippet: Following the usual tradition, the Apple Store is down ahead of this morning’s September Apple event, kicking off at 10 AM Pacific Time. We are expecting Apple to announce the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12, and updated AirPods (fifth-generation). more…
fullText:
Following the usual tradition, the Apple Store is down ahead of this morning’s September Apple event, kicking off at 10 AM Pacific Time. 

We are expecting Apple to announce the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12, and updated AirPods (fifth-generation).

This is the first event led by new CEO John Ternus, who has a bunch of new products to announce including the debut of the folding iPhone Duo. 

The Duo will have a ~5.5-inch outer display when closed, and a ~7.8-inch display when opened up, a bit smaller than an iPad mini in size. The Duo’s big screen, when unfolded, enables immersive media experiences, and more productivity with split-screen multitasking of two apps at once. 

Apple is expected to differentiate itself from other foldables on the market by focusing on premium build quality, including a custom-designed hinge. The crease along the center of the inner screen is expected to be minimal. 

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will also be launched today, including new processors, improved camera system, and a new cherry red color option. The Dynamic Island on the new Pro models is shrinking in width, resulting in even less bezel. The starting price of the 18 Pro line is anticipated to rise by about $100.

The base model iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 will not make an appearance at this event. Apple is shifting the release schedule, so the entry-level iPhone will no longer launch in the fall. Instead, we expect it to arrive in the spring. Apple will presumably keep selling the base iPhone 17 until then.

Also today, we expect unveilings of the new Apple Watch lineup, Series 12 and Ultra 4, and new AirPods 5. The new Watches will reportedly include revamped health tracking functionality and a new AI feature that generates recaps of your daily whereabouts and conversations.

Other upcoming new Apple hardware includes a smart home display product, Apple TV and HomePod mini refreshes, and a MacBook Pro featuring an OLED touch screen. Most reports indicate these products will launch later in the year, likely as part of an October event.

9to5Mac is on the ground in Cupertino today, and we will have live coverage of all the iPhone announcements as they happen — so stay tuned for all the latest.

title: What Is Stuff? All About the Third-Party App Featured During Apple’s Latest Event
snippet: Siri AI got a few more details during the iPhone Event, including a tie-in with Stuff. Here’s what the third-party app can do for you.
fullText:
During the long-awaited annual September iPhone event on Wednesday, Apple spent some time detailing the latest upgrades to Siri AI. Among those was that it “already works seamlessly with over 300,000 apps,” and one of the apps mentioned was Stuff.

“You can let Siri see what you see, and combine it with up-to-date broad-world knowledge to answer your questions. Add the rest of the ingredients I’ll need to my grocery list, and Siri can take action in the apps you already use, including third-party apps like Stuff,” Apple said during the event where the foldable iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max were unveiled.

Stuff is a third-party app for iPhone, iPad and Mac that helps you organize your notes into to-do lists, tasks, deadlines and plans. There’s also a Listen Mode that works with Siri AI to create tasks from your voice commands.

“Stuff will recognize tasks and dates from your speech and present them as a list. You can review and edit the tasks before saving them,” the Stuff website says.

You can additionally scan handwritten notes into Stuff using your iPhone camera. The app has handwriting recognition and will create tasks for you, whether you’ve written them out in bullet points or paragraph form. It’ll also pick up on any notes you write with the words “today” and “next week” and create dated tasks with deadlines for you.

Stuff allows you to invite up to 25 people to your lists (five people if you have the free version of the app), so you can use it for things like planning grocery lists, birthday presents, events and vacations. Editing is in real-time, so you and anyone else you invite can make changes simultaneously.

The app is free, but if you want to invite more people or access Listen Mode and Scan Mode, it costs $3 per month or $30 per year.

In addition to Stuff, other third-party apps mentioned by Apple that are compatible with Siri AI include Audible, WhatsApp, Outlook, Notability and Tripsy. 

During the event on Wednesday, Apple also unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5, all of which have compatibility with Siri AI.

title: Apple Watch SE 3 is now unavailable ahead of launch event

fullText:
Tomorrow is Apple’s biggest product launch event of the year, with new Apple Watch models expected to debut. And now in an unusual move, the Apple Watch SE 3 is completely unavailable in all configurations on Apple’s website.

Apple’s website says ‘Currently Unavailable’ for all Apple Watch SE 3 models

Apple is expected to launch new iPhones, Apple Watch models, and likely AirPods and more at its September 9 event.

And now ahead of the event, one current Watch model—Apple Watch SE 3—has become unavailable for purchase on Apple’s website.

As spotted by MacRumors, you can configure any version of Apple Watch SE 3, then find at the end of the process that Apple’s site says the model is “Currently Unavailable.” That’s true for delivery options as well as local Apple Store pickup.

Apple doesn’t typically remove stock of a product ahead of its replacement.

But what makes this move especially odd is that there have been no rumors about an Apple Watch SE 4 coming tomorrow.

Instead, we’re expecting Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 to be the only new models.

Perhaps the current lack of availability is a system bug that will be resolved shortly. But for now, it seems to suggest that a next-generation Apple Watch SE might debut tomorrow.

We’ll keep you posted on any relevant updates to Apple Watch SE 3 availability.

fullText:
The prestigious television Emmy Awards began this weekend, with the winners announced for Creative Arts categories. The Primetime award ceremony is coming up on September 14th, which will include the big categories like Best Drama and Best Comedy.

So far, though, Apple will be very happy with the recognition it has gotten, with Apple TV leading the weekend with a record 20 wins. A lot of that success is attributable to the breakout comedy Widows Bay, which earned 8 wins, and is now looking likely to sweep up all the top prizes in the comedy categories.

So far, for the 2026 Emmys, Apple has 20 wins followed by HBO Max with 16 and Netflix with 13. The latter streamers’ totals will probably overtake Apple after all the Primetime Emmys are announced, but Apple will hold a respectable third place.

Apple is expected to dominate in comedy, but lose out to the likes of The Pitt in drama. We’ll find out next Monday.

As it stands right now, Widows Bay has earned eight wins, Pluribus got four, Margo’s Got Money Troubles won three, Palm Royale also got three, and documentary Mr Scorsese also earned one. 

That’s 19 across Apple TV titles; Apple also counts a win for the company’s “I’m Not Remarkable” commercial in its headline total of 20:

“Widow’s Bay”

Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy: Betty Gilpin

Outstanding Production Design for a Narrative Program (Half-Hour)

Apple TV went into the season with a record 89 Emmy nominations for itself, and we’ll see how many more wins it can convert during the Primetime Emmy’s ceremony on September 14. It is all just another indicator of how much industry critics like Apple’s programming overall.

title: Apple’s new CEO is reviving a Steve Jobs strategy from 25 years ago
snippet: John Ternus made the case in his first keynote as Apple CEO that the iPhone isn't going anywhere.
fullText:
Apple CEO John Ternus wants you to know that the iPhone isn’t going anywhere.

Ternus threw his weight behind the venerable device on Wednesday during his first keynote as CEO, placing it firmly at the center of Apple’s product strategy for the AI era. 

“There’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,” he said. 

This contrasts with the approach taken by former CEO Tim Cook, who tried time and again to convince Wall Street that Apple was more than just the iPhone.

Ternus’ pitch is also a rebuttal to pundits who have recently cast doubt on the iPhone. “The smartphone’s days are numbered,” said one headline. “The Tim Cook era is coming to a close with an existential challenge for Apple: figuring out what comes after the iPhone,” said another article.

But it’s not just about the hardware. Ternus has put the iPhone at the center of his “intelligent personal assistant” strategy, a vision that could define the company for years to come. Steve Jobs did something similar in 2001 with the Mac, less than 10 months before he announced the iPod.

At the time, many observers thought the PC’s days were numbered. At a Macworld New York keynote, Jobs called out bearish quotes from industry wonks like Walt Mossberg and the leaders of Compaq and Gateway. 

“This is what everyone else is telling us. That our PC is waning if not the hole being dug,” Jobs said at the time, pointing at a tombstone for the “Beloved PC” on the screen behind him. “We don’t think the PC is dying at all. We don’t think the PC is moving away from the center at all. We think it’s evolving, just like it has since it was invented.”

“We think the PC is on the threshold of entering its third great age,” Jobs added, a prediction driven by the proliferation of digital devices at the time, including camcorders, digital cameras, and DVD players. 

The Mac would form the center of a “digital hub” that would connect these disparate devices and, in Jobs’ words, “add value” to all of them.

Later that year, Jobs pulled the iPod out of his pocket, a device seemingly developed to answer the question, “Why do you still need a PC?” The device turned out to be an enormous hit, driving Apple’s profits quarter after quarter and ultimately helping lead to the development of the iPhone.

Today, with the iPhone on the cusp of its 20th anniversary, Ternus is facing a version of the same question Jobs took on in 2001. We don’t know if Ternus is quietly sitting on an iPod-like product, one that will secure the iPhone’s position as Apple’s hub for years to come. But he is firmly rebutting the idea that the iPhone is past its prime.

“If you were designing the ideal version of this hub from scratch, how would you do it?” Ternus asked before listing the ingredients: a powerful processor, high-resolution cameras, persistent networking, and on-device AI.

It helps that the iPhone is one of the most powerful personal computing devices around, giving it an edge in the compute-hungry AI era. Its portability and adaptability make it, for many people, the only computing device they need. Even among those who own laptops and iPads, the iPhone is often the one device they can’t live without. Plenty of people leave home without their laptops. Almost no one leaves without their phones.

That combination of power and portability has given Apple a privileged position in the AI world. Other companies have attempted to unseat the iPhone with all manner of wearable devices, but none have succeeded.

Instead of sidelining the iPhone in favor of the next flashy thing, Ternus is leaning into it instead. In a way, he’s bringing Apple around to what the rest of us already know: The iPhone is pretty great, and maybe we don’t need to replace it with something else. Yet.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

title: My Favorite Things From Apple’s iPhone 18 Event
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and the buzzy foldable iPhone Duo bring some great stuff. But there are some downsides, too.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable, automatically adjusts its display to its orientation.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

We may not want to pay $2,000 for it, or couldn’t spend that even if we wanted to, thanks to RAMaggedon-high prices, but there’s no doubt that the centerpiece of Apple’s primary iPhone launch this year was the foldable iPhone Duo. From a bread-and-butter perspective, though, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, despite a price increase, were the highlight of the “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday. Apple took the opportunity to raise the prices of much of the rest of the line, though.

Much of what we’re treated to during these launch events is a recap of the new capabilities of their operating systems, which have usually been available in beta since the developers conferences where they get announced. 

	

			

For Apple, that means demonstrations of its updated iOS 27 and WatchOS 27, announced at WWDC in June, running on the new hardware. But we’ve been using the OSes for a while and don’t have to rely on passing demos during the hardware announcement: Here’s our experience with the beta and what to know about iOS 27 before you start using it, as well as our take on the new Siri in WatchOS. 

On the upside, the memetic reaction to the Duo brought out the creative snarkers of social media.

Check out our complete coverage of Apple’s September 2026 iPhone launch and play-by-play commentary on the event in our archived live blog.

Preorders for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and Watches start soon, and they ship a week later. The Duo is up for preorder starting and ships at the end of October. And don’t forget the cases.

John Ternus’ event debut as CEO

After the initial cinematic opening promoting the new variable-aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, Tim Cook delivered a clever, well-done segue into Ternus’ first Apple launch as CEO.

	

			

Ternus came up through product design, and it showed during the event. If memory serves, we were provided with more specific hardware information about chips, device builds, cooling systems and so on than in a lot of earlier launches. That might not appeal to everyone, but it’s the type of thing that keeps me awake as we head into the second hour of these things.

There also seemed to be a lot more video shot across many locations around LA. This was likely to drive home the association between Apple and “pro” cameras, but it made a very nice change from a lot of static Apple Park and heartwarming family video.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Perks of the iPhone Duo

In addition to being its first foldable, the iPhone Duo brought a much longed-for feature back into the…fold.

Touch ID disappeared along with the iPhone’s Home button; the last holdout was the iPhone SE, which was discontinued in 2022. Even if you’re fine with Face ID, having a fallback method for logging in and approving purchases makes sense, and it’s certainly more convenient than having to enter a PIN code.

But it replaced Face ID rather than supplementing it. 

We had some in-chat mockery about the ability to register multiple fingerprints for the Touch ID, but as someone who occasionally has dirty, greasy or otherwise electronics-objectionable hands, being able to use a clean finger sounds nice to me.

I like the simultaneous front and rear camera feeds, which lets you use the outer screen flipped toward the subject. It reminds me of methods introduced to get pets’ attention in the early days of phones and before phones had cameras; I remember using an app that mimicked different cat vocalizations, though I really spent a lot of time wiggling my fingers above my head.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

I’m also a huge fan of the nano-texture screen layer, which comes from Apple’s desktop displays and MacBook Pros. With its excellent anti-reflective properties, it makes the most sense on a phone. I’d like to see it on more than just the Duo.

My biggest concern about the Duo was the size. The iPhone 16 Pro Max I currently have occasionally feels a hair too big to use comfortably single-handed. But the folded Duo is a bit narrower.

Variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

Apple made a big deal about its mechanical aperture for the new 48MP main cameras on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and it is a breakthrough for a phone. 

Electronic apertures used by most small cameras and phones simply limit or increase the amount of light the sensor absorbs. A mechanical, bladed aperture physically changes the shape of the hole, which controls the exposure, and that determines what bokeh and bright highlights look like, as well as how naturally the depth of field is rendered.

So, introducing a mechanical aperture should allow for more control over the quality of the look (as opposed to the quality of the image) of photos and videos. That’s notable.

But don’t expect a truly pro-lens look, though. It’s a six-bladed diaphragm, which isn’t even as good as some entry-level kit lenses, and eight blades is more or less the minimum for really nice-looking, soft bokeh. In its video showing off the camera, there was very little of it.

There are four aperture settings, f1.48-f4, which highlight the constraint of the small phone sensor and module. At f4 on a sensor that small, you’re essentially at infinite focus, whereas on a larger sensor, you might get up to f16 or f32. The bottom line is you don’t have a lot of depth-of-field variability to play with for that variable aperture.

I’m reserving judgment on the underscreen front camera for the moment, though.

The new iPhone Duo folding phone folds like a book or a passport.CNET

Burgundy Pro, night sky Duo

I’m a fan of deep, rich colors for phones, though I usually just cram them into a case and never see them again. At least based on the livestream, the burgundy looks like a nice change from the aggressive orange of the previous generation (though I do like it), and the navy-black night sky seems a lovely choice after my MacBook Pro-favorite space gray. 

A20 Pro 

In a switch-up from previous years, Apple launched its new laptop and desktop chip, the M6, ahead of the A20 Pro, which powers all three iPhones. Usually, the mobile processor comes first, and the computer chip inherits its major architectural changes from that. In this case, the A20 has the same 2nm process size as the M6, down from 3nm in previous generations. 

A smaller process size allows for a denser die, which ultimately lets you fit more circuitry in the same size package. 

In this case, it has the doubled Neural Engine of the M6, used for the on-device AI processing, from 16 to 32 cores. That’s likely an essential upgrade for decent performance with on-device Siri AI. 

There are also more cores, both GPU and CPU, plus a shift from performance cores to super cores, which run at higher clock speeds. 

It also has the packaging with the memory placement optimized for better heat dissipation because smaller process sizes and denser dies can generate a lot more heat than bigger ones. That, plus the switch to super cores, required it.

Apple also dealt with heat by adding a vapor chamber and a dissipation layer beneath the screen.

Efficiencies introduced by the chip theoretically improve battery life, according to the company.

iPhone Handoff

If you’ve got two iPhones, iPhone Handoff will let you share a single phone number, designating one eSIM as primary and the other as a companion. It sounds interesting, and would let you leave one phone at home or, with careful scheduling, let someone else pick up (for say an elderly relative or young child), but it’s one of those features that could suffer if it’s badly implemented. I’m not sure if it lets you save on the cost of a second line, since you still need to have an active SIM in the companion phone. I also wish it could work with a non-Apple phone.

It’s also kind of confusing, since Apple already has Handoff for sharing tasks across devices.

Watch Ultra 4 has improved sensors 

More sensitive, frequently polling sensors are an unambiguous win if you use them in a watch, as long as they don’t overwhelm the rest of the system (which I have no reason to think they do here). Better sensors in the Watch Ultra 4 mean more accurate readings and more easily recognized outliers.

Audio Intelligence sound recognition

The watches’ Audio Intelligence can, among other things, decode sounds into visual notifications for the hearing impaired. That’s a nice accessibility perk. 

An AI-driven feature that I could really use, though, is real-time accent compensation in AirPods; the AirPods 5 received some tweaks inherited from the higher-end model, including improved active noise canceling. Translation is nice, but I have a lot of trouble understanding people with heavy accents of all kinds — a big drawback when you live in New York City.

It’s not all sunshine, though. There are a lot of things I just say “nope” about.

Always-on AI

On one hand, I like the idea of a watch that can catch parts of conversations I routinely miss (Live Rewind), either because I’ve gone space cadet or because my hearing glitched, as it tends to do. But I’m also one of those Luddites who don’t like or use devices with always-on listening or recording.

I’m not a big fan of Apple’s “it only stays on our servers” Private Cloud Compute privacy narrative, which resurfaced Wednesday, especially since Apple Intelligence/Siri AI can also use hybrid (local plus cloud) and third-party-integration models. Even if it stays on your device, you still never know until after the fact what has obtained access to your data — and it may now include a lot of health data. 

It may also be because I don’t find a lot of the commonly trotted-out use cases very compelling. Apple Intelligence and the upcoming dedicated Siri app can do the things everybody’s on-device AI can, which seems to be writing email, summarizing calendars, travel scheduling, creating shopping lists, generating wallpaper and so on. 

To me, a lot of the AI used by the Watch Series 12/Ultra Health and related apps and on similar devices, such as Stuff, goes too far into the micromanaging-your-life zone. If it’s going to give a Readiness score of my ability to handle activities, I’m going back to bed and pulling the covers up over my head, because my body tells me it’s not ready for anything. 

The iPhone Duo’s drawbacks

While the Duo has the same 48-megapixel main camera as the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, it doesn’t have the same mechanical aperture or high-end features. This is actually a notable negative that I’d weight heavily when considering the phone.

The other thing I suspect will make things awkward is the screen aspect ratios. Folded, each side is just shy of 3:2 — it’s 1.45 instead of 1.5 — which has become nonstandard. 1.5 is the aspect ratio of full-frame camera sensors, which conceivably makes it nice for displaying them, but neither video or games use it. Opened, the large screen has a 1.4 aspect ratio, which is even more novel.

As a result, Apple has had to alter iOS 27’s screen layout settings, both to take advantage of the extra screen real estate (good), as well as to change where controls appear so you can use them comfortably (bad). Apple spins these as “optimizations.” But it means inconsistent user experiences and interface conventions between the Duo and the rest of the iPhone line.

Additionally, it means that the operating system will have to adapt a lot of existing non-Apple apps and content on the fly to run right on the device. That’s always a bumpy road.

While the Duo supports the Apple Pencil, it’s just plain odd. It works with the original, USB-C Pencil rather than the more recent Bluetooth version, which seems inconvenient for carrying around and using — it requires physical pairing with the device and plugged-in charging. Plus, it’s not really designed to be used with the phone, since there’s no way to dock it. It seems like the least-effort solution possible to a stylus.

snippet: The main event was the tech giant's highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.
fullText:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its latest iPhones and Apple Watches at its first fall event under newly appointed CEO John Ternus. The main event was the tech giant’s highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Apple also announced its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with new AirPods, and more.

We’ve compiled all of the announcements from today’s “Surprise and Shine” event.

iPhone Duo

Image Credits:Apple

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, features a 7.6-inch Retina display when unfolded, while its outer display measures 5.4 inches. The company said that the new device was “inspired by the versatility of iPad.” The inner display features an “underdisplay” camera that gives users an all-screen feel.

Apple says the iPhone Duo delivers up to 31 hours of video playback on its inner display and up to 44 hours on its outer display.

The phone features a 48-megapixel fusion main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera with 2x optical zoom. As with other foldable phones, users can take rear-camera selfies and look at previews on the outer display. 

The Duo’s hinge is made from Grade 5 aluminum and comprises more than 100 specially engineered components designed to ensure smooth opening and closing.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and is available in two colors. Preorders for Apple’s new foldable open October 16, with the device hitting stores on October 23.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max

Image Credits:Apple

The new iPhone 18 Pro lineup retains the same design as its predecessors, but its biggest upgrade comes in the form of enhanced cameras.

The new Pro series camera features a 48-megapixel sensor with a variable aperture controlled by six thin blades. This system is expected to improve low-light photography while also increasing shooting speed. The camera software also introduces new Pro controls, including white balance, shutter speed, aperture, and a histogram. In addition, new “Photographic Styles” offer greater customization with texture and grain controls.

The new camera can record 4K video in Dolby HDR Vision and apply cinematic effects after shooting the footage.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299, which is $100 more than last year’s models. Preorders will open Saturday, with both devices officially available on September 18.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4

Image Credits:Apple

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying, providing helpful alerts for people who are hard of hearing. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, but they are getting some significant software updates.

Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI-powered wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that can rewind moments and help users remember details from their everyday conversations.

The smartwatches are introducing a “Live Rewind” feature that shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, and a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499. Preorders open today, with availability in stores beginning September 18.

AirPods 5

Image Credits:Apple

The latest generation of Apple’s wireless earbuds, the AirPods 5 introduces several upgrades, including improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and expanded Siri and Apple Intelligence features.

Apple says AirPods 5 can reduce background noise by 50% more than the previous generation. They also feature volume control on the stem, which was previously only available on Apple’s more expensive AirPods Pro.

Transparency mode on AirPods 5 has also been improved to allow users to hear nearby voices and ambient sounds more naturally.

The AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of listening with active noise cancellation on a single charge. The charging case brings total listening time up to 22 hours.

AirPods 5 start at $129, while the version with a Wireless Charging Case costs $149. Preorders begin today, with the earbuds set to arrive on September 18.

Revamped Health app

Image Credits:Apple

Apple announced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data. 

The updates introduce a new Insights tab with a summary of the most timely health information, along with personalized guidance, assessments, a new “Readiness” score, and a calculation of your “Health Age.” The updates also introduce a new Longevity tab that uses metrics from your Apple Watch and iPhone to assess your overall health across factors such as sleep, movement, heart health, and more.

The revamped Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

title: Apple adds 37 hardware identifiers ahead of ‘Surprise and Shine’ event
snippet: Apple has added new hardware identifiers for iPhones, iPads, Macs, and other devices, some of which could be announced as soon as tomorrow at its “Surprise and Shine” event. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has added new hardware identifiers for iPhones, iPads, Macs, and other devices, some of which could be announced as soon as tomorrow at its “Surprise and Shine” event. Here are the details.

Apple’s back end adds new products

With less than 24 hours to go until Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, the company appears to be preparing its back end for upcoming devices.

As spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has added nearly 40 new hardware identifiers to its backend, including seven for iPhones.

A bunch of upcoming Apple device identifiers have been found on Apple’s backend. Interestingly, there are 7 iPhone models listed. We only know of 6.

iPhone19,1

iPhone19,2

iPhone19,3

iPhone19,4

iPhone19,5

iPhone19,6

iPhone19,7

Mac17,10

Mac17,11

Mac17,12

Mac17,13

Mac18,1

Mac18,2…

— Aaron (@aaronp613) September 8, 2026

Interestingly, the new iPhone hardware identifiers include one more identifier than the six models currently rumored to make up the full iPhone 18 lineup. Current rumors point to three iPhones being announced tomorrow (iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Ultra), with the rest of the lineup expected to be announced early next year (iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, iPhone 18e).

That said, it is possible that the extra hardware identifier could simply be a variant of one of the six other devices, rather than a new device altogether.

Back to the list, it also features nine Mac identifiers, eight for iPads, nine for Apple Watches, one for Apple TV, and three for products in Apple’s HomeAccessory category.

While most of the identifiers cannot yet be tied to specific devices, some align with products Apple is known to be developing and could announce as early as tomorrow.

That includes the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, a new Apple TV, the long-rumored smart home hub, M6-powered iMac and MacBook Pro models, and a new OLED iPad mini, among others.

9to5Mac will be at Apple Park tomorrow, so be sure to check out our coverage before, during, and after the “Surprise and Shine” event.

What’s your best guess for some of the new device identifiers? Let us know in the comments.
